student.title: Introduction
student.html:
Welcome to B1 Medical English

In 12 weeks you will learn to talk about the body, symptoms, health history, numbers and medicines in English, and to speak with patients and instructors with confidence. This book is yours: write in it, tick things off, and bring it to every lesson.

My details
Name
Level B1 Foundation
Teacher
Class days and time
Start date
My nursing goal

How the course works

  • 3 lessons a week, 60 minutes each. Lesson A: learn new words. Lesson B: practice and listen. Lesson C: perform and record.
  • You speak more than your teacher. Mistakes are normal. Your teacher corrects numbers, names and left/right at once, and other mistakes at the end.
  • Homework: 15–20 minutes a day. After Lesson A: learn words and listen. After Lesson B: speak and record. After Lesson C: send your weekly voice note.
  • Voice notes. Every week you send one 60–90 second voice note. In Weeks 6 and 12 you will hear how much you have improved.
  • Three checks. Lesson 1 (start), Lesson 18 (middle) and Lesson 36 (final).
  • Uzbek Bridge. You will practice moving between Uzbek and English, a real skill for nursing in the USA.

How to learn a new word: say it, write it, use it in a sentence about your life, then check its English definition in the Vocabulary Book.

Grammar help: look up any grammar point in the Doc (Part 1). Every unit ends with a short practice and the answers.

Word help: every word in your week tables has an English definition and an example in the Doc (B1 section). Read the definition, then say the example aloud.

Cards and texts. Each week ends with the cards, charts, labels and frames you use in class and for homework. All of them are fictional. When your teacher plays a patient, keep your book closed unless your teacher says to open it.

All patients, charts and medicine labels in this book are fictional. This course teaches English; clinical skills are taught in nursing school.

student.title: Healthcare Basics
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ give a 60-second introduction about my nursing goals
  • ☐ explain who works where in a hospital
  • ☐ check in for an appointment and ask someone to repeat

Words

Lesson Word Example
1 nursing school I plan to apply to nursing school next year.
1 registered nurse (RN) My goal is to become a registered nurse.
1 patient The patient is waiting.
1 healthcare I want to work in healthcare.
1 career Nursing is a good career.
1 goal My goal is to work in a hospital.
1 experience I don't have hospital experience yet.
1 degree A nursing degree takes two to four years.
2 physician A physician is a doctor.
2 nursing assistant A nursing assistant helps patients wash and eat.
2 pharmacist A pharmacist prepares medicines.
2 receptionist The receptionist checks patients in.
2 emergency department (ED) Urgent patients go to the ED.
2 unit She works on a hospital unit.
2 pharmacy The pharmacy is on the first floor.
2 shift I work the night shift.
3 appointment I have an appointment at ten thirty.
3 check in Please check in at the front desk.
3 insurance card Do you have your insurance card?
3 date of birth My date of birth is March 12, 1998.

Useful phrases

  • At the moment I'm studying… / I plan to… / I hope to…
  • A pharmacist is someone who… / The ED is a place where…
  • Could you repeat that, please? / Could you speak more slowly? / Could you spell that?
  • In the USA, dates are written month/day/year: 03/12/1998 = March 12, 1998.

Practice: checking in

Receptionist: Good morning. How can I help you?

Patient: Hi, I have an appointment at ten thirty with Dr. Lee.

Receptionist: Can I have your full name, please?

Patient: Dilnoza Karimova.

Receptionist: Could you spell your last name?

Patient: K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A.

Receptionist: And your date of birth?

Patient: March twelfth, nineteen ninety-eight.

Receptionist: Do you have your insurance card?

Patient: Sorry, could you repeat that more slowly, please?

Receptionist: Of course. Do you have your insurance card? … Thank you. Please take a seat in the waiting room.

Homework: after Lesson 1, learn the words and listen to your teacher's model introduction. After Lesson 2, record 3 role descriptions with who and where. After Lesson 3, send your voice note.

Voice note: introduce yourself, then explain how to check in at a clinic (60–90 seconds).

Cards and texts · Week 1

Question card (Lesson 1): Where are you from? Where do you live now? What are you studying at the moment? Why do you want to be a nurse? What is your goal?

Appointment cards (fictional, Lesson 3):

Card Patient Date of birth Appointment Twist
A Aziz Rakhimov 07/04/1990 Tuesday 9:15, Nurse Practitioner Brown None
B Malika Yusupova 11/30/2001 Thursday 2:40 p.m., Dr. Patel Forgot insurance card
C Jasur Toshev 01/13/1985 Monday 10:15, Dr. Lee Arrives at 10:50

Observer checklist (Lesson 3, groups):

  • ☐ Name spelled
  • ☐ Date of birth
  • ☐ Appointment time
  • ☐ One polite request

student.title: The Human Body
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ name and locate 16 body parts
  • ☐ explain what 8 organs do
  • ☐ describe exactly where pain is

Words

Lesson Word Example
4 abdomen The pain is in my abdomen.
4 chest Put your hand on your chest.
4 shoulder My left shoulder hurts.
4 elbow The elbow is between the shoulder and the wrist.
4 wrist She broke her wrist.
4 hip His hip is stiff.
4 knee Can you bend your knee?
4 ankle Her ankle is swollen.
5 brain The brain controls the body.
5 heart The heart pumps blood.
5 lungs The lungs take in oxygen.
5 liver The liver cleans the blood.
5 kidneys The kidneys filter the blood and make urine.
5 intestines The intestines absorb food and water.
5 bladder The bladder stores urine.
5 pancreas The pancreas produces insulin.
6 upper The pain is in my upper back.
6 lower I have lower back pain.
6 anterior (front) Anterior means the front of the body.
6 posterior (back) Posterior means the back of the body.

Useful phrases

  • The ___ is between the ___ and the ___. / It's above / below / next to the ___.
  • The ___ is responsible for ___. / The ___ helps to ___.
  • The pain is in the lower right part of my abdomen.
  • So the pain is in your lower back. Is that correct?

Homework: after Lesson 4, label a body diagram and say each word. After Lesson 5, record 4 organ sentences. After Lesson 6, send your voice note.

Voice note: name 8 body parts and 4 organs with their jobs, then describe one pain location.

Cards and texts · Week 2

Organ cards (Lesson 5): brain · heart · lungs · liver · kidneys · intestines · bladder · pancreas

Function cards (Lesson 5; cut them up and mix them): stores urine · pumps blood · produces insulin and helps digestion · filters the blood and makes urine · controls the body · absorb food and water · take in oxygen · cleans the blood and helps digestion

Mystery Patient question card (Lesson 6): Is it on the front or the back? Is it above or below the waist? Is it on the left, on the right, or on both sides? Is it in the head, the chest, the abdomen, the back, an arm or a leg? Is it near the shoulder, the hip or the knee? → So the pain is in your… Is that correct?

student.title: Symptoms and Pain
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ describe 8 common symptoms
  • ☐ ask about pain location, type and score
  • ☐ say when a symptom started and how long it has lasted

Words

Lesson Word Example
7 symptom What symptoms do you have?
7 fever I have a fever.
7 chills She has chills at night.
7 nausea I have nausea. / I feel nauseous.
7 vomiting He has vomited twice since this morning.
7 dizziness I feel dizzy when I stand up.
7 fatigue I have no energy. It's fatigue.
7 weakness I have weakness in my legs.
8 sharp It's a sharp pain.
8 dull It's a dull ache.
8 burning I have a burning pain after meals.
8 aching My back is aching.
8 throbbing I have a throbbing headache.
8 constant The pain is constant.
8 comes and goes The pain comes and goes.
8 pain scale On a pain scale from 0 to 10, it's a 6.
9 onset The onset was sudden.
9 duration What is the duration of the pain?
9 suddenly It started suddenly.
9 gradually It got worse gradually.

Useful phrases

  • I feel dizzy. / I have a fever.
  • Where does it hurt? What kind of pain is it? Is it constant, or does it come and go?
  • On a scale from 0 to 10, how bad is the pain?
  • It started three days ago. / I've had it for three days. / I've had it since Monday.

Practice: Uzbek Bridge. Say it in English: Uch kundan beri boshim og‘riyapti. · Ko‘nglim ayniyapti, lekin qusmadim. · Ikki kundan beri isitmam bor.

Homework: after Lesson 7, record 4 symptom sentences. After Lesson 8, write and record 5 pain questions. After Lesson 9, send your voice note.

Voice note: tell the story of a fictional symptom: what, where, type, score, when it started and how long you've had it.

Cards and texts · Week 3

Symptom cards (fictional, Lesson 7): 1 – fever and chills since last night. 2 – nausea, vomited twice. 3 – dizziness when standing up. 4 – fatigue and weakness in both legs.

Pain cards (fictional, Lesson 8): A – sharp, lower right abdomen, constant, 7/10. B – burning, upper abdomen after meals, comes and goes, 4/10. C – throbbing headache at the front of the head, 6/10, worse with bright light.

Pain question card (Lessons 8 and 16): Where is the pain? What kind of pain is it? Is it constant, or does it come and go? On a scale from 0 to 10, how bad is it?

student.title: Health History
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about long-term conditions
  • ☐ describe past surgeries and injuries with dates
  • ☐ take a basic health history in 5 parts

Words

Lesson Word Example
10 medical history Let's go over your medical history.
10 condition Do you have any medical conditions?
10 chronic Asthma is a chronic condition.
10 diabetes My mother has diabetes.
10 hypertension Hypertension means high blood pressure.
10 asthma He uses an inhaler for asthma.
10 infection She had a kidney infection last spring.
10 diagnosis There is no diagnosis yet.
11 surgery Have you ever had surgery?
11 operation The operation took two hours.
11 procedure It was a small procedure.
11 injury He had a knee injury.
11 fracture A fracture is a broken bone.
11 hospital stay She had a three-day hospital stay.
11 recovery Recovery took six weeks.
11 scar There is a small scar on my abdomen.
12 allergic to I'm allergic to penicillin.
12 reaction What reaction did you have?
12 rash I got a rash on my arms.
12 family history Do you have a family history of heart disease?

Useful phrases

  • Have you ever had…? / Have you ever been told you have…?
  • How long have you had it?
  • I had surgery in 2015. / I broke my wrist two years ago.
  • Are you allergic to anything? What happens when you take it?
  • Does anyone in your family have…? / It runs in the family.
  • The 5-part history: conditions → surgery → medicines → allergies → family.

Homework: after Lesson 10, make 8 everyday-to-medical word pairs. After Lesson 11, record a 60-second past-health history for card S2. After Lesson 12, send your voice note.

Voice note: give the full health-history summary of the patient you interviewed in Lesson 12 (card M2), from your notes.

Cards and texts · Week 4

Condition cards (fictional, Lesson 10): H1 – hypertension for 5 years; asthma as a child, none now; no diabetes. H2 – type 2 diabetes for 2 years; a kidney infection last spring.

Surgical cards (fictional, Lesson 11): S1 – appendix surgery in 2015, 3 days in the hospital; broke her left wrist in 2019, no surgery. S2 – C-section in 2020; knee injury playing football two years ago, recovery took 6 weeks.

5-part order card (Lesson 12): conditions → surgery → medicines → allergies → family.

student.title: Vital Signs and Measurements
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ hear, say and check numbers and units
  • ☐ read a vital-signs chart aloud
  • ☐ report a change between two readings

Words

Lesson Word Example
13 decimal point Thirty-seven point five.
13 degree Her temperature is 38 degrees.
13 kilogram (kg) He weighs 72 kilograms.
13 pound (lb) She weighs 160 pounds.
13 centimeter (cm) The cut is 2 centimeters long.
13 inch (in) He is 5 feet 4 inches tall.
13 percent (%) Oxygen saturation is 98 percent.
13 unit Always say the unit with the number.
14 vital signs Let me check your vital signs.
14 blood pressure (BP) Your blood pressure is 120 over 80.
14 pulse / heart rate (HR) His heart rate is 72.
14 respiratory rate (RR) Her respiratory rate is 16.
14 temperature (T) Your temperature is normal.
14 oxygen saturation (SpO2) SpO2 is 95 percent on room air.
14 beats per minute 72 beats per minute.
14 breaths per minute 16 breaths per minute.
15 reading The first reading was 118 over 76.
15 baseline His baseline heart rate is 74.
15 increase His heart rate has increased.
15 decrease Her oxygen saturation has decreased.

Useful phrases

  • Did you say thir-TEEN or THIR-ty?
  • Could you spell that, please? / Let me repeat that back.
  • The blood pressure was 138 over 86 at 9 a.m.
  • The temperature has gone up from 36.8 to 38.3. It's higher than this morning.

Practice: say these aloud. 13 · 30 · 15 · 50 · 98.6 °F · 37.5 °C · 120/80 · 72 kg · 160 lb · 98%

Homework: after Lesson 13, record the 10 numbers in the practice list, with units. After Lesson 14, record yourself reading charts V1 and V2. After Lesson 15, send your voice note.

Voice note: report how the vital signs changed from chart V1 to chart V2. Include every unit.

Cards and texts · Week 5

Mock charts (fictional, Lessons 14–15):

Chart Time BP HR RR T SpO2
V1 8 a.m. 118/76 74 16 36.8 °C 98%
V2 2 p.m. 142/90 96 22 38.3 °C 94%

Blank chart (Lesson 14):

Chart Time BP HR RR T SpO2

Report frame (Lesson 15): I'm reporting the vital signs for ___ in room ___. At ___ his / her temperature was ___. At ___ it was ___, so it has gone up / down. His / her heart rate has increased / decreased from ___ to ___. His / her oxygen saturation is ___ percent on room air. His / her blood pressure is ___ over ___.

student.title: Heart and Lungs · Midpoint
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about chest symptoms
  • ☐ ask about breathing and give breathing directions
  • ☐ do an interview, read a chart and give a 1-minute report on my own (midpoint check)

Words

Lesson Word Example
16 heartbeat I can feel my heartbeat.
16 circulation Exercise helps circulation.
16 artery Arteries carry blood from the heart.
16 vein Veins carry blood back to the heart.
16 chest pain Do you have chest pain now?
16 palpitations My heart is racing. I have palpitations.
16 swelling (edema) There is swelling in both ankles.
16 irregular Her heartbeat is irregular.
17 breath Take a deep breath.
17 breathe Breathe in slowly.
17 shortness of breath I get shortness of breath on the stairs.
17 cough I have had a cough for two days.
17 wheezing I hear wheezing when she breathes.
17 sputum (phlegm) Do you cough up any sputum?
17 inhale Inhale through your nose.
17 exhale Exhale slowly through your mouth.

Useful phrases

  • My heart is beating fast right now. Usually it beats slowly.
  • Does it happen when you walk or when you rest?
  • I have trouble breathing. / I get short of breath when I climb stairs.
  • Take a deep breath in… and breathe out slowly.
  • I'm going to get the nurse right away.

Midpoint check (Lesson 18): a 3-minute interview, reading a chart, and a 1-minute report. Your teacher will compare it with your Lesson 1 recording.

Homework: after Lesson 16, label a heart diagram. After Lesson 17, record 5 breathing sentences. After Lesson 18, send your voice note.

Voice note: record your midpoint report again, with your 2 improvements.

Cards and texts · Week 6

Chest cards (fictional, Lesson 16): C1 – tight chest when climbing stairs, goes away with rest, for 2 weeks. C2 – heart racing at night for 3 days; ankles swollen in the evening.

Midpoint report checklist (Lesson 18):

  • ☐ Name and age
  • ☐ Main symptoms
  • ☐ When they started
  • ☐ History and allergy
  • ☐ All 5 values with units and the time

student.title: Digestion, Urination and Nutrition
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about eating, drinking and swallowing
  • ☐ ask personal questions respectfully
  • ☐ combine a digestion and urinary interview

Words

Lesson Word Example
19 appetite I have a poor appetite this week.
19 diet My diet has a lot of bread.
19 nutrition Good nutrition helps recovery.
19 fluids Please drink plenty of fluids.
19 intake What is your daily fluid intake?
19 hydration Hydration is important in hot weather.
19 dehydration Diarrhea can cause dehydration.
19 swallow Food gets stuck when I swallow.
20 bowel movement When was your last bowel movement?
20 stool Was the stool hard or soft?
20 constipation I've had constipation for four days.
20 diarrhea He has had diarrhea since yesterday.
20 bloating I have bloating after meals.
20 cramps I have stomach cramps.
20 regular Are your bowel movements regular?
20 usual Is that usual for you?
21 urinate (pass urine) Does it burn when you urinate?
21 frequency Frequency means going very often.
21 urgency Urgency means you can't wait.
21 burning There is burning when I pass urine.

Useful phrases

  • I need to ask a few personal questions. These are routine questions we ask everyone. Is that OK?
  • How much water do you drink a day? How many meals do you eat?
  • When was your last bowel movement? Was it normal for you?
  • How often do you pass urine? Do you get up at night to go?

Homework: after Lesson 19, record a 60-second description of your own food and drink. After Lesson 20, record 5 respectful bowel questions. After Lesson 21, send your voice note.

Voice note: give your 30-second summary of the patient you interviewed in Lesson 21 (card U2), from your notes, then say 3 respectful questions you would ask any patient.

Cards and texts · Week 7

Intake cards (fictional, Lesson 19): F1 – 3 meals; poor appetite this week; 4 glasses of water and 3 cups of tea a day. F2 – 2 meals with a lot of bread; 1 bottle of soda a day; trouble swallowing pills.

Bowel cards (fictional, Lesson 20): B1 – last bowel movement 4 days ago (usually every day); hard stool; bloating; cramps 5/10. B2 – diarrhea 6 times since yesterday; cramps; drinking very little.

Urinary card (fictional, Lesson 21): U1 – burning when urinating for 2 days; goes every hour, 3 times a night; urgency; darker urine; drinks 2 glasses a day.

4-part order card (Lesson 21): food → fluids → bowels → urine.

student.title: Movement, Skin and Sensation
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ give polite movement directions and offer help
  • ☐ describe a wound without guessing what it is
  • ☐ ask about feeling, name, place and time

Words

Lesson Word Example
22 muscle My leg muscles are weak.
22 joint The knee is a joint.
22 mobility Her mobility is limited.
22 balance He has poor balance.
22 stiff My back is stiff in the morning.
22 cane She walks with a cane.
22 walker Please use your walker.
22 wheelchair Would you like a wheelchair?
23 wound The wound is on her left arm.
23 cut There is a 2 cm cut on his palm.
23 bruise There is a purple bruise on her leg.
23 redness I can see some redness.

Useful phrases

  • Could you lift your right arm for me? / Bend your knee, please.
  • May I help you stand up? / Let me get someone to help us.
  • There is a red area about 3 cm wide on the left forearm.
  • I can see some redness. I'll tell the nurse so she can check it.
  • Can you tell me your name? Do you know where you are? Can you tell me what day it is?

Homework: after Lesson 22, describe 3 mobility situations. After Lesson 23, record 4 wound descriptions. After Lesson 24, send your voice note.

Voice note: give the 1-minute factual summary of card N1, then 3 polite movement directions.

Cards and texts · Week 8

Direction verbs (Lesson 22): lift · bend · straighten · turn · squeeze · push

Wound cards (fictional, Lesson 23): W1 – cut on the right palm, 2 cm long, dressing dry and clean. W2 – purple bruise on the left shin, about 5 cm. W3 – red area around a scratch on the left forearm, 3 cm wide, warm, a small amount of yellow drainage.

Wound description frame (Lesson 23): There is a ___ on the ___ (where). It is about ___ cm (size). It is ___ (color). The dressing is ___ (dressing).

Sensation cards (fictional, Lesson 24): N1 – Rustam Nazarov, 70; tingling in both feet for a month; numbness in the left hand since this morning (new); alert; knows his name and where he is, not the day. N2 – Zarina Kamolova, 58; dizzy when standing; poor balance; uses a cane; alert and oriented.

Summary frame (Lesson 24): The patient reports… She / He is alert and…

student.title: Medicines
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ name medicine forms and routes
  • ☐ read a medicine label correctly
  • ☐ ask about medicines and check understanding with teach-back

Words

Lesson Word Example
25 tablet Take one tablet.
25 capsule Swallow the capsule with water.
25 liquid This medicine is a liquid.
25 injection The vaccine is an injection.
25 inhaler Use your inhaler when needed.
25 cream Apply the cream to the skin.
25 by mouth (oral, PO) This tablet is taken by mouth.
25 IV (intravenous) IV means into a vein.
26 dose What is the dose?
26 milligram (mg) Each tablet is 10 milligrams.
26 milliliter (mL) Take 10 milliliters.
26 once daily Take it once daily in the morning.
26 twice daily Apply it twice daily.
26 every 8 hours Take it every 8 hours.
26 as needed (PRN) Use it as needed for cough.
26 with food Take it with food.
27 side effect This medicine can make you sleepy. That's a side effect.
27 missed dose I had a missed dose yesterday.
27 refill You have two refills.
27 teach-back Let's do teach-back: tell me how you will take it.

Practice: read label L1 aloud (Cards and texts · Week 9).

Useful phrases

  • This medicine is taken by mouth. / You take it by mouth.
  • Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily with food. (amount → route → how often)
  • I want to make sure I explained this clearly. Can you tell me how you will take this medicine?
  • That's a good question for your pharmacist or doctor.

Homework: after Lesson 25, make 8 picture flashcards. After Lesson 26, record 2 labels with exact units. After Lesson 27, send your voice note.

Voice note: explain label L2 to a patient, then ask for teach-back.

Cards and texts · Week 9

Labels (fictional, Lessons 26–27):

Label Medicine Directions
L1 CALMEXA 10 mg tablets Take 1 tablet by mouth once daily in the morning. Qty 30. Refills: 2.
L2 RESPIRA-X syrup 5 mg/5 mL Take 10 mL by mouth every 8 hours as needed for cough. Do not take more than 3 doses in 24 hours.
L3 DERMOSOL cream 1% Apply a thin layer to the affected skin twice daily. For external use only.

Label map (Lesson 26): name → strength → amount → route → how often.

student.title: Tests and Procedures
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ explain a sample instruction card
  • ☐ explain an imaging test from a card
  • ☐ explain a handwashing sequence and give a polite reminder

Words

Lesson Word Example
28 blood test You have a blood test tomorrow.
28 urine sample Please give a urine sample.
28 specimen The specimen goes to the lab.
28 laboratory (lab) The lab is on the second floor.
28 result The doctor will explain the result.
28 fasting This is a fasting blood test.
28 collect Collect the first urine of the morning.
28 container Use the clean container.
29 X-ray You need a chest X-ray.
29 CT scan The CT scan takes 10 minutes.
29 MRI Remove all metal before the MRI.
29 ultrasound A gel is used for the ultrasound.
29 imaging Imaging is on the first floor.
29 contrast (dye) Some scans use contrast.
29 procedure The procedure doesn't hurt.
29 consent form Please sign the consent form.
30 hand hygiene Hand hygiene stops infections.
30 gloves Put on gloves before you start.
30 mask Please wear a mask in this room.
30 isolation This room is in isolation.

Useful phrases

  • You have to / need to come at 8 a.m. You don't have to fast for this test.
  • The instructions say only water.
  • You're going to have an MRI tomorrow. It will take about 30 minutes.
  • The radiology team will check that with you.
  • Excuse me, before you go in, could you please clean your hands and put on a mask?
  • Clean your hands before touching the patient and after removing your gloves.

Homework: after Lesson 28, record one test-card explanation. After Lesson 29, make 4 imaging flashcards. After Lesson 30, send your voice note.

Voice note: explain card T1 or card I1, then give the isolation reminder.

Cards and texts · Week 10

Test cards (fictional, Lesson 28): T1 – blood test, fasting: no food or drink except water for 8 hours before; come to the lab at 8 a.m.; bring your ID. T2 – urine sample: first urine of the morning; use the clean container; write your name and the time on the label; bring it to the lab within 1 hour.

Imaging cards (fictional, Lesson 29): I1 – MRI of the knee, Tuesday 3:00 p.m., Radiology, 1st floor; takes 30–45 minutes; remove all metal (jewelry, watch); the machine is loud, earplugs are given; tell staff if you have metal in your body. I2 – abdominal ultrasound, Friday 9:30 a.m.; no food for 6 hours before; a gel is put on the skin; it does not hurt.

4-part frame (Lesson 29): what → when → how long → how to prepare.

Handwashing steps (Lesson 30): wet your hands → soap → rub for at least 20 seconds → rinse → dry → turn off the tap with the towel.

student.title: Patient Communication and Teamwork

This week I can:

  • ☐ respond kindly to a worried patient
  • ☐ give a short SBAR report
  • ☐ confirm a handoff and write a 3-sentence note

Words

31 reassure I tried to reassure her.
32 handoff I'm giving the handoff to the night nurse.
32 report Let me give you a quick report.
32 situation S is for situation.
32 background B is for background.
32 assessment A is for assessment.
32 recommendation R is for recommendation.
32 update I'm calling with an update.
32 read-back Please do a read-back of the numbers.
33 confirm Let me confirm the room number.
33 reported The patient reported pain.
33 observed I observed swelling.
33 document Please document the time.

Useful phrases

  • I can see you're worried. / It sounds like… / Would you like…?
  • I'm calling about… in room… (S) → She was admitted… (B) → Her vital signs are… (A) → Could you come and see her, please? (R)
  • Let me confirm: room 5, headache since this morning, 6 out of 10.
  • "I feel dizzy" → The patient said she felt dizzy. / Patient reports dizziness.

Practice: SBAR. I'm calling about Mrs. Rahimova in room 8. She has had new shortness of breath since 3 p.m. She was admitted yesterday with a chest infection. Her respiratory rate is 26 and her oxygen saturation is 91 percent on room air. Could you come and see her, please?

Homework: after Lesson 31, record 3 caring responses to cards E1–E3. After Lesson 32, record one SBAR report from card SB2. After Lesson 33, send your voice note.

Voice note: give the SBAR report for card SB2, then read your 3-sentence note aloud.

Cards and texts · Week 11

Empathy cards (fictional, Lesson 31): E1 – worried about MRI results. E2 – does not want her son to hear her history. E3 – an older Uzbek speaker with very little English.

SBAR case cards (fictional, Lessons 32–33):

SB1 – Dilfuza Rahimova, 64, room 8 SB2 – Anvar Qodirov, 59, room 3
Situation New shortness of breath since 3 p.m. Shaky and sweaty; blood sugar 58 mg/dL at 11 a.m.
Background Admitted yesterday with a chest infection; history of asthma Type 2 diabetes; took insulin at 7 a.m.; ate very little breakfast
Assessment (supplied) RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air, HR 104, T 38.4 °C Alert; HR 102
Recommendation (supplied) Could you come and see her, please? Could you come and see him now, please?

SBAR frame (Lesson 32): S – I'm calling about ___ in room ___. She / He has had ___ since ___. B – She / He was admitted ___ with ___. She / He has a history of ___. A – Her / His ___ is ___ (values from the card only). R – Could you come and see her / him, please? Read-back: Can you repeat that back to me?

Note template (Lesson 33): 1. Patient reports ___ since ___. 2. ___ (what happened, with the time). 3. ___ (a value you observed, with the time); alert and oriented.

teacher.title: Introduction
teacher.html:
1. About this book

This is the teacher's book for B1 Medical English, the first of three ShifoLife levels (B1 → B2 → C1). It covers 12 weeks, 36 lessons of 60 minutes, three per week. A matching Student Edition holds the timetable, the word lists and every card and text students use, without answer keys or hidden cards.

Who it is for: Uzbek-speaking adults preparing to study nursing in English-speaking countries (primarily the USA). It works for one-to-one and small-group classes (2–6 students).

What it is not: clinical training. Every patient, chart and label in this book is fictional. Students learn the language of healthcare; clinical knowledge is taught in nursing school.

How to use it:

  1. Place each student with the placement check (section 3, run during the free trial class) before Lesson 1.
  2. Run every lesson on the SHIFO cycle (section 4). The timings are fixed; the content changes.
  3. Follow the weekly rhythm: Lesson A Learn, Lesson B Practice, Lesson C Perform.
  4. Score students at Lessons 1, 18 and 36 with the rubric (section 7).

Grammar companion: every grammar point in this book is explained in full in the Doc (Part 1, Units 1–18), with examples, common mistakes and practice.

Vocabulary companion: every new word in this book has an English definition, a word type and an example sentence in the Doc (B1 section, by week and lesson). Use it for Picture Reveal, Odd One Out and the weekly word review.

Copyright. © 2026 Shifo Life. All rights reserved. ShifoLife Medical English, the SHIFO Lesson Cycle and the Learn · Practice · Perform week are proprietary to Shifo Life. No part of this book may be copied, adapted or used to teach outside Shifo Life without written permission. Version 1.0 (draft for review).

2. The three-level system: B1, B2, C1

ShifoLife Medical English has three levels of 36 lessons each (108 hours in total). Each level takes a student from talking about healthcare (B1), to running patient conversations (B2), to working professionally in nursing school and on placement (C1).

B1: Foundation B2: Clinical C1: Professional
Entry level (general English) A2+ / low B1: can hold a simple everyday conversation B1 completed, or placement score 18–27 B2 completed, or placement score 28+
Core aim Name, describe and ask about the body, symptoms, history, numbers and medicines Run a structured patient interview, report changes, and give SBAR handoffs Follow lectures, present cases, handle difficult conversations, and write clinical and academic notes
By Week 12 the student can Give a 2-minute self-introduction; take a basic history; read vital signs and a medicine label accurately; ask an instructor for help Run a 5-minute focused interview; report numbers without errors; give a 1-minute SBAR; do discharge teach-back Present a full case in 3 minutes; take notes from a 10-minute lecture; manage a complaint or bad-news conversation; interpret Uzbek↔English in a clinic
Topics (12 weeks) Healthcare basics, body, symptoms, history, vital signs, heart and lungs, digestion, skin and movement, medicines, tests, teamwork, nursing school Advanced interviews, neuro, cardio, respiratory, diabetes, GI and renal, emergency, surgery, medication safety, mental health, documentation, simulation Lectures, textbooks, case presentations, chronic illness, patient education, consent and ethics, bad news, conflict, rounds, clinical writing, interpreting, OSCE-style final
Grammar band Present simple and continuous, past simple, present perfect, comparatives, modals (can, should, need to), will and going to; for recognition and short use: relative clauses (who, where), the passive, reported speech, the first conditional Present perfect continuous, passive voice, reported speech, conditionals 1–2, hedging (may, might, appears to) Advanced hedging, nominalization, cleft sentences, register shifts, academic linking
New words per week 16–20 24–27 24–30, plus academic word list
Student talk time 50% rising to 65% 60–70% 70–80%

These CEFR labels describe the target of each book. They are not an official certificate. For admission, students still need the English test each nursing school requires (usually TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic).

C1 at a glance (to be written after B1 and B2 are approved):

Week C1 topic Week C1 topic
1 Lectures and note-taking 7 Breaking difficult news
2 Reading nursing textbooks 8 Complaints and de-escalation
3 Case presentations 9 Rounds, care conferences, read-back
4 Chronic illness and complex histories 10 Care plans, incident reports, reflective writing
5 Patient education and health literacy 11 Medical interpreting, Uzbek ↔ English
6 Consent, ethics and patient rights 12 OSCE-style final simulation

3. Placement: which book does the student start?

The free trial class doubles as the placement check, so no extra test is needed. It takes 20 minutes inside the trial and gives a score out of 36. Record it in the student's placement record. All items and the scoring key are printed below the table.

Part Task Time Points
A. Warm-up Three warm-up questions: Tell me about your English. How often do you use English in healthcare? What are your goals? Score fluency, accuracy and range, 0–3 each. 4 min 9
B. Picture and match Name 4 symptom pictures (headache, cough, abdominal pain, fever). Match 4 everyday phrases to medical terms (items below). 1 point each. 4 min 8
C. Listening and numbers The teacher reads the script below twice. The student answers 3 questions, then writes 4 numbers the teacher dictates. 1 point each. 4 min 7
D. Interview and interpreting The student asks the placement patient (below) 4 questions (where, when, how bad, other symptoms), then interprets 2 Uzbek sentences into English. Score question forms, accuracy, detail and interpreting, 0–3 each. 8 min 12

Placement items (fictional):

  • B. Match: My belly hurts → abdominal pain · I feel like throwing up → nausea · The room is spinning → dizziness · I have no energy → fatigue.
  • C. Script (teacher reads twice): "I have had a fever and cough for two days. I took pain medicine this morning." Questions: What are the two symptoms? How long has the patient had them? What did the patient take this morning? Key: fever and cough; two days; pain medicine.
  • C. Numbers (teacher dictates): thirteen · thirty · one-twenty over eighty · thirty-seven point five. Key: 13 · 30 · 120/80 · 37.5.
  • D. Placement patient (teacher answers only what is asked): pain in the lower back since yesterday morning; 6 out of 10; worse when sitting; no other symptoms.
  • D. Uzbek sentences (teacher reads; the student says them in English): Kechadan beri qornim og‘riyapti. → I have had stomach pain since yesterday. · Ikki kundan beri isitmam bor, boshim ham aylanyapti. → I have had a fever for two days, and I also feel dizzy.

Scoring key. Parts B and C: 1 point per correct item (B = 8, C = 7). Parts A and D: score each skill 0–3 with this table. Total = 36.

Skill 0 1 2 3
A. Fluency, accuracy, range (each) No answer or single words Short phrases; many pauses or errors Full sentences; some errors Fluent, accurate and varied
D. Question forms No correct question 1–2 correct questions 3 correct questions All 4 correct
D. Accuracy Hard to understand Many errors Some errors; meaning clear Almost no errors
D. Detail No details found 1–2 details found 3 details found All 4 details found and repeated back
D. Interpreting Not attempted One sentence, partly right Both sentences; one detail missing Both complete and accurate
Score Place in Note to student
0–8 General English first Join B1 once everyday conversation is comfortable.
9–17 B1 Foundation Start at Lesson 1.
18–27 B2 Clinical Start B2 Lesson 1, or B1 Week 5 if numbers or history are weak.
28–36 C1 Professional Start C1 Lesson 1.

Mixed groups. Keep a group within one band. If a group must mix, every B1 lesson has a Stretch line for stronger students (see each lesson card). Never mix students more than one band apart.

4. The SHIFO Lesson Cycle and the Learn · Practice · Perform week

Every lesson runs through the same five stages, so students always know what comes next. What changes is the weight of each stage, set by the lesson's place in the week.

Stage What happens Teacher rule
S — Start English-only check-in; student recalls 3 recycled words from earlier lessons without notes. Ask, don't teach.
H — Hear and learn New words: picture → say → use in a sentence. Everyday-to-clinical bridge (belly → abdomen). Drill 2 hard sounds. Max 8 new words.
I — Interact Teacher models a short dialogue; student practices the pattern; a listening task on B lessons. Grammar explanation max 4 minutes.
F — Field practice Role-play in three rounds: with prompts, fewer prompts, one new detail. Roles swap. The week's Spark activity usually lives here. Student talks more than the teacher.
O — Own it Feedback on max 2 errors, then a retry; exit check (2 words + 1 pattern, no notes); homework set. End on success, not on correction.

The week has a shape. Lesson A teaches, Lesson B practices with listening, Lesson C performs a recorded task with only 4 new words. Students meet new language on Monday and use it confidently by Friday.

Lesson type New words S H I F O
A — Learn 8 0–6 6–24 24–32 32–50 50–60
B — Practice 8 0–6 6–16 16–30 30–50 50–60
C — Perform 0–4 (recycle) 0–5 5–12 12–20 20–50 50–60

All times are minutes from the start of the lesson.

Correct immediately only when a mistake changes meaning: a name, number, unit, left/right, time, or a missing not. Save every other correction for stage O.

5. Intensive without overload: the rules and the Spark bank

Intensity comes from how much the student speaks, not from how much the teacher covers. These limits keep every lesson full but light enough to remember.

Load limits (never break these):

  • Max 8 new words in Lessons A and B and 4 in Lesson C: 20 a week (16 in Weeks 6 and 12, when Lesson C is the assessment).
  • Max one grammar point per lesson, explained in 4 minutes or less.
  • 3 recycled words in every Start stage, from earlier lessons; at least one from an earlier week (Week 1: from the lessons before).
  • At least 4 activity changes per lesson; no single activity runs longer than 20 minutes.
  • Homework: 15–20 minutes a day, 5 days a week. After Lesson A: words and listening. After Lesson B: speak and record. After Lesson C: the weekly voice note and review.
  • Weeks 6 and 12 are lighter: the C lesson is the assessment.

Against boredom:

  • Rotate the student's role every week: nursing student, patient, receptionist, colleague, interpreter, student asking an instructor. In every nurse role the student speaks as a nursing student: they report to the nurse in charge and refer; they never diagnose.
  • One Spark per lesson, never the same Spark twice in a row. Odd One Out is a Start warm-up, not the lesson's Spark.
  • Personal hooks: the student's own goal, city and family appear in examples (fictional health details only).
  • Visible progress: each Lesson C ends with a voice note. The student hears Week 1 against Week 6 and Week 12.

The Spark bank (short game-like activities for stage F):

Spark How it works Time Best in
Picture Reveal Show a picture. What do you see? Describe it in a full sentence. Then reveal the word. 5 min A
Match and Speak Match everyday phrases to medical terms, then say: The patient reports … When did it start? 6 min A, B
Uzbek Bridge Teacher reads a patient line in Uzbek; student says it in English in the first person, then reverses. 8 min B, C
Number Catch Teacher reads values (13/30, 15/50, 37.5, 120/80); student writes them and reads them back. 5 min B
Listen and Answer Teacher reads a short patient report; student answers 3 questions. 5 min B
Error Hunt Teacher gives a report with 3 planted errors (side, number, time); student finds and fixes them. 6 min B, C
Mystery Patient Teacher holds a hidden card; student has 10 questions to find the complaint, start and severity. 8 min C
60-Second Report Student speaks for 60 seconds from a card; teacher ticks each target word used. 4 min C
Odd One Out Four words, one does not belong; the student explains why in a full sentence. 3 min Start warm-up (any lesson)

Uzbek Bridge is the ShifoLife signature. It builds interpreting skill, and it uses the student's first language as a strength.

6. B1 timetable: 36 lessons at a glance

Three lessons a week on fixed days, with at least one day between lessons (for example Mon / Wed / Fri or Tue / Thu / Sat). Never move Lesson C before Lesson B: the week only works in order.

# Wk Type Lesson Goal: the student can… Grammar (B1) Spark
1 1 A Introductions and nursing goals give a 60-second introduction about their nursing goals Present simple vs continuous; want / plan / hope to Picture Reveal
2 1 B Healthcare roles and workplaces explain who works where in a hospital Relative clauses who / where Listen and Answer
3 1 C Appointments and asking for help check in for an appointment and ask for repetition Polite requests could / would; at / on / in for time Number Catch
4 2 A Body parts name and locate 16 body parts There is / are; prepositions of place Picture Reveal
5 2 B Organs and what they do explain what 8 organs do Present simple for facts; helps to, is responsible for Match and Speak
6 2 C Where exactly? Location words describe exactly where pain is Compound nouns (lower back pain) Mystery Patient
7 3 A Common symptoms describe 8 common symptoms feel + adjective, have + noun Picture Reveal
8 3 B Describing pain ask about pain location, type and score How + adjective questions Listen and Answer
9 3 C When did it start? ask and say when a symptom started and how long it has lasted Present perfect with for / since vs past simple Uzbek Bridge
10 4 A Common medical conditions ask about long-term conditions Have you ever…? Match and Speak
11 4 B Surgeries and past health events describe past surgeries and injuries with dates Past simple vs present perfect; ago Error Hunt
12 4 C Allergies, medicines, family history take a basic health history be allergic to; runs in the family Mystery Patient
13 5 A Numbers, units and spelling hear, say and confirm numbers and units Clarifying: Did you say…? Number Catch
14 5 B Vital signs read a vital-signs chart aloud Saying values (120 over 80) Listen and Answer
15 5 C Reporting measurements report a change in measurements Comparatives; has gone up from… to… Error Hunt
16 6 A Heart and circulation ask about chest symptoms Present continuous vs simple Picture Reveal
17 6 B Breathing ask about breathing symptoms and give breathing directions have trouble + -ing; when clauses Uzbek Bridge
18 6 C Midpoint check complete an interview, a chart reading and a 1-minute report Review Assessment
19 7 A Food, fluids and swallowing ask about eating and drinking How much / how many; quantifiers Picture Reveal
20 7 B Bowel habits ask bowel questions respectfully Past questions; softeners Match and Speak
21 7 C Urinary symptoms combine a digestion and urinary interview Frequency: How often…? Mystery Patient
22 8 A Movement and mobility give movement directions and offer help can; Could you… for me?; May I…? Picture Reveal
23 8 B Skin and wounds describe a wound neutrally Size and shape (about 2 cm long) Error Hunt
24 8 C Sensation and orientation ask about sensation and orientation Indirect questions: Can you tell me…? 60-Second Report
25 9 A Medicine forms and routes name medicine forms and routes Passive: is taken by mouth Match and Speak
26 9 B Dose, timing and labels read a medicine label accurately Frequency: twice daily, every 8 hours Number Catch
27 9 C Medicine questions and teach-back ask about medicines and check understanding will; sequencing first, then Uzbek Bridge
28 10 A Lab tests and samples explain a sample instruction card have to / don't have to Picture Reveal
29 10 B Imaging and procedures explain an imaging test from a card will vs going to Listen and Answer
30 10 C Infection prevention explain a handwashing sequence and give a polite reminder before / after + -ing 60-Second Report
31 11 A Empathy, privacy, interpreters respond to a worried patient Would you like…?; I can see… Match and Speak
32 11 B SBAR reports give a short SBAR report I'm calling about… Error Hunt
33 11 C Clarifying and writing a note confirm a handoff and write a 3-sentence note Reported speech: The patient said that… Uzbek Bridge
34 12 A Classroom and assignments ask an instructor about an assignment Indirect questions: Could you tell me when…? Match and Speak
35 12 B Skills lab and simulation follow and question skills-lab instructions First conditional Listen and Answer
36 12 C Final assessment complete five speaking tasks Review Assessment

7. Assessment: Lessons 1, 18 and 36

The student is scored three times on the same four skills, so progress is easy to see. A student moves to B2 with 9 or more out of 12 at Lesson 36 and no skill below 2.

Skill 0 1 2 3
Vocabulary use Not yet shown Uses target words only with prompts Uses most target words correctly Uses target words naturally, without notes
Clear speech Hard to understand Understood with effort Mostly clear; some sounds unclear Clear throughout; stresses key words
Listening and clarifying Misses the main point Gets the main point; does not check Gets details; sometimes checks Gets details and always checks (Did you say…?)
Accurate details Numbers, times or sides wrong Several errors One error, corrected when asked All names, numbers, units and times right
When Tasks Recording kept
Lesson 1 (baseline) 60-second introduction; 3 warm-up questions Introduction voice note
Lesson 18 (midpoint) 3-minute interview with an unfamiliar patient card; read a vital-signs chart; 1-minute report Report voice note
Lesson 36 (final) Five tasks: introduction; patient interview; measurement report; label explanation with teach-back; instructor-help request All five, compared with Lessons 1 and 18

Every lesson: note 5 target words and 1 speaking goal on the student's card. Every Lesson C: the student sends one voice note (60–90 seconds).

Completion. Students who attend at least 32 of 36 lessons and reach the score above receive the ShifoLife B1 Medical English certificate of completion. It is a course certificate, not a CEFR or clinical qualification.

teacher.title: Healthcare Basics
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can introduce themselves and their nursing goal, say who works where in a hospital, and check in for an appointment.

Student roles this week: future nursing student; patient at reception; receptionist.

Prepare: 8 healthcare-role pictures; a phone to record voice notes. The question card, appointment cards A–C and the observer checklist are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 1).

Lesson 1 · A Learn · Introductions and nursing goals
Goal Give a 60-second introduction about my nursing goals.
New words (8) nursing school, registered nurse (RN), patient, healthcare, career, goal, experience, degree
Recycle None (first lesson). Use the warm-up questions instead.
Grammar Present simple for facts (I live in Ohio) vs continuous for now (I'm studying English); want / plan / hope to + verb
Spark Picture Reveal (healthcare people)
Assessment Baseline. Record the introduction and score it with the section 7 rubric.
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Warm-up questions: Tell me about your experience with English. How often do you use English in healthcare? What is your goal? Listen; do not correct.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words with pictures; the student makes a sentence for each. Sounds: nurse (one smooth vowel, no rolled r); career (ca-REER, not KO-rea). Bridge: doctor's office → clinic; nurse → registered nurse, RN.
24–32 I Read the model introduction twice. The student names 3 facts. Grammar in 4 minutes: always true vs happening now; I want / plan / hope to become…
32–50 F Round 1: the student interviews the teacher with the question card. Round 2: swap roles. Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal with 4 healthcare people. Round 3: the student introduces themselves to a nursing-school instructor (the teacher) in 60 seconds. Record it (baseline).
50–60 O Two priority errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 new words + 1 plan to / hope to sentence, without notes. Set homework.

Model introduction (teacher reads): Hello, my name is Dilnoza. I'm from Samarkand, and I live in Ohio now. At the moment I'm studying English, because I plan to apply to nursing school next year. I don't have experience in healthcare yet, but I often help my grandmother with her clinic visits. My goal is a career as a registered nurse. I hope to work in a big hospital one day.

Question card: Where are you from? Where do you live now? What are you studying at the moment? Why do you want to be a nurse? What is your goal?

Stretch (stronger students): add a reason with because and a time plan (next year, in two years). Support: give starters: At the moment I'm… / My goal is…

Groups: pairs interview each other in Rounds 1–2; each student gives Round 3 to the whole group.

Homework: learn the 8 words (say each in a sentence); listen to the teacher's model voice note twice and write 3 facts.

Lesson 2 · B Practice · Healthcare roles and workplaces
Goal Explain who works where in a hospital.
New words (8) physician, nursing assistant, pharmacist, receptionist, emergency department (ED), unit, pharmacy, shift
Recycle patient, registered nurse, goal
Grammar Relative clauses: A pharmacist is someone who prepares medicines. The ED is a place where urgent patients go.
Spark Listen and Answer (Who am I?)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student repeats their introduction from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words with role cards. Sounds: ph = f (pharmacist, physician: fi-ZI-shun).
16–30 I Grammar in 4 minutes: who for people, where for places. Spark: Listen and Answer, 2 texts (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the teacher plays three roles; the student asks What do you do? Where do you work? and names each role. Round 2: the student plays roles; the teacher guesses. Round 3 (new detail): a lost patient asks for help; the student directs them: For your medicine, please ask the pharmacist, who works in the pharmacy on the first floor.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 roles in who / where sentences, without notes. Set homework.

Listen and Answer, text 1: I work on a hospital unit, usually on the night shift. I help patients wash, eat and walk. I check their temperature and tell the nurse if something changes. Questions: Who am I? Where do I work? Who do I tell about changes? Key: nursing assistant; hospital unit; the nurse.

Text 2: I sit at the front desk of the clinic. I check patients in, ask for their insurance card and make appointments. Questions: Who am I? Where do I work? What do I do? Key: receptionist; at the front desk of a clinic; checks patients in, asks for insurance cards and makes appointments.

Stretch: explain the difference between a registered nurse and a nursing assistant. Support: fill-in frame A ___ is someone who ___.

Groups: Round 2 as a team guessing game; one point per correct role.

Homework: record 3 role descriptions using who and where (60 seconds in total).

Lesson 3 · C Perform · Appointments and asking for help
Goal Check in for an appointment and ask for repetition.
New words (4) appointment, check in, insurance card, date of birth
Recycle receptionist, physician, shift
Grammar Polite requests: Could you repeat that? Could you spell your last name? Time: at 10:30, on Tuesday, in March
Spark Number Catch (dates and times)
Perform task Recorded check-in, played as patient and as receptionist
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Odd One Out: pharmacist, physician, pharmacy, receptionist (pharmacy is a place). Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Spelling drill for letters Uzbek speakers often mix up: A/E/I, G/J, B/V.
12–20 I Model the dialogue below. Spark: Number Catch. Teach US date order: month/day/year.
20–50 F Round 1: the student checks in using Card A, dialogue in view. Round 2: dialogue hidden, Card B. Round 3 (problem): Card C; the patient is late and asks what to do. Then the performance: the student records the check-in twice, once as patient and once as receptionist.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Model dialogue:

Receptionist: Good morning. How can I help you?

Patient: Hi, I have an appointment at ten thirty with Dr. Lee.

Receptionist: Can I have your full name, please?

Patient: Dilnoza Karimova.

Receptionist: Could you spell your last name?

Patient: K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A.

Receptionist: And your date of birth?

Patient: March twelfth, nineteen ninety-eight.

Receptionist: Do you have your insurance card?

Patient: Sorry, could you repeat that more slowly, please?

Receptionist: Of course. Do you have your insurance card? … Thank you. Please take a seat in the waiting room.

Appointment cards (fictional):

Card Patient Date of birth Appointment Twist
A Aziz Rakhimov 07/04/1990 Tuesday 9:15, Nurse Practitioner Brown None
B Malika Yusupova 11/30/2001 Thursday 2:40 p.m., Dr. Patel Forgot insurance card
C Jasur Toshev 01/13/1985 Monday 10:15, Dr. Lee Arrives at 10:50

Number Catch (teacher reads, student writes and reads back): 13 · 30 · 10:15 · 10:50 · 07/04/1990 · 11/30/2001 · 2:40 p.m. Key: 07/04/1990 = July 4, 1990; 11/30/2001 = November 30, 2001.

Stretch: in Round 3, the student also apologizes and asks to reschedule. Support: keep the dialogue visible in Round 2.

Groups: threes: patient, receptionist, observer with a checklist (name spelled, date of birth, time, one polite request). Rotate.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): introduce yourself, then explain how to check in at a clinic.

teacher.title: The Human Body
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can name and locate body parts and organs, say what each organ does, and describe exactly where pain is.

Student roles this week: anatomy student; nurse explaining to a patient; patient describing pain.

Prepare: front and back body diagrams; an organ diagram; 4 body-map pain cards (below, teacher only). The organ cards, function cards and Mystery Patient question card are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 2).

Lesson 4 · A Learn · Body parts
Goal Name and locate 16 body parts.
New words (8) abdomen, chest, shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, ankle
Review (known) head, neck, back, arm, leg, hand, foot, finger
Recycle appointment, date of birth, physician
Grammar There is / are; place: above, below, between, next to, on the left / right side of
Spark Picture Reveal (close-up photos of body parts)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Play 20 seconds of the student's Week 1 voice note; they say one thing they'd improve. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Label the diagram: 8 known words fast, then the 8 new ones. Sounds: abdomen (AB-do-men), silent k in knee, silent w in wrist. Bridge: belly / tummy → abdomen. The stomach is an organ; the abdomen is the area.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: The elbow is between the shoulder and the wrist. There are two knees. The student makes 4 location sentences.
32–50 F Round 1: the teacher gives a clue (It's between the hip and the ankle); the student names and points. Round 2: the student gives clues; the teacher guesses. Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal with close-ups. Round 3 (new detail): add left and right: your right wrist, her left ankle.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 new words + 1 between sentence. Set homework.

Stretch: add upper arm, forearm, thigh, calf. Support: keep the labeled diagram visible in Round 1.

Groups: Round 2 as a team clue race.

Homework: label the front and back diagrams and say each word aloud; listen to the teacher's 16-word voice note.

Lesson 5 · B Practice · Organs and what they do
Goal Explain what 8 organs do.
New words (8) brain, heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, intestines, bladder, pancreas
Recycle abdomen, chest, physician
Grammar Present simple for facts: pumps, filters, stores, produces; helps to; is responsible for
Spark Match and Speak (organ ↔ function)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Point-and-say: 10 body parts in 60 seconds. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 organs on the diagram, one plain-English function each (key below). Sounds: lungs (one syllable), kidneys (KID-neez).
16–30 I Spark: Match and Speak; the student says The ___ is responsible for ___. Listening: the teacher reads the organ tour twice and asks 3 questions.
30–50 F Round 1: the student explains 3 organs to a teacher-patient, who asks Where is it? each time. Round 2: the teacher explains 3 organs with one mistake; the student corrects it. Round 3 (new detail): What does the pancreas do? My mother has diabetes. The student explains in plain English and refers medical questions to the doctor.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 organs + their functions without notes. Set homework.

Function key: brain – controls the body; heart – pumps blood; lungs – take in oxygen; liver – cleans the blood and helps digestion; kidneys – filter the blood and make urine; intestines – absorb food and water; bladder – stores urine; pancreas – produces insulin and helps digestion.

Organ tour (listening): The kidneys are in the back of the abdomen, one on each side. They filter the blood and make urine. The urine goes to the bladder, which stores it. Questions: Where are the kidneys? What do they make? What does the bladder do?

Stretch: explain one organ's location and function in a single sentence with which. Support: function cards stay face-up.

Groups: Match and Speak as a card race in pairs.

Homework: record 4 organ-and-function sentences (60 seconds).

Lesson 6 · C Perform · Where exactly? Location words
Goal Describe exactly where pain is.
New words (4) upper, lower, anterior (front), posterior (back)
Recycle date of birth, kidneys, shoulder
Grammar Word order: pain in the lower right abdomen; right lower back pain
Spark Mystery Patient (find the pain location)
Perform task Recorded: describe 3 pain locations, then confirm one as the nurse
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Odd One Out: heart, lungs, knee, liver. Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Anterior and posterior are for recognition: students hear them in nursing school but say front and back to patients.
12–20 I Model: The pain is in the lower right part of my abdomen. Nurse check: So the pain is in your lower right abdomen. Is that correct?
20–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient. The teacher hides a body-map card; the student asks up to 10 yes/no questions (Is it on the front? Is it above the waist? Left or right?), then states the location. Round 1 with card A, Round 2 with card B. Round 3: cards C and D, student as the patient. Then the performance: record 3 locations as the patient and 1 confirmation as the nurse.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Body-map cards (fictional; hidden, teacher only): A – lower right abdomen; B – upper left chest; C – back of the right knee; D – lower back, both sides.

Stretch: recognize 4 word parts: cardi/o (heart), neur/o (nerve), gastr/o (stomach), -itis (inflammation). Support: give the Mystery Patient question card (below).

Mystery Patient question card: Is it on the front or the back? Is it above or below the waist? Is it on the left, on the right, or on both sides? Is it in the head, the chest, the abdomen, the back, an arm or a leg? Is it near the shoulder, the hip or the knee? → So the pain is in your… Is that correct?

Groups: one student hides the card and answers; the rest take turns asking.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): name 8 body parts and 4 organs with their functions, then describe one pain location.

teacher.title: Symptoms and Pain
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can describe common symptoms, ask about pain step by step, and say when a symptom started and how long it has lasted.

Student roles this week: nurse asking questions; patient describing symptoms; interpreter (Uzbek Bridge).

Prepare: 4 symptom pictures; a 0–10 pain scale; a timeline strip. Symptom cards 1–4, pain cards A–C and the pain question card are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 3).

Lesson 7 · A Learn · Common symptoms
Goal Describe 8 common symptoms.
New words (8) symptom, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, fatigue, weakness
Recycle abdomen, lower, kidneys
Grammar feel + adjective (I feel dizzy); have + noun (I have a fever); word pairs: dizziness / dizzy, weakness / weak, nausea / nauseous
Spark Picture Reveal (symptom pictures)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Where is it? The teacher names 5 places; the student points and says It's in the lower… Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words. Make the difference clear: dizzy = the room spins or you feel unsteady; fatigue = tired, no energy; weakness = muscles are not strong. Everyday-to-clinical bridge: I feel like throwing up → nausea; My head is spinning → dizziness.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: the noun/adjective pairs. The student turns 4 nouns into I feel… sentences.
32–50 F Round 1: the teacher plays a patient with symptom card 1; the student asks How are you feeling? Do you have…? Round 2: swap, card 2. Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal. Round 3 (new detail): cards 3 and 4 add a location (I feel dizzy, and I have pain in my lower abdomen).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 symptoms, one with feel, one with have. Set homework.

Symptom cards (fictional): 1 – fever and chills since last night; 2 – nausea, vomited twice; 3 – dizziness when standing up; 4 – fatigue and weakness in both legs.

Stretch: add lightheaded and vertigo and explain the difference. Support: a two-column card: I feel… / I have…

Groups: symptom charades: one student acts, the others name it in a full sentence.

Homework: learn the 8 words; record 4 symptom sentences.

Lesson 8 · B Practice · Describing pain
Goal Ask about pain location, type and score.
New words (8) sharp, dull, burning, aching, throbbing, constant, comes and goes, pain scale
Recycle chest, nausea, upper
Grammar How questions: How bad is it? How long does it last? How often does it come? On a scale from 0 to 10…
Spark Listen and Answer (a patient's pain report)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student describes yesterday's symptom card from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words with a 0–10 scale and gestures. Sounds: throbbing (th + short o), aching (AY-king).
16–30 I Model a short pain interview. Spark: Listen and Answer (below), heard twice.
30–50 F Round 1: the teacher-patient uses pain card A; the student asks where, what type, constant or not, and the score, then summarizes: So you have a sharp pain in your lower right abdomen, 7 out of 10. Round 2: card B, fewer prompts. Round 3 (new detail): card C, and halfway through the patient says Now it's worse, about 8; the student updates the summary.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 pain words + 1 How question. Set homework.

Listen and Answer: The pain is in my lower back. It's a dull, aching pain, and it's there all the time. Right now it's about a six out of ten. It gets worse when I sit for a long time. Questions: Where is the pain? What type is it? What is the score? What makes it worse? Key: lower back; dull, aching, constant; 6/10; sitting for a long time.

Pain cards (fictional): A – sharp, lower right abdomen, constant, 7/10. B – burning, upper abdomen after meals, comes and goes, 4/10. C – throbbing headache at the front of the head, 6/10, worse with bright light.

Correct at once: any wrong score or wrong side.

Stretch: add What makes it better? What makes it worse? Support: a 4-question card (where / type / constant? / score).

Groups: pairs swap pain cards; one listener writes the summary.

Homework: write 5 pain questions and record yourself asking them.

Lesson 9 · C Perform · When did it start?
Goal Ask and say when a symptom started and how long it has lasted.
New words (4) onset, duration, suddenly, gradually
Recycle dizziness, constant, lower
Grammar Past simple for the start (It started three days ago); present perfect for up to now (I've had it for three days / since Monday)
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Perform task Recorded 60-second symptom story, then the nurse's summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Pain-word quick fire: the teacher acts, the student names (throbbing!). Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words on a timeline strip. Onset = when it started; duration = how long.
12–20 I Grammar on the timeline: ago with past simple; for / since with present perfect. Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
20–50 F Round 1: the student interviews the teacher-patient: When did it start? Did it start suddenly? How long have you had it? Round 2: swap. Round 3 (new detail): the teacher changes one fact (Actually, it started on Sunday); the student asks again and updates. Then the performance: record a 60-second symptom story as the patient (onset, duration, type, score), then a 20-second nurse summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Uzbek Bridge (teacher reads the Uzbek; student says it in English, first person):

Uzbek Model English
Uch kundan beri boshim og‘riyapti. I have had a headache for three days.
Boshim qattiq og‘riyapti, ba’zan boshim aylanadi. I have a severe headache, and sometimes I feel dizzy.
Ko‘nglim ayniyapti, lekin qusmadim. I feel nauseous, but I haven't vomited.
Ikki kundan beri isitmam bor. I have had a fever for two days.

Reverse: the teacher says Where does it hurt? and Do you have a fever or a cough?; the student says them in Uzbek. Rule: keep every detail, add nothing, no advice.

Stretch: add a second time detail: It started suddenly on Monday, and I've had it since then. Support: timeline strip in view during Round 1.

Groups: Uzbek Bridge round-robin; each student takes one line.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): tell the story of a fictional symptom: what, where, type, score, when it started and how long you've had it.

teacher.title: Health History
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about long-term conditions, past surgeries and injuries, allergies, medicines and family history, then give a short summary.

Student roles this week: nurse taking a history; patient with a fictional history.

Prepare: a timeline strip. Condition cards H1–H2, surgical cards S1–S2 and the 5-part order card are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 4); history cards M1–M2 (below) are teacher only.

Lesson 10 · A Learn · Common medical conditions
Goal Ask about long-term conditions.
New words (8) medical history, condition, chronic, diabetes, hypertension (high blood pressure), asthma, infection, diagnosis
Recycle symptom, onset, fatigue
Grammar Have you ever…? Have you ever been told you have…? and Do you have…?
Spark Match and Speak (everyday ↔ medical)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S When did it start? The teacher gives 3 symptoms; the student answers with ago / for / since. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words. Key difference: a symptom is what you feel; a condition is the illness. Chronic = long-term. Teach hypertension together with high blood pressure.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: Have you ever…? for any time in life; Do you have…? for now.
32–50 F Spark (6 min): Match and Speak (below). Round 1: the teacher plays patient H1; the student asks about 3 conditions and How long have you had it? Round 2: swap, H2. Round 3 (new detail): the patient says I think my sugar is a bit high, but no doctor told me. The student notes no diagnosis; patient is unsure and does not guess.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 conditions in Have you ever…? questions. Set homework.

Match and Speak: high blood pressure ↔ hypertension; a problem with blood sugar ↔ diabetes; a long-term illness ↔ chronic condition; uses an inhaler for breathing ↔ asthma; germs got into the cut ↔ infection; the doctor found out what it is ↔ diagnosis.

Condition cards (fictional): H1 – hypertension for 5 years; asthma as a child, none now; no diabetes. H2 – type 2 diabetes for 2 years; a kidney infection last spring.

Stretch: explain one condition in plain English: Hypertension means your blood pressure is often too high. Support: question card with 3 starters: Have you ever had…? Do you have…? How long have you had it?

Groups: Match and Speak as a pair race; then pairs interview each other with H1 and H2.

Homework: make 8 everyday-to-medical word pairs and say them aloud.

Lesson 11 · B Practice · Surgeries and past health events
Goal Describe past surgeries and injuries with dates.
New words (8) surgery, operation, procedure, injury, fracture (broken bone), hospital stay, recovery, scar
Recycle chronic, diagnosis, onset
Grammar Present perfect to ask (Have you ever had surgery?), past simple for details (I had surgery in 2015); ago, in, last
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student asks the teacher 3 Have you ever…? questions. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Sounds: surgery (SUR-jer-ee), fracture (FRAK-cher). Bridge: broken bone → fracture.
16–30 I The teacher models a surgical history on a timeline; the student retells it. Grammar in 4 minutes: question in present perfect, answer in past simple. Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student interviews the teacher-patient with card S1 and repeats the history back. Round 2: swap, card S2. Round 3 (new detail): the patient gives a date as about five years ago; the student turns it into a year and checks it.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 question + 1 answer with a year. Set homework.

Surgical cards (fictional): S1 – appendix surgery in 2015, 3 days in the hospital; broke her left wrist in 2019, no surgery. S2 – C-section in 2020; knee injury playing football two years ago, recovery took 6 weeks.

Error Hunt (teacher reads; card S1 in front of the student): The patient had appendix surgery in 2016 and stayed in the hospital for five days. She broke her right wrist in 2019. Key: 2016 → 2015; five → three days; right → left wrist.

Stretch: add What was the recovery like? Support: timeline strip with years marked.

Groups: pairs; the listener fills in a blank timeline.

Homework: record a 60-second past-health history for card S2.

Lesson 12 · C Perform · Allergies, medicines, family history
Goal Take a basic health history.
New words (4) allergic to, reaction, rash, family history
Recycle surgery, chronic, nausea
Grammar Are you allergic to anything? What happens when you take it? Does anyone in your family have…? It runs in the family.
Spark Mystery Patient (full history)
Perform task Recorded 90-second history interview and a 30-second summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Odd One Out: asthma, diabetes, fracture, hypertension (fracture is an injury). Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Allergy = the body reacts (rash, swelling, trouble breathing). Side effect = an expected unwanted effect (feeling sleepy).
12–20 I Model the 5-part history order: conditions → surgery → medicines → allergies → family.
20–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient with card M1 hidden; the student asks in the 5-part order. Round 2: card M2, no prompt sheet. Round 3: the student plays M1, the teacher asks. Then the performance: record a 90-second interview with M2 and a 30-second summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

History cards (fictional; hidden, teacher only):

Card Conditions Surgery Medicines Allergies Family
M1 – Gulnora, 46 Hypertension, 6 years Gallbladder removed, 2018 One blood-pressure tablet every morning Penicillin – rash Mother: diabetes. Father: heart attack at 60
M2 – Bekzod, 33 Asthma None Inhaler when needed Peanuts – lips swell High blood pressure runs in the family

Correct at once: a missed not (I'm not allergic vs I'm allergic).

Stretch: ask one follow-up for every yes. Support: 5-part order card in view.

Groups: threes: nurse, patient, observer ticking the 5 parts.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): give the full health-history summary of the patient you interviewed in the performance (card M2), from your notes.

teacher.title: Vital Signs and Measurements
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can hear and say numbers and units without errors, read a vital-signs chart aloud, and report a change between two readings.

Student roles this week: nurse reading a chart; colleague receiving a report.

Prepare: a phone to record. Charts V1–V2, a blank chart, the number list and the report frame are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 5).

This week is about accuracy. Correct every wrong number, unit or time at once.

Lesson 13 · A Learn · Numbers, units and spelling
Goal Hear, say and confirm numbers and units.
New words (8) decimal point, degree, kilogram, pound, centimeter, inch, percent, unit
Recycle allergic to, family history, surgery
Grammar Clarifying: Did you say thirteen or thirty? Could you spell that? Let me repeat that back.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student spells their full name and says their date of birth US-style. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words, metric and US units side by side. Stress: thir-TEEN vs THIR-ty, the same for 14–19. Decimals: thirty-seven point five.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: three clarifying phrases. The teacher reads fast; the student must use one.
32–50 F Spark (5 min): Number Catch (below). Round 1: the teacher dictates a fictional name and 5 measurements; the student writes them and reads them back. Round 2: the student dictates; the teacher mishears one on purpose; the student corrects. Round 3 (new detail): the teacher speaks quickly; the student must clarify before writing.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 3 numbers with units, read back correctly. Set homework.

Number Catch: 13 · 30 · 15 · 50 · 98.6 °F · 37 °C · 72 kg · 160 lb · 5 feet 4 inches · 165 cm.

Stretch: convert roughly: 1 kg is about 2.2 lb; 1 inch is about 2.5 cm. Support: a number line 13–19 / 30–90 to point at.

Groups: dictation chain; each student passes 3 numbers to the next.

Homework: record the 10 numbers in the Student Edition Week 5 practice list, with units; listen to the teacher's teen/ty voice note.

Lesson 14 · B Practice · Vital signs
Goal Read a vital-signs chart aloud.
New words (8) vital signs, blood pressure (BP), pulse / heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), temperature (T), oxygen saturation (SpO2), beats per minute, breaths per minute
Recycle decimal point, degree, allergic to
Grammar Saying values: 120 over 80; 37.5 degrees; 98 percent; 72 beats per minute. With a time: At 8 a.m. the BP was…
Spark Listen and Answer (a vital-signs report)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Number Catch warm-up: 5 quick values. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the full term first, then the abbreviation. Use this example: BP 120/80 mmHg, T 37.5 °C (99.5 °F), SpO2 98%, HR 72 bpm.
16–30 I Model reading chart V1 aloud. Spark: Listen and Answer (below), heard twice.
30–50 F Round 1: the student reads chart V1; the teacher fills a blank chart; compare. Round 2: swap with V2. Round 3 (new detail): chart V2 again; the student says the full term for every abbreviation.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: read 3 values with units. Set homework.

Listen and Answer: At 9 a.m., Mr. Karimov's blood pressure was 138 over 86, pulse 92, respiratory rate 20, temperature 38.1 degrees, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. Questions: What was the BP? The temperature? The oxygen saturation? Key: 138/86; 38.1 °C; 95%.

Mock charts (fictional):

Chart Time BP HR RR T SpO2
V1 8 a.m. 118/76 74 16 36.8 °C 98%
V2 2 p.m. 142/90 96 22 38.3 °C 94%

Stretch: say the temperature in °F too. Support: chart with full terms printed.

Groups: pairs; one reads, one fills the blank chart, then swap.

Homework: record yourself reading charts V1 and V2 with units.

Lesson 15 · C Perform · Reporting measurements
Goal Report a change between two readings.
New words (4) reading, baseline, increase, decrease
Recycle blood pressure, oxygen saturation, chronic
Grammar Comparatives and change: higher than this morning; it has gone up from 36.8 to 38.3; it has decreased to 94 percent
Spark Error Hunt
Perform task Recorded 45-second report comparing V1 and V2
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S The student reads chart V2 from memory as far as possible. Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Baseline = the first or usual reading you compare with.
12–20 I Model report (below). Spark: Error Hunt (below).
20–50 F Round 1: the student reports V1 → V2 with the model in view. Round 2: model hidden; the teacher, as a colleague, asks What time was that? What unit? Round 3 (new detail): the teacher adds a third reading at 6 p.m. (T 37.6 °C, HR 84); the student reports the new change. Then the performance: a recorded 45-second report. Values, units and times only; no diagnosis.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Model report: I'm reporting the vital signs for Mr. Karimov in room 12. At 8 a.m. his temperature was 36.8 degrees. At 2 p.m. it was 38.3, so it has gone up. His heart rate has increased from 74 to 96, and his oxygen saturation has decreased from 98 to 94 percent on room air. His blood pressure is 142 over 90, higher than this morning.

Error Hunt: His temperature has gone up from 36.8 to 38.8. His heart rate has decreased from 74 to 96. At 2 p.m. his oxygen saturation was 98 percent. Key: 38.8 → 38.3; decreased → increased; 98 → 94 percent.

Stretch: add the respiratory rate change and a closing line: I wanted to let you know about these changes. Support: report frame with gaps for values.

Report frame (Support): I'm reporting the vital signs for ___ in room ___. At ___ his / her temperature was ___. At ___ it was ___, so it has gone up / down. His / her heart rate has increased / decreased from ___ to ___. His / her oxygen saturation is ___ percent on room air. His / her blood pressure is ___ over ___.

Groups: threes: reporter, colleague asking questions, observer checking every number.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): the full V1 → V2 report, every unit included.

teacher.title: Heart and Lungs · Midpoint
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about chest and breathing symptoms and complete the midpoint check: an interview, a chart reading and a 1-minute report.

Student roles this week: nursing student interviewing; patient; interpreter.

Prepare: 4 pictures (hand on chest, swollen ankles, person out of breath on stairs, pulse check); a simple heart diagram; the Lesson 1 recording. Chest cards C1–C2 and the report checklist are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 6); card MP1 and chart MP (below) are unseen, teacher only.

Lesson 16 · A Learn · Heart and circulation
Goal Ask about chest symptoms.
New words (8) heartbeat, circulation, artery, vein, chest pain, palpitations, swelling (edema), irregular
Recycle pulse, increase, baseline
Grammar Present continuous for now vs simple for usual: My heart is beating fast right now. Usually it beats slowly.
Spark Picture Reveal
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student reads one line of chart V2 and says what changed from V1. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words with a simple heart diagram. Bridge: heart racing / pounding → palpitations; swollen ankles → swelling, edema (for recognition). Sounds: artery (AR-ter-ee), vein (one syllable, like rain).
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: right now vs usually. Model: Do you have chest pain now? Does it happen when you walk or when you rest?
