32–50 F Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal with the 4 pictures. Round 1: the teacher plays patient C1; the student asks where, what type, when and what helps, then summarizes. Round 2: swap, card C2. Round 3 (new detail): the patient says The pain is getting worse right now. The student says I'm going to get the nurse right away. Language only, no clinical decisions.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 right now + 1 usually sentence. Set homework.

Chest cards (fictional): C1 – tight chest when climbing stairs, goes away with rest, for 2 weeks. C2 – heart racing at night for 3 days; ankles swollen in the evening.

Stretch: add Does the pain spread anywhere? Support: 4-question card from Lesson 8.

Groups: pairs with C1 and C2; swap.

Homework: label a heart diagram; record two chest-symptom descriptions.

Lesson 17 · B Practice · Breathing
Goal Ask about breathing symptoms and give breathing directions.
New words (8) breath, breathe, shortness of breath, cough, wheezing, sputum (phlegm), inhale, exhale
Recycle palpitations, swelling, baseline
Grammar have trouble + -ing (I have trouble breathing); when clauses (I get short of breath when I climb stairs)
Spark Uzbek Bridge (breathing lines)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Mini-interview: the student asks the teacher 3 chest questions. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Sounds: breath (short e, noun) vs breathe (long ee, verb). Bridge: phlegm → sputum.
16–30 I Listening: I have had a fever and cough for two days. Questions: main symptoms? how long? Key: fever and cough; two days. Grammar in 4 minutes: when clauses. Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the teacher describes cough and breathing symptoms; the student asks follow-ups (When do you get short of breath? Do you cough anything up? What color is it?). Round 2: swap. Round 3 (new detail): the student gives directions: Take a deep breath in… and breathe out slowly.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: breath and breathe in one sentence each. Set homework.

Uzbek Bridge (the teacher may adjust wording to the student's dialect):

Uzbek Model English
Kechadan beri yo‘talayapman. I have had a cough since yesterday.
Zinadan chiqqanimda nafasim qisiladi. I get short of breath when I climb stairs.
Balg‘am oq rangda. The phlegm is white.
Ikki kundan beri isitmam bor, yo‘talim ham bor. I have had a fever for two days, and I also have a cough.

Stretch: describe the sputum: color, amount, how often. Support: follow-up question card: When do you get short of breath? Do you cough anything up? What color is it? How long have you had the cough?

Groups: Uzbek Bridge in pairs: one reads the Uzbek, one interprets.

Homework: record 5 breathing sentences and the breathing directions.

Lesson 18 · C Perform · Midpoint check
Goal Complete an interview, a chart reading and a 1-minute report without help.
New words None. Review Weeks 1–6.
Assessment Midpoint. Score with the section 7 rubric and compare with Lesson 1.
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Relaxed warm-up: What was the hardest week so far? Why?
5–10 — Explain the 3 tasks and the 4 rubric skills. No coaching during tasks.
10–25 Task 1 3-minute interview with card MP1 (unseen). The teacher answers only what is asked. Record it.
25–32 Task 2 The student reads chart MP aloud. Record it.
32–42 Task 3 2 minutes to prepare, then a 1-minute report to the teacher as a colleague. Record it.
42–50 Review Play 20 seconds of Lesson 1, then 20 seconds of today. The student names 2 improvements.
50–60 O Share scores, 2 strengths and 2 goals for Weeks 7–12. Write them on the student's card.

Card MP1 (fictional; unseen, teacher only): Nodira Aliyeva, 52. Cough and shortness of breath for 4 days, worse when walking. White sputum. Fever started 2 days ago. History: asthma. Medicines: inhaler when needed. Allergy: aspirin – wheezing.

Chart MP (fictional; unseen, teacher only): 10 a.m. · BP 128/82 · HR 98 · RR 24 · T 38.0 °C · SpO2 93%.

Report checklist (tick each): name and age · main symptoms · when they started · history and allergy · all 5 values with units and the time.

Groups: run tasks one student at a time while the others prepare their own report with a second card; or book short individual slots.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): re-record the Task 3 report with your 2 improvements.

teacher.title: Digestion, Urination and Nutrition
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about eating, drinking, bowel and urinary habits respectfully, and combine them in one interview.

Student roles this week: nurse asking personal questions with respect; embarrassed patient.

Prepare: food and drink pictures (include plov, non, tea and water bottles). Intake cards F1–F2, bowel cards B1–B2, urinary card U1 and the 4-part order card are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 7); card U2 (below) is hidden, teacher only.

Respect first. These questions can feel embarrassing, especially in Uzbek culture. Teach the opener: I need to ask a few personal questions. These are routine questions we ask everyone. Is that OK?

Lesson 19 · A Learn · Food, fluids and swallowing
Goal Ask about eating and drinking.
New words (8) appetite, diet, nutrition, fluids, intake, hydration, dehydration, swallow
Recycle cough, sputum, breathe
Grammar How much / how many; a little, a few, a lot of, not much (How much water do you drink a day? How many meals do you eat?)
Spark Picture Reveal (food and drink)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Personal hook: What did you eat and drink yesterday? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words. US units: cup, glass, ounce (oz), bottle; 8 oz is about 240 mL. Bridge: I'm not hungry → poor appetite; not drinking enough → risk of dehydration.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: countable (meals, glasses) vs uncountable (water, bread).
32–50 F Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal. Round 1: the student interviews the teacher about card F1 and summarizes. Round 2: swap, F2. Round 3 (new detail): Food gets stuck when I swallow. The student asks: solids or liquids? since when?
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 how much + 1 how many question. Set homework.

Intake cards (fictional): F1 – 3 meals; poor appetite this week; 4 glasses of water and 3 cups of tea a day. F2 – 2 meals with a lot of bread; 1 bottle of soda a day; trouble swallowing pills.

Stretch: summarize in one sentence with a quantifier: She drinks very little water. Support: question card: How much water do you drink a day? How many meals do you eat? How is your appetite? Do you have any trouble swallowing?

Groups: pairs compare their real daily intake, then swap to F1 and F2.

Homework: record a 60-second food-and-fluid description of your own day.

Lesson 20 · B Practice · Bowel habits
Goal Ask bowel questions respectfully.
New words (8) bowel movement, stool, constipation, diarrhea, bloating, cramps, regular, usual
Recycle appetite, intake, cough
Grammar Past questions: When was your last bowel movement? Was it normal for you? Softeners: I need to ask…; Is that OK?
Spark Match and Speak (everyday ↔ medical)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student summarizes card F1 from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words in a neutral, calm voice. Sounds: diarrhea (dye-uh-REE-uh), bowel (rhymes with towel).
16–30 I Model the opener and 4 questions. Spark: Match and Speak (below). Listening: the teacher reads the bowel report (below) twice; the student answers 3 questions.
30–50 F Round 1: the teacher plays patient B1; the student opens respectfully and asks about timing, frequency and symptoms. Round 2: card B2, no notes. Round 3 (new detail): the patient is embarrassed and gives a vague answer; the student reassures and rephrases.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: the opener + 1 bowel question without notes. Set homework.

Match and Speak: I can't go ↔ constipation; loose, watery stools ↔ diarrhea; my stomach feels full of air ↔ bloating; poo ↔ stool, bowel movement; my stomach keeps squeezing ↔ cramps.

Bowel cards (fictional): B1 – last bowel movement 4 days ago (usually every day); hard stool; bloating; cramps 5/10. B2 – diarrhea 6 times since yesterday; cramps; drinking very little.

Bowel report (listening, fictional; teacher reads): Mr. Saidov is 67. His last bowel movement was three days ago. Usually he goes every morning. The stool was hard, and he has some cramps in his lower abdomen, about 4 out of 10. He drinks only two glasses of water a day. Questions: When was his last bowel movement? What is usual for him? How bad are the cramps? Key: three days ago; every morning; 4 out of 10.

Stretch: add Have you noticed any change in color? Support: opener and 4 questions on a card: When was your last bowel movement? Was it normal for you? How often do you usually go? Do you have any pain or bloating?

Groups: pairs; the observer rates respectfulness from 1 to 3.

Homework: practice 5 bowel-history questions aloud and record them.

Lesson 21 · C Perform · Urinary symptoms
Goal Combine a digestion and urinary interview.
New words (4) urinate (pass urine), frequency, urgency, burning
Recycle bowel movement, usual, wheezing
Grammar Frequency: How often do you…? every hour; three times a night; Does it burn when you urinate?
Spark Mystery Patient (combined card)
Perform task Recorded 2-minute combined interview and a 30-second summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Match and Speak replay, fast. Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Bridge: pee → urinate, pass urine; I have to go all the time → frequency; I can't wait → urgency.
12–20 I Model a short urinary interview with card U1.
20–50 F Round 1: the student interviews the teacher with U1. Round 2: swap. Spark: Mystery Patient with card U2 hidden; the student must cover food, fluids, bowels and urine. Then the performance: a recorded 2-minute interview with U2 and a 30-second summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Urinary cards (fictional): U1 – burning when urinating for 2 days; goes every hour, 3 times a night; urgency; darker urine; drinks 2 glasses a day. U2 (combined; hidden, teacher only) – poor appetite; constipation for 3 days; urinates less than usual; dark urine; drinks 1 glass of water a day.

Stretch: recognize hesitancy (hard to start) and retention (cannot empty). Support: a 4-part order card: food → fluids → bowels → urine.

Groups: threes: nurse, patient, observer ticking the 4 parts.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): your 30-second summary of U2 (from your notes), then 3 respectful questions you would ask any patient.

teacher.title: Movement, Skin and Sensation
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can give polite movement directions, describe a wound neutrally, and ask about sensation and orientation.

Student roles this week: nursing student giving directions; nursing student observing; patient with limited mobility.

Prepare: mobility pictures (walker, wheelchair, cane, someone losing balance); a direction-verb picture card; 3 illustrated wound cards drawn from W1–W3 (below), not photos; picture cards for the 8 skin words. Wound cards W1–W3 (text), sensation cards N1–N2, the direction verbs and the summary frame are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 8).

Describe, don't diagnose. Students say what they see (There is redness), never what it is (It's infected).

Lesson 22 · A Learn · Movement and mobility
Goal Give movement directions and offer help.
New words (8) muscle, joint, mobility, balance, stiff, cane, walker, wheelchair
Recycle frequency, urgency, swallow
Grammar can / can't for ability; polite directions: Could you lift your right arm for me?; permission: May I help you stand up?
Spark Picture Reveal (mobility aids)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student asks the teacher 3 urinary questions. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words. Direction verbs: lift, bend, straighten, turn, squeeze, push. Sounds: muscle (silent c: MUS-ul).
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: Lift your arm → Could you lift your arm for me? Always ask before helping: May I…?
32–50 F Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal. Round 1: the student gives 5 directions; the teacher follows, sometimes with the wrong side; the student corrects. Round 2: swap. Round 3 (new detail): the patient wants to walk to the bathroom but is unsteady; the student asks permission, offers the walker and says Let me get someone to help us. Verbal practice only.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 Could you… for me? + 1 May I…? Set homework.

Stretch: add Tell me if it hurts and Take your time. Support: direction verb card with pictures.

Groups: "nurse says": one student gives directions, the group follows; wrong side = out.

Homework: describe 3 mobility situations in a voice note.

Lesson 23 · B Practice · Skin and wounds
Goal Describe a wound neutrally.
New words (8) wound, cut, bruise, redness, drainage, dressing, intact, itchy
Recycle swelling, joint, stiff
Grammar There is / are + size, color, place: There is a red area about 3 cm wide on the left forearm.
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student gives the teacher 3 movement directions. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words with illustrated cards. Intact = whole, not broken. Bridge: bandage → dressing; liquid coming out → drainage.
16–30 I Model describing W1 in the order: where → size → color → dressing. Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student describes W1; the teacher picks the matching card from three. Round 2: the teacher describes W2; the student chooses and checks details. Round 3 (new detail): with W3 the patient asks Is it infected? The student answers: I can see some redness. I'll tell the nurse so she can check it.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: describe one card in 4 parts. Set homework.

Wound cards (fictional, illustrated): W1 – cut on the right palm, 2 cm long, dressing dry and clean. W2 – purple bruise on the left shin, about 5 cm. W3 – red area around a scratch on the left forearm, 3 cm wide, warm, a small amount of yellow drainage.

Error Hunt (W1 in front of the student): There is a 5 cm cut on the left palm. The dressing is wet. Key: 5 cm → 2 cm; left → right palm; wet → dry and clean.

Stretch: compare two cards with comparatives (larger, redder). Support: 4-part description frame (Student Edition, Week 8 cards): There is a ___ on the ___ (where). It is about ___ cm (size). It is ___ (color). The dressing is ___ (dressing).

Groups: pairs play "describe and draw": one describes, one sketches.

Homework: write and record 4 card descriptions.

Lesson 24 · C Perform · Sensation and orientation
Goal Ask about sensation and orientation, then give a factual summary.
New words (4) numbness, tingling, alert, confused
Recycle balance, redness, constipation
Grammar Indirect questions: Can you tell me your name? Do you know where you are? Can you tell me what day it is?
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded 1-minute factual summary of card N1
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Odd One Out: bruise, cut, wound, walker. Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Numbness = no feeling; tingling = pins and needles. Alert = awake and aware; confused = mixed up about name, place or time.
12–20 I Grammar in 4 minutes: direct → indirect questions. The three orientation checks: person, place, time.
20–50 F Round 1: the teacher plays N1; the student asks about movement, sensation and orientation. Round 2: N2, no notes. Round 3 (new detail): N1 says My left hand went numb this morning. The student notes this is new and says I'll tell the nurse now. Spark: 60-Second Report on N1. Then the performance: record the 1-minute summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Sensation cards (fictional): N1 – Rustam Nazarov, 70; tingling in both feet for a month; numbness in the left hand since this morning (new); alert; knows his name and where he is, not the day. N2 – Zarina Kamolova, 58; dizzy when standing; poor balance; uses a cane; alert and oriented.

Stretch: separate what the patient said from what you saw. Support: summary frame: The patient reports… She is alert and…

Groups: pairs; the listener ticks target words during the 60-Second Report.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): the N1 summary, then give 3 polite movement directions.

teacher.title: Medicines
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can name medicine forms and routes, read a label accurately, ask about medicines and check understanding with teach-back.

Student roles this week: nurse explaining a label; patient with questions; interpreter.

Prepare: pictures of medicine forms; form and route cards; labels L1–L3 (below), printed large. All medicine names here are invented. Labels L1–L3 and the label map are also in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 9).

Language, not advice. Students read what the label says and send every other question to the pharmacist or doctor. They never suggest a dose or a change.

Lesson 25 · A Learn · Medicine forms and routes
Goal Name medicine forms and routes.
New words (8) tablet, capsule, liquid, injection, inhaler, cream, by mouth (oral, PO), IV (intravenous)
Recycle numbness, alert, confused
Grammar Passive for recognition: is taken by mouth; is given by injection; is applied to the skin; is inhaled
Spark Match and Speak (abbreviations ↔ plain English)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Orientation questions: the student asks the teacher name, place and day. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words with pictures, full term before abbreviation. Sounds: capsule (CAP-sool), intravenous (in-tra-VEE-nus).
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: the passive is for recognizing labels; patients hear the active: You take it by mouth.
32–50 F Spark (6 min): Match and Speak: PO ↔ by mouth; IV ↔ into a vein; topical ↔ on the skin; inhaled ↔ breathed in. Round 1: the teacher shows form and route cards; the student explains 3 in everyday words. Round 2: the teacher explains with one wrong route; the student corrects. Round 3 (new detail): Can I crush this tablet? The student says That's a good question for the pharmacist.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 forms + 1 route in a sentence. Set homework.

Stretch: add drops, patch, suppository for recognition. Support: picture card for each form.

Groups: card race: the first to say the route in plain English wins the card.

Homework: make 8 picture or audio flashcards.

Lesson 26 · B Practice · Dose, timing and labels
Goal Read a medicine label accurately.
New words (8) dose, milligram (mg), milliliter (mL), once daily, twice daily, every 8 hours, as needed (PRN), with food
Recycle tablet, by mouth, wound
Grammar Imperatives with frequency: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily with food.
Spark Number Catch (mg vs mL)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student explains 3 routes from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Separate amount per dose from times per day. Spark: Number Catch: 5 mg · 50 mg · 15 mL · 0.5 mL · every 8 hours · 3 doses in 24 hours.
16–30 I Listening: the teacher reads label L2 aloud. Questions: how much per dose? how often? the most per day? Key: 10 mL; every 8 hours when needed; 3 doses in 24 hours.
30–50 F Round 1: the student reads L1 to the teacher-patient; the teacher repeats it back; the student checks amount, route and timing. Round 2: swap with L2. Round 3 (new detail): with L3 the patient says twice a week; the student corrects: twice a day.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: read one label line with exact units. Set homework.

Labels (fictional):

Label Medicine Directions
L1 CALMEXA 10 mg tablets Take 1 tablet by mouth once daily in the morning. Qty 30. Refills: 2.
L2 RESPIRA-X syrup 5 mg/5 mL Take 10 mL by mouth every 8 hours as needed for cough. Do not take more than 3 doses in 24 hours.
L3 DERMOSOL cream 1% Apply a thin layer to the affected skin twice daily. For external use only.

Correct at once: mg vs mL; daily vs weekly; any wrong number.

Stretch: explain Qty and Refills. Support: a label map: name → strength → amount → route → how often.

Groups: pairs; one reads, one repeats back; swap labels.

Homework: record yourself reading labels L1 and L2 with exact units.

Lesson 27 · C Perform · Medicine questions and teach-back
Goal Ask about medicines and check understanding.
New words (4) side effect, missed dose, refill, teach-back
Recycle dose, twice daily, numbness
Grammar will for future actions: Tell me how you will take it. Sequencing: first, then, after that
Spark Uzbek Bridge (medicine lines)
Perform task Recorded medicine interview, label explanation and teach-back
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Read label L3 aloud from the card. Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Teach-back = the patient explains it back in their own words, so you know your explanation was clear.
12–20 I Model teach-back (below). Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
20–50 F Round 1: the student asks the teacher-patient What medicines do you take? How often? Any side effects? Round 2: the student explains L1, then asks for teach-back; the teacher leaves out one detail; the student clarifies from the label. Round 3 (new detail): I missed my dose yesterday. Should I take two today? The student refers: Please ask your pharmacist or doctor about that. Then the performance: record Rounds 2 and 3 with L2.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Teach-back model: I want to make sure I explained this clearly. Can you tell me how you will take this medicine? Patient: One tablet every evening. Nurse: Almost. Let's check the label again: it says in the morning.

Uzbek Bridge:

Uzbek Model English
Ha, kecha og‘riq qoldiruvchi dori ichdim. Yes, I took pain medication yesterday.
Bugun ertalab dori ichishni unutdim. I forgot to take my medicine this morning.
Bu dori uyqumni keltiradi. This medicine makes me sleepy.
Kuniga ikki marta, ovqatdan keyin ichaman. I take it twice a day, after meals.

Reverse: Have you taken any medication today? → Uzbek.

Stretch: ask about over-the-counter medicines and supplements. Support: teach-back phrase card.

Groups: threes: nurse, patient who "forgets" one detail, observer.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): explain label L2 to a patient, then ask for teach-back.

teacher.title: Tests and Procedures
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can explain a test instruction card, describe an imaging test from supplied information, and give a polite infection-prevention reminder.

Student roles this week: nurse explaining instructions; nervous patient; visitor at an isolation room.

Prepare: pictures of a blood tube, urine cup, lab, X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound; a 6-picture handwashing sequence. Test cards T1–T2, imaging cards I1–I2, the 4-part frame and the handwashing steps are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 10).

Read from the card. Preparation depends on the real order. Students explain only what the card says.

Lesson 28 · A Learn · Lab tests and samples
Goal Explain a sample instruction card.
New words (8) blood test, urine sample, specimen, laboratory (lab), result, fasting, collect, container
Recycle side effect, refill, teach-back
Grammar have to / need to / don't have to: You don't have to fast for this test. You need to collect the sample in the morning.
Spark Picture Reveal (lab items)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student explains label L1 and asks for teach-back. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words with pictures. Fasting = no food for a set time; what you may drink depends on the card. Sounds: laboratory (LAB-ruh-tor-ee), specimen (SPESS-i-men).
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: have to (necessary) vs don't have to (not necessary). Model explaining T1.
32–50 F Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal. Round 1: the student explains T1 to the teacher-patient. Round 2: the teacher repeats T2 with one step missing; the student clarifies from the card. Round 3 (new detail): Can I drink tea before the test? The student answers from T1: The instructions say only water.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 have to + 1 don't have to sentence. Set homework.

Test cards (fictional): T1 – blood test, fasting: no food or drink except water for 8 hours before; come to the lab at 8 a.m.; bring your ID. T2 – urine sample: first urine of the morning; use the clean container; write your name and the time on the label; bring it to the lab within 1 hour.

Stretch: add Your doctor will tell you the results. Support: the card stays in view.

Groups: pairs; each explains one card, the other repeats it back.

Homework: record one explanation from card T2.

Lesson 29 · B Practice · Imaging and procedures
Goal Explain an imaging test from a card.
New words (8) X-ray, CT scan, MRI, ultrasound, imaging, contrast (dye), procedure, consent form
Recycle specimen, fasting, side effect
Grammar going to for plans (You're going to have an MRI tomorrow); will for facts and promises (It will take about 30 minutes. The doctor will explain the results.)
Spark Listen and Answer (imaging card)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student explains card T1 from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words with pictures. Say the letters: C-T, M-R-I. Consent = the patient agrees and signs.
16–30 I Grammar in 4 minutes: going to vs will. Spark: Listen and Answer: the teacher reads I1. Questions: When? How long? What to remove? Key: Tuesday 3 p.m.; 30–45 minutes; all metal, such as jewelry and a watch.
30–50 F Round 1: the student explains I1 to the teacher-patient. The teacher asks one question the card answers and one it doesn't (Is an MRI safe for me?); the student refers: The radiology team will check that with you. Round 2: card I2. Round 3 (new detail): the patient is nervous about the noise; the student reassures, using only facts from the card.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 going to + 1 will sentence about a test. Set homework.

Imaging cards (fictional): I1 – MRI of the knee, Tuesday 3:00 p.m., Radiology, 1st floor; takes 30–45 minutes; remove all metal (jewelry, watch); the machine is loud, earplugs are given; tell staff if you have metal in your body. I2 – abdominal ultrasound, Friday 9:30 a.m.; no food for 6 hours before; a gel is put on the skin; it does not hurt.

Stretch: explain why a consent form is signed, in plain English. Support: a 4-part frame: what → when → how long → how to prepare.

Groups: pairs; one patient asks a question the card can't answer; the partner refers.

Homework: make 4 imaging-term flashcards and record an I2 explanation.

Lesson 30 · C Perform · Infection prevention
Goal Explain a handwashing sequence and give a polite reminder.
New words (4) hand hygiene, gloves, mask, isolation
Recycle procedure, consent form, refill
Grammar before / after + -ing: Clean your hands before touching the patient and after removing your gloves.
Spark 60-Second Report (picture sequence)
Perform task Recorded 45-second sequence explanation and a polite reminder to a visitor
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Odd One Out: X-ray, MRI, ultrasound, specimen. Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words; gown and PPE (protective equipment) for recognition. Clean = no visible dirt; sterile = no germs at all.
12–20 I Model the 6-step sequence with first, then, after that, finally: wet hands → soap → rub for at least 20 seconds → rinse → dry → turn off the tap with the towel.
20–50 F Spark: 60-Second Report on the sequence. Round 1: the student gives a visitor (the teacher) a polite reminder (below). Round 2: the visitor is in a hurry; the student stays polite and firm. Round 3 (new detail): a child visitor; the student uses simpler words. Then the performance: record the sequence and the reminder.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Polite reminder model: Excuse me, before you go in, could you please clean your hands and put on a mask? This room is in isolation. Thank you for helping keep the patient safe.

Stretch: add the order for putting on a mask and gloves. Key: clean your hands, put on the mask, then put on the gloves (gloves go on last). Support: sequence pictures stay in view.

Groups: threes: nurse, visitor, observer ticking before / after sentences.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): explain card T1 or I1, then give the isolation reminder.

teacher.title: Patient Communication and Teamwork
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can respond to a worried patient, give a short SBAR report, confirm a handoff and write a 3-sentence factual note.

Student roles this week: caring nurse; colleague giving and receiving reports; interpreter.

Prepare: empathy cards E1–E3, SBAR cards SB1–SB2, the SBAR frame and the note template are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 11). The teacher reads the mock handoff (below) aloud.

Lesson 31 · A Learn · Empathy, privacy, interpreters
Goal Respond to a worried patient.
New words (8) concern, worried, uncomfortable, privacy, confidential, interpreter, respect, reassure
Recycle isolation, consent form, procedure
Grammar I can see (that) you're worried. It sounds like… Would you like…?
Spark Match and Speak (patient words ↔ caring response)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student gives the isolation reminder from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words. Rule: acknowledge the feeling, don't promise an outcome. Everything will be fine ✗ → I understand this is worrying. Let me find the nurse to answer your questions ✓.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: three caring frames. Intonation: soft and slow, falling at the end.
32–50 F Spark (6 min): Match and Speak (below). Round 1: the teacher plays E1; the student acknowledges and asks a helpful question. Round 2: E2, a privacy request. Round 3 (new detail): E3 needs an interpreter; the student offers a professional interpreter rather than a family member, for accuracy and privacy.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 caring frame + 1 Would you like…? Set homework.

Match and Speak: I'm scared about the surgery ↔ I can see you're worried. Would you like to talk about it? · I don't want my son to hear this ↔ Of course. Would you like some privacy? · I don't understand the doctor ↔ Would you like an interpreter? · Nobody tells me anything! ↔ I'm sorry you feel that way. Let me find out for you.

Empathy cards (fictional): E1 – worried about MRI results. E2 – does not want her son to hear her history. E3 – an older Uzbek speaker with very little English.

Stretch: add a check: Is there anything else worrying you? Support: the three frames on a card.

Groups: pairs; the observer rates warmth and clarity from 1 to 3.

Homework: record 3 caring responses to E1–E3.

Lesson 32 · B Practice · SBAR reports
Goal Give a short SBAR report.
New words (8) handoff, report, situation, background, assessment, recommendation, update, read-back
Recycle worried, privacy, isolation
Grammar I'm calling about…; present perfect for change: She has had shortness of breath since 3 p.m.
Spark Error Hunt (SBAR)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S Respond to 2 Match and Speak lines from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words and SBAR. Assessment uses only the findings on the card; recommendation uses only the request on the card. No invented diagnosis.
16–30 I Listening: the teacher reads the model SBAR; the student labels each part S, B, A or R. Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student puts SB1 into the frame and reports to the teacher as a colleague; the teacher asks one clarifying question. Round 2: SB2, fewer prompts. Round 3 (new detail): the teacher interrupts: Sorry, what was the oxygen? The student reads it back exactly.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: say S and R for SB2 without notes. Set homework.

Case cards (fictional):

SB1 – Dilfuza Rahimova, 64, room 8 SB2 – Anvar Qodirov, 59, room 3
Situation New shortness of breath since 3 p.m. Shaky and sweaty; blood sugar 58 mg/dL at 11 a.m.
Background Admitted yesterday with a chest infection; history of asthma Type 2 diabetes; took insulin at 7 a.m.; ate very little breakfast
Assessment (supplied) RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air, HR 104, T 38.4 °C Alert; HR 102
Recommendation (supplied) Could you come and see her, please? Could you come and see him now, please?

Model SBAR (SB1): Hello, this is Dilnoza on Unit 4. I'm calling about Mrs. Rahimova in room 8. She has had new shortness of breath since 3 p.m. She was admitted yesterday with a chest infection and has a history of asthma. Her respiratory rate is 26, oxygen saturation 91 percent on room air, heart rate 104 and temperature 38.4. Could you come and see her, please?

Key (labeling the model): S = new shortness of breath since 3 p.m.; B = admitted yesterday with a chest infection, history of asthma; A = RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air, HR 104, T 38.4; R = Could you come and see her, please?

Error Hunt: …Mrs. Rahimova in room 18… shortness of breath since 5 p.m.… oxygen saturation 97 percent… Key: room 8; 3 p.m.; 91 percent.

Stretch: finish with read-back: Can you repeat that back to me? Support: SBAR frame with sentence starters.

SBAR frame (Support): S – I'm calling about ___ in room ___. She / He has had ___ since ___. B – She / He was admitted ___ with ___. She / He has a history of ___. A – Her / His ___ is ___ (values from the card only). R – Could you come and see her / him, please? Read-back: Can you repeat that back to me?

Groups: pairs on the phone, back to back, so there are no visual cues.

Homework: record one SBAR report from card SB2.

Lesson 33 · C Perform · Clarifying and writing a note
Goal Confirm a handoff and write a 3-sentence factual note.
New words (4) confirm, reported, observed, document
Recycle handoff, situation, consent form
Grammar Reported speech: "I feel dizzy" → The patient said she felt dizzy; in notes: Patient reports…
Spark Uzbek Bridge (interpret, then write)
Perform task Recorded read-back and handoff, plus a written 3-sentence note
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S The student gives SB1 as SBAR from memory. Recall 3 words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Reported = the patient told you. Observed = you saw or measured it.
12–20 I Grammar in 4 minutes: tense back-shift. Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below); the student says each line in English, then writes it as a note.
20–50 F Round 1: the teacher gives the mock handoff; the student confirms key details: Let me confirm: room 5, headache since this morning, 6 out of 10… Round 2: the student writes a 3-sentence note; review together against the model. Round 3: the student delivers the handoff to the teacher as the next nurse. Then the performance: record the read-back and handoff, and hand in the note.
50–60 O Play the recording back and check the note. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Uzbek Bridge:

Uzbek English As a note
Ertalabdan beri boshim aylanyapti. I've felt dizzy since this morning. Patient reports dizziness since this morning.
Tushlikdan keyin bir marta qusdim. I vomited once after lunch. Patient said she vomited once after lunch.
Qornimning o‘ng tomoni og‘riyapti. The right side of my stomach hurts. Patient reports right-sided abdominal pain.

Mock handoff (teacher reads): Room 5, Ms. Usmanova, 45. She says she has had a headache since this morning, 6 out of 10. She vomited once at 12:30. I checked her blood pressure at 1 p.m.: 150 over 95. She is alert and oriented.

Model note: Patient reports headache since this morning, 6/10. Vomited once at 12:30. BP 150/95 at 1 p.m.; alert and oriented.

Stretch: mark each fact in the note R (reported) or O (observed). Support: a note template with 3 lines.

Note template (Support): 1. Patient reports ___ since ___. 2. ___ (what happened, with the time). 3. ___ (a value you observed, with the time); alert and oriented.

Groups: chain handoff: each student passes the report to the next, who confirms it.

Weekly voice note (60–90 seconds): the SB2 SBAR report, then read your 3-sentence note aloud.

teacher.title: Nursing-School Readiness · Final
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask an instructor for clarification, follow skills-lab instructions, and complete the five-task final assessment.

Student roles this week: nursing student; new student on a clinical placement.

Prepare: the Lesson 1 and Lesson 18 recordings; the completion certificate. Assignment cards A1–A2, the mock syllabus page and skills-lab card SL1 are in the Student Edition (Cards and texts · Week 12); the final-assessment cards (below) are unseen, teacher only.

Lesson 34 · A Learn · Classroom and assignments
Goal Ask an instructor about an assignment.
New words (8) lecture, syllabus, assignment, due date (deadline), rubric, quiz, chapter, office hours
Recycle confirm, document, report
Grammar Indirect questions: Could you tell me when the assignment is due? Do you know where I can find the rubric?
Spark Match and Speak (US college terms ↔ meaning)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student reads their Lesson 33 note aloud. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 8 words with the mock syllabus page (below). Sounds: syllabus (SIL-uh-bus), rubric (ROO-brik).
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes: When is it due? → Could you tell me when it is due? (the word order changes).
32–50 F Spark (6 min): Match and Speak: syllabus ↔ the course plan with dates and rules; rubric ↔ the scoring guide; office hours ↔ when the instructor meets students; due date ↔ the last day to hand in work; quiz ↔ a short test. Round 1: the teacher plays the instructor with card A1; the student asks for clarification and restates the task and deadline. Round 2: card A2. Round 3 (new detail): the student missed a lecture and asks: I'm sorry I missed Monday's lecture. Could I come to your office hours to ask about it?
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 indirect questions without notes. Set homework.

Mock syllabus page: ShifoLife B1 Medical English · 12-week course. Teacher: Mrs. Karimova. Office hours: Tuesday 2–4 p.m., online, or by email. Lessons: Monday, Wednesday and Friday, 6:00–7:00 p.m. Week 3: read the Vocabulary Book, B1 Week 3; Word quiz 1 on Friday (10 questions, 15 minutes). Assignment 1: a 1-minute recorded patient report; due Friday of Week 5 at 11:59 p.m.; scored with the rubric in My progress. Late work loses 10% per day. Questions to practice: When is Word quiz 1? What do we read for Week 3? When is Assignment 1 due? Where can I find the rubric? When are office hours? Key: Friday of Week 3; the Vocabulary Book, B1 Week 3; Friday of Week 5, 11:59 p.m.; in My progress; Tuesday 2–4 p.m.

Assignment cards: A1 – Doc, B1 Week 10: read the definitions and examples for Lessons 28–29; write one new sentence for each word; check your work with the 4-skill rubric in My progress; due Friday 11:59 p.m., send to your teacher by email. A2 – word quiz on B1 Weeks 9–10 next Tuesday in class; 20 multiple-choice questions; 30 minutes.

Stretch: write the same request as a 3-sentence email. Support: question starters on a card: Could you tell me when…? Do you know where…? Could you explain…? Could I…?

Groups: one student plays the instructor; the others each ask one question.

Homework: record an instructor-help request for card A1.

Lesson 35 · B Practice · Skills lab and simulation
Goal Follow and question skills-lab instructions.
New words (8) clinical placement, simulation, skills lab, mannequin, demonstrate, preceptor, care plan, feedback
Recycle syllabus, due date, read-back
Grammar First conditional: If I don't understand, I'll ask. Requests: Could you show me again? Could you repeat the second step?
Spark Listen and Answer (skills-lab instructions)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S The student asks the teacher 2 questions about card A2. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. A preceptor is the nurse who guides a student on placement. The focus is on vocabulary, not clinical procedures.
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer (below), heard twice. Grammar in 4 minutes: If…, I'll…
30–50 F Round 1: the student explains skills-lab card SL1 (below) to the teacher-instructor. Round 2: the teacher reads the Round 2 instructions (below) too fast; the student asks to repeat a step. Round 3 (new detail): the first day on placement; the student introduces themselves to a preceptor, an upgraded version of the Lesson 1 introduction.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 If…, I'll… + 1 repeat request. Set homework.

Listen and Answer: Today in the skills lab you will practice taking vital signs on the mannequin. First, clean your hands and introduce yourself. Then check the patient's name and date of birth. After that, take the blood pressure and pulse and write the results on the form. I will give feedback at the end. Questions: What will they practice? What do they do first? What two things do they check before measuring? Key: taking vital signs; clean hands and introduce themselves; name and date of birth.

Skills-lab card SL1 (fictional): Skills lab 2 · Vital signs on the mannequin. 1. Clean your hands. 2. Introduce yourself to the patient. 3. Check the patient's name and date of birth. 4. Take the blood pressure and pulse. 5. Write the results on the form. 6. Tell the instructor when you finish; feedback comes at the end.

Round 2 instructions (fictional; teacher reads fast): Now take a temperature on the mannequin. Clean your hands, then check the ID band. Put a new cover on the thermometer, place it under the tongue and wait for the beep. Read the number aloud, write it on the form and throw the cover away. Model repeat requests: Sorry, could you repeat the step after the ID band? / Could you show me again how to put on the cover?

Stretch: add What should I do if…? questions. Support: sequence words on a card.

Groups: one student gives instructions, one follows, one checks the order.

Homework: prepare and record your final introduction (90 seconds); review the words you find hardest.

Lesson 36 · C Perform · Final assessment
Goal Complete five speaking tasks without help.
New words None. Review Weeks 1–12.
Assessment Final. Score with the section 7 rubric; compare with Lessons 1 and 18; decide the certificate and the B2 recommendation.
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Relaxed warm-up: What are you proudest of from this course?
5–8 — Explain the 5 tasks and the rubric. No coaching during tasks. Record everything.
8–14 Task 1 Introduction and nursing goals (90 seconds).
14–24 Task 2 Patient interview with card FA1 (unseen), 3–4 minutes.
24–30 Task 3 1-minute measurement report from chart FA.
30–38 Task 4 Explain label FA, then ask for teach-back; the teacher leaves out one detail.
38–43 Task 5 Instructor-help request about assignment FA.
43–50 Review Play 20 seconds each from Lessons 1, 18 and 36. The student names 3 improvements.
50–60 O Share scores; certificate decision; the student writes a next-step plan: 10 words and 3 speaking goals.

Final cards (fictional; unseen, teacher only):

Card Content
FA1 – Shoira Tursunova, 38 Burning upper abdominal pain for 5 days, after meals, 5/10; nausea, no vomiting; no conditions; antacid tablets when needed; no allergies; father had a stomach ulcer
Chart FA 9 a.m.: BP 124/80, HR 78, RR 16, T 36.9 °C, SpO2 98% · 3 p.m.: BP 132/84, HR 92, RR 18, T 37.8 °C, SpO2 97%
Label FA GASTRONIL 20 mg capsules. Take 1 capsule by mouth once daily, 30 minutes before breakfast.
Assignment FA Read B1 Week 11 in the Vocabulary Book and write one sentence for each of the 8 Lesson 31 words. Due Monday 9 a.m., by email.

Groups: book individual 30-minute slots for Tasks 2–5; run Task 1 as a group presentation.

Final voice note: the Task 1 introduction. The student keeps the Lesson 1 and Lesson 36 introductions and the Lesson 18 report voice note as their progress record.

student.title: Introduction
student.html:
Welcome to B2 Clinical Medical English

In B1 you learned to talk about healthcare. In B2 you will run real patient conversations: full interviews, exact reports, urgent calls, SBAR handoffs and caring, sensitive talk. This book is yours: write in it and bring it to every lesson.

My details
Name
Level B2 Clinical
Teacher
Class days and time
Start date
My B1 final score
My goal for B2

What's new in B2

  • You lead. Every lesson starts with 60 seconds of free speaking, and in the last role-play you get a card you have never seen.
  • Every detail counts. Your teacher corrects these at once: numbers, units, left/right, times and the word not.
  • Report and refer. You collect facts and pass them on. You never diagnose or give medical advice. Learn these by heart:
  • I'll let the nurse know right away.
  • That's a question for your doctor or pharmacist.
  • I'm not able to advise on that, but I'll find someone who can.
  • I'm concerned about this change. Could you come and see the patient?
  • Hot Seat Interpreting. You will interpret longer Uzbek turns into English, in the first person, adding nothing.
  • Homework: 20 minutes a day. After Lesson A: words and listening. After Lesson B: speak and record. After Lesson C: a 90–120 second voice note.

Grammar help: look up any grammar point in the Doc (Part 2 for B2; Part 1 to review). Every unit ends with a short practice and the answers.

Word help: every word in your week tables has an English definition and an example in the Doc (B2 section). Read the definition, then say the example aloud.

All patients, charts and labels in this book are fictional. This course teaches English, not clinical skills.

student.title: Advanced Patient Interviews
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ open an interview and get the chief complaint without leading
  • ☐ take a structured symptom history (OLDCARTS)
  • ☐ interview for 5 minutes and summarize in 60 seconds
Lesson Word Example
1 intake Let's start your intake.
1 verify I need to verify your date of birth.
1 preferred language What is your preferred language?
1 chief complaint Her chief complaint is fatigue.
1 reason for visit What is the reason for your visit?
1 concern What concerns you most?
1 bothersome Which symptom is most bothersome?
1 clarify Can I clarify one thing?
1 leading question Is it sharp? is a leading question.
2 location Where exactly is the pain?
2 character How would you describe the pain?
2 aggravating factor Walking is an aggravating factor.
2 relieving factor Rest is a relieving factor.
2 timing Is it constant, or does it come and go?
2 associated symptoms Any associated symptoms, like nausea?
2 pertinent negative No diarrhea is a pertinent negative.
2 radiate Does the pain radiate anywhere?
3 social history Let's go over your social history.
3 occupation What is your occupation?
3 tobacco Do you use tobacco in any form?
3 alcohol How much alcohol do you drink in a week?

Useful phrases: What brings you in today? · Tell me more about that. · How would you describe it? · How long have you been having this pain? · He reports… He denies…

OLDCARTS: Onset · Location · Duration · Character · Aggravating · Relieving · Timing · Severity.

Voice note: a 60-second history summary, then 3 open questions you would ask next.

Cards and texts · Week 1

Intake script: Hello, I'm Dilnoza, a nursing student. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth? What language would you prefer to use today? What brings you in today? Tell me more about that.

Match and Speak (Lesson 1): make each question open. Do you have pain? · Is it bad? · Did it start today? · Are you worried?

Complaint cards (fictional): K1 – Feruza, 41: I've been really tired and my feet tingle (3 weeks). K2 – Akmal, 29: My stomach has been bad since the weekend (upper abdominal pain and nausea, 3 days).

OLDCARTS grid:

Part What the patient says
Onset
Location
Duration
Character
Aggravating factors
Relieving factors
Timing
Severity (0–10)
Associated symptoms
Pertinent negatives

Observer checks: Lesson 1 – open question first · identity confirmed (name and date of birth) · no leading questions · one-sentence summary. Lesson 2 – all 8 OLDCARTS parts · one pertinent negative asked · timing and severity repeated back · no leading questions. Lesson 3 – 6 history parts covered (chief complaint, symptom details, past history, medicines and allergies, family history, social history) · denies used correctly · numbers right · summary 60 seconds or less.

student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about neurological symptoms and exact timing
  • ☐ describe mental status in neutral words
  • ☐ report a new change with side and time
Lesson Word Example
4 migraine She has had migraines since she was a teenager.
4 fainting Have you had any fainting?
4 seizure He had a seizure last year.
4 slurred speech Her speech is slurred.
4 blurred vision Do you have blurred vision?
4 double vision Any double vision?
4 vertigo The room spins: that's vertigo.
4 sensitivity to light Bright light makes the headache worse.
4 warning sign Sudden weakness is a warning sign.
5 awake He is awake and talking.
5 drowsy She is drowsy but wakes to voice.
5 agitated He is agitated and pulling at his IV.
5 oriented She is oriented to person, place and time.
5 disoriented He is disoriented to time.
5 attention She can't keep her attention on the question.
5 memory How is his memory today?
5 baseline Is this his baseline?
5 responds to He responds to his name.
6 strength His strength is equal on both sides.
6 grip Her left grip is weaker.
6 gait His gait is unsteady.
6 unequal Grip strength is unequal.

Useful phrases: When did you first notice it? · Have you noticed any changes in your vision? · He appears drowsy. · I'm calling about a new change: new weakness in his left hand since 4 p.m.

Remember: never say a diagnosis (stroke). Say what you see and when.

Voice note: a change report with side and both times, then describe a patient's mental status.

Cards and texts · Week 2

Neuro cards (fictional): N1 – Gulchehra, 34: throbbing headache on the left side for 2 days; sensitive to light; nausea; has had similar headaches before. N2 – Bobur, 48: the room spins when he turns his head, for 1 week; no change in hearing.

Neuro follow-up card: Vision: Have you noticed any changes in your vision? · Speech: Have you had any trouble speaking or finding words? · Weakness: Have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs? · Numbness: Do you have any numbness or tingling? Where?

Mental-status card M2 (fictional): Kamila, 25: alert, oriented ×3, anxious, answers all questions.

Says / observe sorting table:

The patient or family says I observe

Change card R1 (fictional): Nodir Saidov, 66, room 14. 2 p.m.: grip equal, speech clear. 4 p.m.: left grip weaker than right; says my left hand feels heavy; gait unsteady; speech clear; alert and oriented ×3.

Observer checks: Lesson 4 – exact onset · neuro follow-ups asked · sudden change escalated at once · no diagnosis named. Lesson 5 – neutral words only · says vs observed kept apart · baseline asked · all three orientation questions. Lesson 6 – side correct · both times given · says vs observed apart · clear request at the end.

student.title: Cardiovascular Conditions and Communication
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about chest symptoms clearly
  • ☐ report blood-pressure readings with position and time
  • ☐ explain an ECG from a card and refer other questions
Lesson Word Example
7 pressure I feel pressure in my chest.
7 tightness My chest feels tight on the stairs.
7 discomfort Any chest discomfort?
7 exertion Does it happen with exertion?
7 at rest Does it happen at rest?
7 spread Does it spread to your arm or jaw?
7 sweating She started sweating.
7 cardiac history Any cardiac history in your family?
7 heart attack His father had a heart attack at 50.
8 systolic Systolic is the top number.
8 diastolic Diastolic is the bottom number.
8 hypotension Hypotension means low blood pressure.
8 orthostatic We'll check orthostatic readings.
8 cuff The cuff will feel tight.
8 lying Lying down: 132 over 80.
8 standing Standing: 104 over 66.
8 lightheaded She feels lightheaded when she stands.
9 electrocardiogram (ECG / EKG) You need an ECG.
9 echocardiogram An echocardiogram is an ultrasound of the heart.
9 electrode Small electrodes are placed on your chest.
9 rhythm The ECG shows the heart's rhythm.

Useful phrases: Does it happen when you walk or when you rest? · The blood pressure was taken at 10:00 lying down. · The doctor will look at the results and explain them to you. · I'm getting the nurse right away.

Voice note: explain the ECG to a patient, then report a lying and standing blood pressure.

Cards and texts · Week 3

Uzbek Bridge (Lesson 7): say each line in English. Ko‘kragimda bosim bor, chap qo‘limga tarqalyapti. · Zinadan chiqqanimda ko‘kragim siqiladi, dam olsam o‘tib ketadi. · Terlab ketdim va ko‘nglim aynidi. · Otam ellik yoshida infarkt bo‘lgan.

Chest cards (fictional): C1 – Rustam, 58: chest tightness walking uphill for 2 weeks; stops with rest. C2 – Madina, 36: heart racing at rest in the evenings for 5 days; 4 cups of coffee a day.

Time-clause card: Does it happen when you walk or when you rest? · Does it go away after you stop? · Does it come on whenever you climb stairs? · Does the discomfort spread anywhere?

Orthostatic chart (fictional): Oydin Nazarova, 70. 10:00 lying: BP 132/80, HR 76. 10:03 standing: BP 104/66, HR 98; says she feels lightheaded.

Test cards (fictional): ECG – about 5–10 minutes; lie still; 10 small stickers (electrodes) on the chest, arms and legs; painless; no preparation; the doctor reviews the results. Echocardiogram – ultrasound of the heart; 30–60 minutes; gel on the chest; you may be asked to turn onto your left side; painless.

Observer checks: Lesson 7 – exertion vs rest · spread asked · urgent case escalated · no diagnosis told to the patient. Lesson 8 – top and bottom numbers in order · position and time for each · she says for symptoms · read-back correct. Lesson 9 – only card facts used · passive used correctly · clinical question referred · calm, reassuring tone.

student.title: Respiratory Conditions and Urgent Communication
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ take a detailed breathing history
  • ☐ report oxygen readings with device and flow, and explain isolation
  • ☐ call for help clearly and calmly
Lesson Word Example
10 trigger What seems to trigger it?
10 allergen Dust is an allergen for her.
10 flare-up She is having an asthma flare-up.
10 congestion I have chest congestion.
10 productive cough A productive cough brings up sputum.
10 dry cough A dry cough brings nothing up.

10 nebulizer He uses a nebulizer at home.
10 peak flow Her peak flow is lower today.

11 oxygen mask He needs an oxygen mask.
11 room air SpO2 is 95% on room air.
11 liters per minute Oxygen at 2 liters per minute.
11 effort Breathing effort has increased.
11 shallow Her breathing is shallow.

Useful phrases: Have you been using your inhaler more than usual? · SpO2 94% on 2 liters via nasal cannula. · This is… in room 6. I need help now. · I'm here with you. Help is coming.

Voice note: an urgent call in 30 seconds, then explain droplet precautions to a visitor.

Cards and texts · Week 4

Match and Speak (Lesson 10): match each patient phrase to a word. Phrases: I'm coughing stuff up · tickly cough, nothing comes up · my chest feels blocked · my asthma attack · my blue inhaler · the cat makes it worse. Words: rescue inhaler · allergen, trigger · dry cough · flare-up · productive cough · congestion.

Breathing cards (fictional): Rb1 – Lola, 22, asthma: flare-up for 3 days; using her rescue inhaler 6 times a day (usually twice a week); trigger: dust at her new job; dry cough at night. teacher.title: Introduction
teacher.html:
1. About this book

This is the teacher's book for B2 Clinical Medical English, the second of three ShifoLife levels (B1 → B2 → C1). It covers 12 weeks, 36 lessons of 60 minutes, three per week. A matching Student Edition holds the timetable, word lists and every card and text students use, without answer keys.

Who it is for: students who completed B1, or scored 18–27 on the placement check (printed in the B1 Teacher Edition, section 3). They can already take a basic history, read vital signs and a medicine label. B2 makes them run full patient conversations, report changes accurately and hand off with SBAR.

What it is not: clinical training. All patients, charts and labels are fictional. Students report and refer; they never diagnose, triage or change treatment.

How to use it: the method is the same as B1: the SHIFO Lesson Cycle, the Learn · Practice · Perform week and the Spark bank. Section 2 lists only what changes at B2.

Grammar companion: B2 grammar is explained in full in the Doc (Part 2, Units 19–27). Review Part 1 with any student who needs it.

Vocabulary companion: every new word in this book has an English definition, a word type and an example sentence in the Doc (B2 section, by week and lesson). Use it for Picture Reveal, Odd One Out and the weekly word review.

Copyright. © 2026 Shifo Life. All rights reserved. ShifoLife Medical English, the SHIFO Lesson Cycle and the Learn · Practice · Perform week are proprietary to Shifo Life. No part of this book may be copied, adapted or used to teach outside Shifo Life without written permission. Version 1.0 (draft for review).

2. The B2 level and what changes from B1

By Week 12 the student can run a 5-minute focused interview without a script, report numbers and changes with no errors, give a 1-minute SBAR, do discharge teach-back, respond to emotional and sensitive situations, and keep reported and observed information apart.

B1 B2
Student talk time 50% rising to 65% 60–70%
New words 8 per A/B lesson, 4 per C 8–9 per A/B lesson, 4 per C; max 22 a week
Start stage (S) Recall 3 words 60 seconds of free speaking on last lesson's topic, then 3 recycled words
Role-play rounds (F) Prompts → fewer prompts → new detail Prompts → no prompts → unseen card led by the student
Teacher's role Models first Models only when the student is stuck; otherwise plays patient, colleague or instructor
Correct at once Numbers, names, side, time, not Same, plus units and anything that changes the clinical meaning
Grammar band Present and past tenses, comparatives, modals Present perfect continuous, passive, reported speech, conditionals, question tags, hedging

The SHIFO timings are the same as in B1: A S 0–6 · H 6–24 · I 24–32 · F 32–50 · O 50–60. B S 0–6 · H 6–16 · I 16–30 · F 30–50 · O 50–60. C S 0–5 · H 5–12 · I 12–20 · F 20–50 · O 50–60.

New Spark for B2: Hot Seat Interpreting. The teacher speaks as an Uzbek patient in turns of 2–3 sentences. The student interprets each full turn into English, in the first person, without notes. Then reverse it with an English-speaking clinician. Score accuracy, completeness and no added words. Eight B1 Sparks appear in the lessons; use the ninth, Odd One Out, for the weekly word review.

Report and refer: phrases students use every week.

  • I'll let the nurse know right away.
  • That's a question for your doctor or pharmacist.
  • I'm not able to advise on that, but I'll find someone who can.
  • I'm concerned about this change. Could you come and see the patient?

SBAR frame (every handoff and urgent call):

  • S – Situation: who you are, where you are, the patient's name and the change now. This is Dilnoza, a nursing student in bay 3. I'm calling about Mrs. Qodirova. She is more drowsy.
  • B – Background: the key facts from the card: age, why the patient is here, what happened and when, important medicines.
  • A – Assessment: what you observed or measured, with values, units and times, and what has changed. No diagnosis.
  • R – Request: what you need, using the supplied request. Could you come and assess her now? Then close the loop: repeat back the reply.

Groups: keep B2 groups to 2–4 students. Each role-play has a third role, the observer, who fills a 4-point checklist printed on each lesson card.

3. B2 timetable: 36 lessons at a glance

Three lessons a week on fixed days with a day between them. Never move Lesson C before Lesson B.

# Wk Type Lesson Goal: the student can… Grammar (B2) Spark
1 1 A Intake and the chief complaint open an interview, confirm identity and language, and get the chief complaint without leading Open vs closed questions; Tell me more about… Match and Speak
2 1 B Detailed symptom history take a structured symptom history Present perfect continuous: How long have you been having…? Listen and Answer
3 1 C History review and summary run a 5-minute interview and give a 60-second summary Reporting verbs: reports, denies, states Mystery Patient
4 2 A Headache and neurological symptoms ask about neurological symptoms and timing When did you first notice…? past vs present perfect Picture Reveal
5 2 B Mental status and orientation describe mental status in neutral words appears, seems, is oriented to Error Hunt
6 2 C Reporting neurological changes report side, time and change without diagnosing Noun phrases: new left-sided weakness 60-Second Report
7 3 A Chest symptoms and cardiac history ask about chest symptoms clearly Time clauses: when, whenever, after; Does it spread? Uzbek Bridge
8 3 B Blood pressure and circulation report supplied cardiovascular readings Passive: was taken, was recorded Number Catch
9 3 C Cardiac tests explain test names from a card and refer other questions Present passive for procedures Listen and Answer
10 4 A Breathing history take a detailed breathing history Present perfect continuous; triggers Match and Speak
11 4 B Oxygen, observations and isolation report breathing observations and explain isolation on 2 L via nasal cannula; on room air Number Catch
12 4 C Urgent respiratory communication call for help clearly and calmly Short urgent sentences 60-Second Report
13 5 A Diabetes: words and symptoms ask about diabetes history and symptoms First conditional: If your sugar is low, you may feel… Uzbek Bridge
14 5 B Glucose monitoring and numbers report glucose values and times with no errors Trends: has been trending up Number Catch

26 9 B Label instructions and clarification spot unclear label wording and ask for clarification Reported instructions: The label says to… Number Catch
27 9 C Side effects and safe referral answer medicine questions safely by referring should for referral; I'm not able to advise… Uzbek Bridge
28 10 A Emotions and supportive language respond with empathy and open questions That must be… Match and Speak
29 10 B Sensitive conversations ask permission and respect preferences Would you prefer…? Would you mind if…? Listen and Answer
30 10 C Reporting mental-health concerns report quotes and observations neutrally Direct quotes; stated Error Hunt
31 11 A Subjective and objective separate reported from measured facts reports, denies, appears Match and Speak
32 11 B Professional SBAR give an organized 1-minute SBAR Compact noun phrases Error Hunt
33 11 C Phone calls and messages pass accurate information by phone Spelling; Could you read that back? Number Catch

35 12 B Integrated patient simulation complete a multi-step patient simulation Sequencing review Mystery Patient
36 12 C Final assessment complete five tasks without help Review Assessment

4. Assessment: Lessons 1, 18 and 36

The four skills are the same as in B1, scored 0–3, but the bar is higher. A student moves to C1 with 10 or more out of 12 at Lesson 36 and no skill below 2.

Skill 1 2 3 (B2 standard)
Vocabulary use Uses B2 words only when prompted Uses most B2 words correctly Chooses the precise term and the plain-English version for each listener
Clear speech Understood with effort Clear; stress sometimes off on long words Clear at natural speed; stresses key facts in a report
Listening and clarifying Gets the main point only Gets details; usually checks Catches every detail, checks numbers, and summarizes back
Accurate details Several errors in numbers, units, side or time One error, self-corrected No errors; keeps reported and observed facts apart

Score 0 when the skill is not yet shown.

When Tasks Recording kept
Lesson 1 (baseline) 3-minute intake interview with unseen card K3 (Lesson 1, Round 3); compare with the student's B1 final score or placement result Interview
Lesson 18 (midpoint) 5-minute focused interview (unseen card); fluid-balance and vital-sign report; 1-minute SBAR All three
Lesson 36 (final) Five tasks: advanced interview; measurement report; SBAR; discharge teach-back; instructor question All five, compared with Lessons 1 and 18

Every lesson: note 5 target words and 1 speaking goal in the student's book. Every Lesson C: one voice note of 90–120 seconds.

Completion: attend at least 32 of 36 lessons and reach the score above for the ShifoLife B2 Clinical Medical English certificate of completion. It is a course certificate, not a CEFR or clinical qualification.

teacher.title: Advanced Patient Interviews
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can open an interview professionally, take a structured symptom history, and summarize a full history in 60 seconds.

Prepare: complaint cards K1–K3; the OLDCARTS grid (Student Edition, Week 1 cards); pain card PC1 and history card H1 (below).

Lesson 1 · A Learn · Intake and the chief complaint
Goal Open an interview, confirm identity and language, and get the chief complaint without leading.
New words (9) intake, verify, preferred language, chief complaint, reason for visit, concern, bothersome, clarify, leading question
Recycle (B1) appointment, date of birth, interpreter
Grammar Open vs closed questions; Tell me more about… How would you describe…?
Spark Match and Speak (closed → open)
Assessment Baseline: record the Round 3 interview.
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds of free speaking: What changed for you during B1? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Leading: Is it a sharp pain? Open: How would you describe the pain? Model the intake script below.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark (4 min): Match and Speak; the student turns closed questions into open ones.
32–50 F Round 1: card K1 with the script in view. Round 2: card K2 without notes; the student sums up the chief complaint in one sentence. Round 3 (unseen): card K3, the patient prefers Uzbek. The student offers a professional interpreter; while waiting for the interpreter, the student practices interpreting her first line (practice only). When the interpreter (the teacher) arrives, the student runs a 3-minute intake interview through them. Record it.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 open questions + 1 one-sentence summary. Set homework.

Intake script: Hello, I'm Dilnoza, a nursing student. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth? What language would you prefer to use today? What brings you in today? Tell me more about that.

Match and Speak: Do you have pain? → Tell me about any pain you've had. · Is it bad? → How would you describe it? · Did it start today? → When did it start? · Are you worried? → What concerns you most?

Complaint cards (fictional): K1 – Feruza, 41: I've been really tired and my feet tingle (3 weeks). K2 – Akmal, 29: My stomach has been bad since the weekend (upper abdominal pain and nausea, 3 days). K3 (unseen) – Hafiza, 67, prefers Uzbek: Oyog‘larim shishib ketyapti (→ My legs are swelling).

Observer checks: open question first · identity confirmed (name and date of birth) · no leading questions · one-sentence summary.

Stretch: add What do you think is causing it? Support: script card stays in view in Round 2.

Homework: record a 90-second interview opening with card K2.

Lesson 2 · B Practice · Detailed symptom history
Goal Take a structured symptom history.
New words (8) location, character, aggravating factor, relieving factor, timing, associated symptoms, pertinent negative, radiate
Recycle chief complaint, onset, duration
Grammar Present perfect continuous for ongoing (How long have you been having this pain?); present perfect simple for counts (How many times have you vomited?)
Spark Listen and Answer (fill the OLDCARTS grid)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the student gives the K2 chief complaint from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words with the OLDCARTS grid: Onset, Location, Duration, Character, Aggravating, Relieving, Timing, Severity. Pertinent negative = an important no (no diarrhea).
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer; the teacher reads the narrative twice, the student fills the grid. Grammar in 4 minutes.
30–50 F Round 1: interview with the grid in view. Round 2: the teacher changes details mid-interview; the student repeats back exact timing and severity. Round 3 (unseen): pain card PC1 (below); the student leads with no grid.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 3 OLDCARTS questions in natural English. Set homework.

Narrative (teacher reads): It started on Sunday night, suddenly, in the middle of my stomach. Now it's moved to the lower right side. It's a sharp, constant pain, about seven out of ten. Walking makes it worse; lying still helps a little. I've also felt sick and I haven't wanted to eat. No diarrhea.

Grid key: Onset – Sunday night, sudden · Location – center, now lower right · Duration – since Sunday · Character – sharp · Aggravating – walking · Relieving – lying still · Timing – constant · Severity – 7/10 · Associated – nausea, poor appetite · Pertinent negative – no diarrhea.

Pain card PC1 (unseen, fictional): Jasur Tojiyev, 45, painter. Pain in his right shoulder for 5 days; it started the day after he painted a ceiling; aching, 5/10; worse when he lifts his arm above his head or lies on that side; rest and a warm shower help a little; worse at night; it does not spread; no numbness or weakness in the arm. Grid key: Onset – 5 days ago, after painting a ceiling · Location – right shoulder · Duration – 5 days · Character – aching · Aggravating – lifting the arm overhead, lying on it · Relieving – rest, warm shower · Timing – worse at night · Severity – 5/10 · Pertinent negatives – does not spread; no numbness or weakness.

Observer checks: all 8 OLDCARTS parts · one pertinent negative asked · timing and severity repeated back · no leading questions.

Stretch: ask Have you had anything like this before? Support: grid in view in Round 2.

Homework: write 6 follow-up questions and record them.

Lesson 3 · C Perform · History review and summary
Goal Run a 5-minute interview and give a 60-second summary.
New words (4) social history, occupation, tobacco, alcohol
Recycle pertinent negative, aggravating factor, chief complaint
Grammar Reporting verbs for summaries: He reports… He denies… He states that…
Spark Mystery Patient
Perform task Recorded 5-minute interview and 60-second summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: the student explains OLDCARTS to an imaginary new classmate.
5–12 H 4 new words. Respectful wording: Do you use tobacco in any form? How much alcohol do you drink in a week?
12–20 I Model summary (below). Focus on denies for pertinent negatives.
20–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient; card H1 is hidden and the student has 5 minutes to cover all 6 history parts (chief complaint, symptom details, past history, medicines and allergies, family history, social history). Round 2: the student plays H1 and the teacher interviews, making 2 errors; the student spots them. Then the performance: record the interview and the 60-second summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

History card H1 (hidden, fictional): Davron Ergashev, 55, taxi driver. Cough for 3 weeks, worse at night. Smokes 15 cigarettes a day for 30 years; no alcohol. History: hypertension; one blood-pressure tablet daily; no allergies. Father had lung problems. Lives with his wife and two sons. Denies fever and weight loss.

Model summary: Mr. Ergashev is a 55-year-old taxi driver with a history of hypertension. He reports a cough for three weeks, worse at night. He has smoked about 15 cigarettes a day for 30 years. He denies fever and weight loss. He takes one blood-pressure tablet daily and has no allergies.

Observer checks: 6 history parts covered · denies used correctly · numbers right · summary 60 seconds or less.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the H1 summary, then 3 open questions you would ask next.

teacher.title: Neurological Assessment and Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about neurological symptoms with exact timing, describe mental status in neutral words, and report a new neurological change.

Prepare: 4 pictures (person holding their head, someone shielding eyes from light, someone fainting, blurred text); neuro cards N1–N3; mental-status cards M1–M2; change cards R1–R2.

Never name a diagnosis. Students say new weakness in the left arm, never stroke. The clinician decides.

Lesson 4 · A Learn · Headache and neurological symptoms
Goal Ask about neurological symptoms and timing.
New words (9) migraine, fainting, seizure, slurred speech, blurred vision, double vision, vertigo, sensitivity to light, warning sign
Recycle onset, radiate, associated symptoms
Grammar When did you first notice…? (past simple for a moment) vs Have you noticed any changes in…? (present perfect up to now)
Spark Picture Reveal
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the H1 summary from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Bridge: I passed out → fainting; my words came out wrong → slurred speech; the room is spinning → vertigo.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Model 4 neuro follow-ups: vision, speech, weakness, numbness.
32–50 F Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal. Round 1: card N1 with OLDCARTS and neuro follow-ups. Round 2: card N2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): card N3, a sudden change; the student says I'm going to get the nurse right away and does not continue the interview.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 When did you first notice…? + 1 Have you noticed…? Set homework.

Neuro cards (fictional): N1 – Gulchehra, 34: throbbing headache on the left side for 2 days; sensitive to light; nausea; has had similar headaches before. N2 – Bobur, 48: the room spins when he turns his head, for 1 week; no change in hearing. N3 (unseen) – Sharofat, 72: sudden slurred speech and weakness in her right arm, starting 20 minutes ago.

Observer checks: exact onset · neuro follow-ups asked · sudden change escalated at once · no diagnosis named.

Stretch: recognize the phrase the worst headache of my life: a patient who says it is escalated at once. Support: the neuro follow-up card (Student Edition, Week 2 cards).

Homework: record 5 neuro questions and their N1 answers.

Lesson 5 · B Practice · Mental status and orientation
Goal Describe mental status in neutral words.
New words (9) awake, drowsy, agitated, oriented, disoriented, attention, memory, baseline, responds to
Recycle confused, alert, fainting
Grammar He appears drowsy. She seems anxious. He is oriented to person and place, not time. She is able / unable to…
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe card N3 and what you did. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Oriented ×3 = knows person, place and time. Baseline = what is normal for this patient. Words to avoid: crazy, senile, demented.
16–30 I Listening: the teacher reads card M1 aloud; the student sorts facts into the patient says and I observe. Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student asks orientation questions to teacher-patient M1 and describes him. Round 2: M2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): a family member says He's not himself today; the student asks how he usually is (baseline).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: describe M1 in 2 neutral sentences. Set homework.

Mental-status cards (fictional): M1 – Tulkin Rahimov, 80: drowsy but wakes when spoken to; knows his name only; says I'm at home (he is in hospital). His daughter says he is usually fully oriented. M2 – Kamila, 25: alert, oriented ×3, anxious, answers all questions.

Error Hunt: Mr. Rahimov is alert and oriented to person and place. His daughter says this is his baseline. Key: drowsy, not alert; oriented to person only; his daughter says this is not his baseline.

Observer checks: neutral words only · says vs observed kept apart · baseline asked · all three orientation questions.

Stretch: add How is his memory compared with last week? Support: the says / observe sorting table (Student Edition, Week 2 cards).

Homework: describe 2 mental-status cards in writing, then read them aloud.

Lesson 6 · C Perform · Reporting neurological changes
Goal Report side, time and change without diagnosing.
New words (4) strength, grip, gait, unequal
Recycle baseline, drowsy, slurred speech
Grammar Compact noun phrases: new left-sided weakness; unequal grip strength; unsteady gait since 4 p.m.
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded 45-second change report for card R1
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: describe card M1 in neutral words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Practice left/right at speed: the teacher points, the student says left grip, right grip.
12–20 I Model the report below. Grammar: long sentence → noun phrase.
20–50 F Spark: 60-Second Report on R1. Round 1: report with the model in view. Round 2: no notes; the teacher interrupts: Which side? What time? Round 3 (unseen): card R2 (below), a change in speech, not strength. Then the performance: record the R1 report.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Change card R1 (fictional): Nodir Saidov, 66, room 14. 2 p.m.: grip equal, speech clear. 4 p.m.: left grip weaker than right; says my left hand feels heavy; gait unsteady; speech clear; alert and oriented ×3.

Model report: I'm calling about Mr. Saidov in room 14. Since 4 p.m. he has had new weakness in his left hand: his left grip is weaker than his right. At 2 p.m. his grip was equal. He says his left hand feels heavy, and his gait is unsteady. He is alert and oriented, and his speech is clear. I'm concerned about this new change. Could you come and see him now?

Change card R2 (unseen, fictional): Saida Normatova, 70, room 8. 9 a.m.: speech clear; grip equal; alert and oriented ×3. 11 a.m.: speech slurred; her daughter says She sounds different; grip equal; coughs when she drinks water; alert; oriented to person and place, not time. Model report: I'm calling about Mrs. Normatova in room 8. Since 11 a.m. her speech has been slurred. At 9 a.m. it was clear. Her daughter says she sounds different. Her grip is equal. She coughs when she drinks water. She is alert and oriented to person and place, but not time. I'm concerned about this new change. Could you come and see her now?

Observer checks: side correct · both times given · says vs observed apart · clear request at the end.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the R1 report, then describe card M1.

teacher.title: Cardiovascular Conditions and Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about chest symptoms clearly, report blood-pressure readings with position and time, and explain a cardiac test from a card.

Prepare: chest cards C1–C3; orthostatic chart and chart BP2 (below); ECG and echocardiogram test cards (below).

Lesson 7 · A Learn · Chest symptoms and cardiac history
Goal Ask about chest symptoms clearly.
New words (9) pressure, tightness, discomfort, exertion, at rest, spread, sweating, cardiac history, heart attack
Recycle palpitations, radiate, swelling
Grammar Time clauses: Does it happen when you walk or when you rest? Does it go away after you stop? Does the discomfort spread anywhere?
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the R1 report from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Many patients say discomfort or pressure, not pain: ask about all three.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
32–50 F Round 1: card C1; the student asks exertion vs rest, spread, associated symptoms. Round 2: C2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): C3, pressure right now; the student stops and says I'm getting the nurse right away. Please stay in bed.
