50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 time-clause questions. Set homework.

Uzbek Bridge:

Uzbek Model English
Ko‘kragimda bosim bor, chap qo‘limga tarqalyapti. I feel pressure in my chest, and it spreads to my left arm.
Zinadan chiqqanimda ko‘kragim siqiladi, dam olsam o‘tib ketadi. My chest gets tight when I climb stairs, and it goes away when I rest.
Terlab ketdim va ko‘nglim aynidi. I started sweating and felt sick.
Otam ellik yoshida infarkt bo‘lgan. My father had a heart attack at fifty.

Chest cards (fictional): C1 – Rustam, 58: chest tightness walking uphill for 2 weeks; stops with rest. C2 – Madina, 36: heart racing at rest in the evenings for 5 days; 4 cups of coffee a day. C3 (unseen) – Hamid, 63: chest pressure for 15 minutes, spreading to his jaw, sweating, now.

Observer checks: exertion vs rest · spread asked · urgent case escalated · no diagnosis told to the patient.

Stretch: ask about family cardiac history with ages. Support: time-clause card (Student Edition, Week 3 cards).

Homework: record 8 chest-symptom questions.

Lesson 8 · B Practice · Blood pressure and circulation
Goal Report supplied cardiovascular readings with position and time.
New words (8) systolic, diastolic, hypotension, orthostatic, cuff, lying, standing, lightheaded
Recycle hypertension, pulse, baseline
Grammar Passive: The blood pressure was taken at 10:00 lying down and was recorded again at 10:03 standing.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe chest card C1. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Systolic = the top number; diastolic = the bottom number. Spark: Number Catch: 118/76 · 180/76 · 90/60 · 160/100 · 104/66.
16–30 I Model the report below. Grammar in 4 minutes: active → passive in reports.
30–50 F Round 1: report the orthostatic chart. Round 2: the teacher asks for exact values, position and time. Round 3 (unseen): chart BP2 (below); the student reports with no model.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 readings with position and time. Set homework.

Orthostatic chart (fictional): Oydin Nazarova, 70. 10:00 lying: BP 132/80, HR 76. 10:03 standing: BP 104/66, HR 98; says she feels lightheaded.

Model report: Mrs. Nazarova's blood pressure was taken at 10:00 lying down: 132 over 80, heart rate 76. At 10:03, standing, it was 104 over 66 and her heart rate was 98. She says she feels lightheaded when she stands.

Chart BP2 (unseen, fictional): Bekzod Hamroyev, 66. 14:00 lying: BP 128/78, HR 72. 14:03 standing: BP 100/62, HR 94; says I feel dizzy. I need to sit down. Model report: Mr. Hamroyev's blood pressure was taken at 14:00 lying down: 128 over 78, heart rate 72. At 14:03, standing, it was 100 over 62 and his heart rate was 94. His systolic pressure dropped from 128 to 100. He says he feels dizzy and needs to sit down.

Observer checks: top and bottom numbers in order · position and time for each · she says for symptoms · read-back correct.

Stretch: describe the change in one sentence with dropped from… to…. Support: chart in view.

Homework: record the orthostatic report.

Lesson 9 · C Perform · Cardiac tests
Goal Explain test names from a card and refer other questions.
New words (4) electrocardiogram (ECG / EKG), echocardiogram, electrode, rhythm
Recycle systolic, exertion, discomfort
Grammar Present passive for procedures: Small stickers called electrodes are placed on your chest. The doctor will explain the results.
Spark Listen and Answer
Perform task Recorded ECG explanation with one referral
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: the orthostatic report from memory.
5–12 H 4 new words. US hospitals often say EKG; both are correct.
12–20 I Spark: Listen and Answer: the teacher reads the echocardiogram card. Questions: What is it? How long does it take? What is put on the chest? Key: an ultrasound of the heart; 30–60 minutes; gel.
20–50 F Round 1: the student explains the ECG card to a nervous teacher-patient. Round 2: the echocardiogram card. Round 3: the patient asks Is my heart damaged?; the student refers: The doctor will look at the results and explain them to you. Then the performance: record Round 1 with the referral.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Test cards (fictional): ECG – about 5–10 minutes; lie still; 10 small stickers (electrodes) on the chest, arms and legs; painless; no preparation; the doctor reviews the results. Echocardiogram – ultrasound of the heart; 30–60 minutes; gel on the chest; you may be asked to turn onto your left side; painless.

Observer checks: only card facts used · passive used correctly · clinical question referred · calm, reassuring tone.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): explain the ECG to a patient, then report the orthostatic chart.

teacher.title: Respiratory Conditions and Urgent Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can take a detailed breathing history, report oxygen observations with device and flow, explain isolation precautions, and call for help clearly in an emergency.

Prepare: breathing cards Rb1–Rb3; observation card O1; pictures of a nasal cannula, an oxygen mask and an N95 respirator; door sign IS1 (below); urgent cards U1–U2.

Lesson 10 · A Learn · Breathing history
Goal Take a detailed breathing history.
New words (9) trigger, allergen, flare-up, congestion, productive cough, dry cough, rescue inhaler, nebulizer, peak flow
Recycle wheezing, sputum, shortness of breath
Grammar Present perfect continuous: Have you been using your inhaler more than usual? What seems to trigger it?
Spark Match and Speak (everyday ↔ clinical)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: explain the ECG card. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Productive = brings up sputum; dry = nothing comes up.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark (4 min): Match and Speak (below).
32–50 F Round 1: card Rb1. Round 2: card Rb2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): Rb3, a parent speaking for a child; the student asks the parent, not the child.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 trigger questions. Set homework.

Match and Speak: I'm coughing stuff up ↔ productive cough · tickly cough, nothing comes up ↔ dry cough · my chest feels blocked ↔ congestion · my asthma attack ↔ flare-up · my blue inhaler ↔ rescue inhaler · the cat makes it worse ↔ allergen, trigger.

Breathing cards (fictional): Rb1 – Lola, 22, asthma: flare-up for 3 days; using her rescue inhaler 6 times a day (usually twice a week); trigger: dust at her new job; dry cough at night. Rb2 – Sobir, 61, smoker: productive cough with yellow sputum for 1 week; short of breath after one flight of stairs. Rb3 (unseen) – a mother: My son is 6. He's breathing fast and wheezing since this morning.

Observer checks: frequency of inhaler use asked · trigger asked · sputum described · proxy handled correctly.

Stretch: compare usual vs now: How often do you usually need it? Support: Match and Speak card in view.

Homework: record a full breathing interview with Rb2.

Lesson 11 · B Practice · Oxygen, observations and isolation
Goal Report breathing observations precisely and explain isolation precautions.
New words (9) nasal cannula, oxygen mask, room air, liters per minute, effort, shallow, droplet precautions, airborne precautions, N95 respirator
Recycle oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, isolation
Grammar Prepositions in reports: SpO2 94% on 2 liters per minute via nasal cannula; 90% on room air.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe Lola's flare-up. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words with pictures. Spark: Number Catch: SpO2 89 / 98 · 2 L / 12 L · RR 28 / 18 · 4 L/min.
16–30 I Model reading card O1. Grammar in 4 minutes: on and via.
30–50 F Round 1: the student reads O1 and confirms every number and device. Round 2: the student reports the change from 8 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. Round 3: the student explains door sign IS1 to a patient and a visitor (the teacher plays both).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 oxygen reading with device and flow. Set homework.

Observation card O1 (fictional): Komil, 68. 8 a.m.: SpO2 95% on room air, RR 18. 12 p.m.: SpO2 90% on room air, RR 26, shallow breathing. 12:15 p.m.: SpO2 94% on 2 L/min via nasal cannula (as ordered).

Door sign IS1 (fictional): DROPLET PRECAUTIONS · Everyone entering: wear a surgical mask · Clean your hands before you go in and when you leave · Patient: wear a mask if you leave the room · Visitors: please ask the nurse before entering.

Isolation model: Your door sign says droplet precautions. That means everyone who comes in wears a mask, and we may ask visitors to keep their distance. Please wear a mask if you leave the room.

Observer checks: device and flow named · room air used correctly · each time given · isolation explained from the sign only.

Stretch: explain the difference between droplet and airborne precautions in plain English. Support: the oxygen report frame (Student Edition, Week 4 cards).

Homework: record 5 observation sentences.

Lesson 12 · C Perform · Urgent respiratory communication
Goal Call for help clearly and calmly.
New words (4) distress, deteriorating, rapid response, reassess
Recycle shallow, room air, nasal cannula
Grammar Short urgent sentences: I need help in room 6 now. Calm imperatives to the patient: Stay sitting up. Breathe slowly with me.
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded 30-second urgent call plus words of reassurance to the patient
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: report card O1.
5–12 H 4 new words. A rapid response team is called by hospital protocol; students learn the words to call for help.
12–20 I Model the urgent call and the reassurance (below). Spark: 60-Second Report on U1.
20–50 F Round 1: the call with the model in view. Round 2: no notes, 30 seconds. Round 3 (unseen): urgent card U2 (below); the student calls for help first, then reassures. Then the performance: record the U1 call and reassurance.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Urgent card U1 (fictional): Nilufar Yusupova, 59, room 6, 3:10 p.m. Sudden difficulty breathing; says I can't breathe; RR 32; SpO2 86% on 2 L nasal cannula (94% at 2 p.m.); sitting upright; frightened.

Model call: This is Dilnoza in room 6. I need help now. Mrs. Yusupova has sudden difficulty breathing. Her oxygen saturation is 86 percent on 2 liters; at 2 p.m. it was 94. Her respiratory rate is 32. Please come now. To the patient: I'm here with you. Help is coming. Stay sitting up and breathe slowly with me.

Urgent card U2 (unseen, fictional): Erkin Sobirov, 72, room 11, 6:40 a.m. Breathing fast and noisy; says I can't get my breath; RR 30; SpO2 88% on room air (96% at 4 a.m.); lips look pale; sitting on the edge of the bed; very anxious. Model call: This is Dilnoza in room 11. I need help now. Mr. Sobirov has sudden difficulty breathing. His oxygen saturation is 88 percent on room air; at 4 a.m. it was 96. His respiratory rate is 30. Please come now. To the patient: I'm here with you. Help is coming. Stay sitting up and breathe slowly with me.

Observer checks: location first · facts in under 30 seconds · old and new value given · calm words to the patient.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the U1 call, then the droplet-precautions explanation.

teacher.title: Diabetes and Endocrine
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about diabetes symptoms and routines, report glucose values with the right unit and time, and summarize endocrine symptoms without diagnosing.

Why this week matters: diabetes is common among Uzbek patients. Spend extra care on numbers and units.

Prepare: diabetes cards D1–D3; glucose log G1; thyroid cards Th1–Th2.

Lesson 13 · A Learn · Diabetes: words and symptoms
Goal Ask about diabetes history and symptoms.
New words (9) glucose, blood sugar, insulin, hypoglycemia (low sugar), hyperglycemia (high sugar), type 1, type 2, thirsty, shaky
Recycle diabetes, pancreas, sweating
Grammar First conditional: If your sugar is low, you may feel shaky and sweaty. Have you checked your blood sugar today?
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the U1 urgent call from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Sounds: hypo-gly-CEE-mia, hyper-gly-CEE-mia. Low sugar: shaky, sweaty, hungry, confused. High sugar: thirsty, urinating often, tired, blurred vision.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
32–50 F Round 1: card D1. Round 2: card D2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): D3, a daughter reports confusion; the student escalates at once.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 If…, you may… + 1 routine question. Set homework.

Uzbek Bridge:

Uzbek Model English
Qandim tushib ketganda qo‘llarim titraydi. When my sugar drops, my hands shake.
Doim chanqayman, kechasi ko‘p marta hojatxonaga turaman. I'm always thirsty, and I get up many times at night to urinate.
Bugun ertalab insulin qilmadim. I didn't take my insulin this morning.
Qandimni o‘lchasam, 250 chiqdi. When I checked my sugar, it was 250.

Diabetes cards (fictional): D1 – Shahlo, 45, type 1: shaky, sweaty and hungry one hour after insulin; skipped lunch. D2 – Farhod, 52, type 2: very thirsty, urinating often, tired for 2 weeks, blurred vision; sugar 280 mg/dL yesterday. D3 (unseen) – Zuhra, 70, type 2: her daughter says she has been confused and sweaty for 20 minutes.

Observer checks: last meal and last insulin asked · numbers with units · confusion escalated · no advice given.

Stretch: ask about routines: meals, activity, checking times. Support: low / high symptom card (Student Edition, Week 5 cards).

Homework: record a 1-minute diabetes interview with card D2.

Lesson 14 · B Practice · Glucose monitoring and numbers
Goal Report glucose values and times with no errors.
New words (8) fingerstick, continuous glucose monitor (CGM), mg/dL, mmol/L, fasting glucose, before meals, after meals, trend
Recycle hypoglycemia, insulin, glucose
Grammar Trends: His bedtime readings have been trending up. It has stayed between 110 and 130. It dropped to 58.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe card D2. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Unit alert: US charts use mg/dL (e.g. 130); Uzbekistan and many countries use mmol/L (e.g. 7.2). Never convert in your head for a report: say the unit given and check it. Spark: Number Catch: 70 / 17 · 58 / 85 · 115 / 150 · 13 / 30 · 6.1 mmol/L.
16–30 I Model reading log G1 and the trend sentence. Grammar in 4 minutes.
30–50 F Round 1: the student reads G1 aloud and confirms each value. Round 2: the student reports the trend. Round 3 (new detail): the patient says My sugar was 4 this morning; the student checks the unit: Was that 4 millimoles per liter? That's low, so I'll tell the nurse now.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 trend sentence with values and unit. Set homework.

Glucose log G1 (fictional, mg/dL):

Day Fasting Before lunch Before dinner Bedtime
Mon 112 145 160 180
Tue 118 150 172 196
Wed 125 158 190 210

Model trend: His readings have been trending up. His bedtime glucose went from 180 on Monday to 210 on Wednesday, and his fasting glucose from 112 to 125.

Observer checks: every value read back · unit said · time of day given · trend direction correct.

Stretch: describe the range: Before-lunch readings stayed between 145 and 158. Support: the log in view.

Homework: read 10 log entries aloud and record them.

Lesson 15 · C Perform · Thyroid and endocrine
Goal Discuss endocrine words without diagnosing.
New words (4) thyroid, hormone, cold / heat intolerance, unexplained weight change
Recycle fatigue, trend, palpitations
Grammar Hedged, neutral summaries: She reports… This may need follow-up. The doctor has ordered…
Spark Match and Speak
Perform task Recorded interview with card Th1 and a 45-second neutral summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: report the G1 trend.
5–12 H 4 new words. The thyroid is in the neck and makes hormones.
12–20 I Spark: Match and Speak: I'm always cold ↔ cold intolerance · I put on weight without eating more ↔ unexplained weight gain · my neck looks bigger ↔ neck swelling · I'm hot and shaky all the time ↔ heat intolerance, tremor.
20–50 F Round 1: interview with Th1. Round 2: the student plays Th1, the teacher interviews and suggests a diagnosis; the student notices and rephrases neutrally. Round 3 (unseen): card Th2 (below), the opposite pattern (heat intolerance). Then the performance: record the Th1 interview and summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Thyroid card Th1 (fictional): Gulnoza Tursunova, 39. Cold all the time and tired for about 3 months; gained 5 kg without changing her diet; dry skin; no medicines. The doctor has ordered a blood test.

Model summary: Ms. Tursunova is 39. She reports feeling cold and tired for about three months. She has gained 5 kilograms in that time without changing her diet, and her skin is dry. She takes no medicines. The doctor has ordered a blood test.

Thyroid card Th2 (unseen, fictional): Zarina Abdullayeva, 31. Feels hot and sweaty all the time for about 2 months; heart racing at rest; hands shake; lost 4 kg without trying; sleeping badly. No medicines. The doctor has ordered a blood test. Model summary: Ms. Abdullayeva is 31. She reports feeling hot and sweaty for about two months. She says her heart races at rest and her hands shake. She has lost 4 kilograms without trying, and she is sleeping badly. She takes no medicines. The doctor has ordered a blood test.

Observer checks: no diagnosis named · duration given · weight with unit · the doctor's plan reported, not invented.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the G1 trend report, then the Th1 summary.

teacher.title: GI and Renal · Midpoint
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask detailed abdominal questions respectfully, read and total an intake-and-output chart, and complete the midpoint tasks.

Prepare: 4 pictures (abdomen in four quadrants, yellow eyes illustration, someone holding the upper abdomen after a meal, antacid tablets); GI cards GI1–GI3; I&O charts F1–F2; midpoint card MP-K (below); the student's Lesson 1 recording.

Lesson 16 · A Learn · Abdominal symptoms
Goal Ask detailed GI questions respectfully.
New words (9) cramping, tenderness, heartburn, indigestion, reflux, change in bowel habit, black stools, jaundice, quadrant
Recycle bloating, nausea, constipation
Grammar Where exactly is the pain? Can you point to where it hurts most? Degree: slightly, quite, very, extremely
Spark Picture Reveal
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the Th1 summary. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words with the quadrant diagram: right/left, upper/lower. Jaundice = yellow skin or eyes. Bridge: a burning feeling going up → heartburn, reflux.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark (4 min): Picture Reveal.
32–50 F Round 1: card GI1 with OLDCARTS. Round 2: card GI2, no notes, with the respectful opener: I need to ask a few personal questions. Is that OK? Round 3 (unseen): GI3, black stools and dizziness; the student escalates.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 Where exactly…? + 1 degree adverb. Set homework.

GI cards (fictional): GI1 – Anvar, 44: burning upper abdominal pain after spicy food and at night for 3 weeks; sour taste; worse lying flat. GI2 – Sevara, 30: lower abdominal cramping; diarrhea 4 times a day for 3 days; mild fever. GI3 (unseen) – Rahim, 66: black stools for 2 days; feels dizzy when standing.

Observer checks: quadrant identified · degree words used · bowel questions respectful · black stools escalated.

Stretch: ask What have you tried for it? Did it help? Support: the quadrant diagram.

Homework: record a 90-second GI history with card GI1.

Lesson 17 · B Practice · Fluid balance
Goal Read and report intake and output.
New words (8) intake and output (I&O), fluid balance, oral intake, IV fluids, urine output, positive balance, negative balance, measured
Recycle dehydration, milliliter, swelling
Grammar A total of 1,950 mL was recorded. Intake was… and output was… over 12 hours.
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe card GI2. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Positive balance = more in than out. Read large numbers: one thousand nine hundred fifty milliliters.
16–30 I Model reading chart F1 and the summary. Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student reads F1 aloud entry by entry. Round 2: the student gives totals and the balance to the teacher as a colleague. Round 3 (unseen): chart F2 (below), with one entry missing a time; the student asks for clarification before reporting.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: report one total with unit and period. Set homework.

I&O chart F1 (fictional, 7 a.m.–7 p.m.): Oral: 8 a.m. tea 200 mL; 12 p.m. water 300 mL; 4 p.m. juice 250 mL (oral total 750 mL). IV fluids: 100 mL per hour for 12 hours (1,200 mL). Total intake 1,950 mL. Output: urine 10 a.m. 250 mL, 2 p.m. 200 mL, 6 p.m. 150 mL (600 mL); vomited 100 mL at 1 p.m. Total output 700 mL. Balance +1,250 mL.

Error Hunt: Total intake was 1,590 mL. Urine output was 650 mL. The patient vomited 200 mL at 1 p.m. Key: 1,950 mL; 600 mL; 100 mL.

I&O chart F2 (unseen, fictional, 7 a.m.–7 p.m.): Odil Rasulov, 58. Oral: 8 a.m. tea 200 mL; water 250 mL (no time recorded); 3 p.m. soup 300 mL. IV fluids: 80 mL per hour for 12 hours. Output: urine 9 a.m. 300 mL, 1 p.m. 250 mL, 5 p.m. 200 mL. Key: before reporting, the student asks What time was the 250 mL of water? Oral 750 mL · IV 960 mL · total intake 1,710 mL · total output 750 mL · balance +960 mL over 12 hours.

Observer checks: every unit said · period stated (12 hours) · totals correct · missing data questioned.

Stretch: state the balance and what changed since the morning. Support: the totals frame (Student Edition, Week 6 cards).

Homework: record the F1 fluid-balance report.

Lesson 18 · C Perform · Kidney and urinary · Midpoint check
Goal Complete the midpoint tasks without help.
New words None. Recognize from the card: urinary tract infection (UTI), flank pain, catheter, dialysis.
Assessment Midpoint. Score with the section 4 rubric; compare with Lesson 1.
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: Which week was hardest, and why?
5–8 — Explain the 3 tasks and the rubric. No coaching. Record everything.
8–23 Task 1 5-minute focused interview with card MP-K (unseen), using respectful urinary questions.
23–33 Task 2 Report the MP-K vital signs and fluid card (2 minutes to prepare, 1 minute to speak).
33–42 Task 3 1-minute SBAR (frame in section 2) to the teacher as a colleague, using the supplied request.
42–50 Review Play 20 seconds of Lesson 1, then today. The student names 2 improvements.
50–60 O Scores, 2 strengths, 2 goals for Weeks 7–12, written in the student's book (My progress).

Card MP-K (unseen, fictional): Sabina Hasanova, 34. Burning on urination for 3 days; going every hour; lower abdominal pain 4/10. Today: right-sided back (flank) pain, fever and chills, nausea, no vomiting. Drinking very little. No allergies; no medicines.

Vital signs and fluids: 6 a.m.: T 37.4 °C, HR 88, BP 118/74. 2 p.m.: T 38.6 °C, HR 108, BP 110/70. 6 a.m.–2 p.m.: intake 400 mL, urine output 250 mL. Supplied request: Please come and assess her.

Report checklist: values with units and times · change stated · intake and output with period · SBAR in order · request at the end.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): re-record Task 3 with your 2 improvements.

teacher.title: Emergency Department Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can take a short arrival history, tell the story of an injury in the right order, and give an urgent SBAR handoff.

Prepare: arrival form AF1 (below); arrival cards E1–E2; injury story I1 (the Hot Seat turns); injury cards I2–I3; ED cards ED1–ED2.

Facts, not urgency. Students collect and report facts. The triage nurse decides who is seen first.

Lesson 19 · A Learn · Arrival and triage language
Goal Take a short arrival history without deciding urgency.
New words (9) triage, arrival, walk-in, by ambulance, waiting area, reassessment, time of onset, last known well, priority
Recycle chief complaint, distress, deteriorating
Grammar Past continuous + past simple: What were you doing when the pain started?
Spark Listen and Answer (fill the arrival form)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: What happens in an emergency department? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Last known well = the last time the patient was known to be normal (at baseline).
24–32 I Spark: Listen and Answer; the teacher reads the narrative and the student fills arrival form AF1. Grammar in 4 minutes.
32–50 F Round 1: arrival interview with card E1. Round 2: card E2, no notes. Round 3 (new detail): the patient asks Am I next? How long will I wait? The student answers: The triage nurse decides the order. I'll let them know about your pain.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 past continuous question + 1 time of onset question. Set homework.

Narrative (teacher reads): I'm Botir Aliyev, born March 3rd, 1979. I was carrying boxes at work when I felt a sharp pain in my lower back, about 11 o'clock. My colleague drove me here. I'm allergic to ibuprofen: I get a rash. I don't take any regular medicines. Form key: Botir Aliyev · 03/03/1979 · sharp lower back pain · about 11:00 while carrying boxes · walk-in (driven by a colleague) · ibuprofen – rash · no medicines.

Arrival form AF1 (fictional): Full name · Date of birth · Chief complaint · Time of onset · What were you doing when it started? · Arrived by: walk-in / ambulance / other · Allergies and reaction · Regular medicines.

Arrival cards (fictional): E1 – Mohira, 27: cut her hand on glass at 7 p.m.; bleeding stopped with pressure; tetanus shot date unknown. E2 – Ulugbek, 50: chest burning since dinner at 8 p.m.; came by taxi; takes blood-pressure medicine.

Observer checks: identity and date of birth · time of onset · allergies and medicines · no urgency promised.

Stretch: ask When were you last completely well? Support: the arrival form.

Homework: record an arrival conversation with card E2.

Lesson 20 · B Practice · Injuries and accidents
Goal Tell what happened in the right order.
New words (9) fall, slip, trip, collision, laceration, loss of consciousness, witnessed, mechanism of injury, head injury
Recycle bruise, cut, swelling
Grammar Narrative tenses and past perfect: She had been standing on a chair when she fell. Had you felt dizzy before the fall?
Spark Hot Seat Interpreting
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: tell Botir's story. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Mechanism of injury = how it happened. Witnessed = someone saw it.
16–30 I Spark: Hot Seat Interpreting (below); the teacher speaks three Uzbek turns, the student interprets each; then one English clinician turn the other way (below). Grammar in 4 minutes.
30–50 F Round 1: from the interpreted story, the student reports mechanism, timing and the patient's words. Round 2: card I2. Round 3 (unseen): injury story I3 (below), told out of order; the student puts it in order.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 past perfect question. Set homework.

Hot Seat turns (injury story I1):

Uzbek Model English
Kecha kechqurun hammomda sirpanib ketdim. Boshimni devorga urdim. Last night I slipped in the bathroom. I hit my head on the wall.
Bir necha soniya hushimni yo‘qotdim, qizim ko‘rib qoldi. Hozir boshim og‘riyapti va ko‘nglim aynayapti. I lost consciousness for a few seconds; my daughter saw it. Now I have a headache and I feel nauseous.
Qon suyultiruvchi dori ichaman. Yiqilishdan oldin boshim aylanmagan edi. I take a blood thinner. I hadn't felt dizzy before the fall.

Reverse turn (the teacher as an English-speaking clinician; the student interprets into Uzbek): When did you last take your blood thinner? Do you have any pain in your neck? Model Uzbek: Qon suyultiruvchi dorini oxirgi marta qachon ichdingiz? Bo‘yningizda og‘riq bormi?

Injury card I2 (fictional): Javlon, 19: cycling at about 5 p.m. when a car door opened; fell onto his right side; laceration on his right elbow; no loss of consciousness; helmet on; witnessed by a friend.

Injury story I3 (unseen, fictional; the teacher tells it in this order): Dildora Rahmonova, 58: My left wrist really hurts. My neighbor drove me here at about 4 o'clock. I was hanging washing on the balcony at around 3. I tripped over a bucket and fell onto my hand. Before that I felt a bit dizzy because I hadn't eaten since breakfast. No, I didn't hit my head, and nobody saw me fall. Key (in order): had not eaten since breakfast and felt dizzy → about 3 p.m., hanging washing on the balcony → tripped over a bucket and fell onto her left hand → left wrist pain → her neighbor drove her in at about 4 p.m. No head injury; not witnessed.

Observer checks: accuracy · nothing added · first person kept · events in order.

Stretch: interpret without asking for any repetition. Support: allow one repetition per turn.

Homework: record a 60-second incident summary for card I2.

Lesson 21 · C Perform · Escalation and handoff
Goal Give an urgent SBAR from supplied facts.
New words (4) stable, unstable, callback, closed-loop communication
Recycle witnessed, loss of consciousness, triage
Grammar I'm calling about a new change in… I'm concerned that… Could you read that back to me?
Spark Error Hunt
Perform task Recorded urgent SBAR for card ED1
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: report card I2.
5–12 H 4 new words. Closed-loop: you say it, they repeat it, you confirm.
12–20 I Model SBAR for ED1 (below), using the SBAR frame in section 2. Spark: Error Hunt (below).
20–50 F Round 1: SBAR with the frame. Round 2: no frame; the teacher asks for one missing detail. Round 3 (unseen): ED card ED2 (below); the student also confirms the reply with closed-loop communication. Then the performance: record the ED1 SBAR.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

ED card ED1 (fictional): Hilola Qodirova, 74, bay 3. Fell at home at 9 p.m., witnessed by her daughter; hit her head; brief loss of consciousness; takes a blood thinner. Now (10:40 p.m.) more drowsy than on arrival; vomited once at 10:30; BP 168/92; HR 58. Supplied request: Please come and assess her now.

Error Hunt: Mrs. Qodirova fell at 7 p.m. The fall was not witnessed. She has vomited twice. Key: 9 p.m.; witnessed by her daughter; vomited once.

Model SBAR (ED1): S: This is Dilnoza, a nursing student in bay 3. I'm calling about Mrs. Qodirova, 74. She is more drowsy than on arrival. B: She fell at home at 9 p.m., and her daughter saw it. She hit her head and had a brief loss of consciousness. She takes a blood thinner. A: At 10:40 p.m. she is more drowsy than on arrival. She vomited once at 10:30. Her blood pressure is 168 over 92 and her heart rate is 58. R: I'm concerned about this change. Please come and assess her now. Closed loop: (Nurse: I'm coming now.) Thank you. You're coming now to bay 3.

ED card ED2 (unseen, fictional): Jamshid Qosimov, 45, bay 5. Fell about 2 meters from a ladder at work at 5:30 p.m.; witnessed by a colleague; landed on his left side; no loss of consciousness. 6 p.m.: BP 126/80, HR 88, left-side pain 5/10. Now (7:30 p.m.): pain 8/10; BP 98/60; HR 112; pale and sweaty. Supplied request: Please come and assess him now. Model SBAR: S: This is Dilnoza, a nursing student in bay 5. I'm calling about Mr. Qosimov, 45. His pain is worse and his blood pressure has dropped. B: He fell about 2 meters from a ladder at 5:30 p.m. and landed on his left side. A colleague saw it. There was no loss of consciousness. A: At 6 p.m. his blood pressure was 126 over 80 and his heart rate was 88. At 7:30 p.m. his blood pressure is 98 over 60 and his heart rate is 112. His left-side pain has gone from 5 to 8 out of 10. He is pale and sweaty. R: Please come and assess him now. Closed loop: (Nurse: I'll be there in two minutes.) Thank you: two minutes, bay 5.

Observer checks: change stated first · times exact · blood thinner mentioned · closed loop completed.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the ED1 SBAR, then Javlon's injury story.

teacher.title: Surgical and Postoperative Care
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can go through a preoperative checklist and spot missing information, ask about postoperative symptoms, orient a new patient, and teach back discharge instructions.

Prepare: checklists P1–P2; postoperative card PO1; discharge sheet DS1.

Lesson 22 · A Learn · Before surgery
Goal Explain a preoperative checklist and spot missing information.
New words (9) preoperative, checklist, nothing by mouth (NPO), anesthesia, ID band, surgical site, site marking, jewelry, dentures
Recycle consent form, fasting, allergic to
Grammar You must not eat or drink. You have to remove your ring. You don't need to… Have you had anything to eat or drink since midnight?
Spark Match and Speak
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the ED1 SBAR. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Sounds: anesthesia (an-es-THEE-zhuh).
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark (4 min): Match and Speak: NPO ↔ nothing to eat or drink · anesthesia ↔ medicine so you sleep or feel no pain · ID band ↔ name bracelet · site marking ↔ the surgeon marks the place on your body.
32–50 F Round 1: go through checklist P1 with the teacher-patient. Round 2: find the 3 problems and report each: You had tea at 6 a.m. I need to tell the nurse right away. Round 3 (unseen): checklist P2 (below).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 must not + 1 since question. Set homework.

Checklist P1 (fictional): Dilshod Murodov, 50; right knee arthroscopy at 8:00 a.m. ID band ✓ · consent signed ✓ · NPO since midnight: patient says I had tea at 6 · allergy: latex · site marked: not yet · dentures: blank · jewelry: wedding ring still on. Problems: tea at 6 a.m.; site not marked; ring on (dentures to be checked).

Checklist P2 (unseen, fictional): Mavluda Toshpulatova, 62; left hip replacement at 10:00 a.m. ID band: date of birth 4 June 1962; the patient says 4 June 1963 · consent form: not signed · NPO since midnight ✓ · allergy: penicillin (rash) · site marked ✓ · dentures: upper denture still in · jewelry: none ✓. Problems: date of birth on the ID band does not match; consent not signed; upper denture still in. The student reports each one to the nurse and repeats the allergy.

Observer checks: every item checked · problems reported, not fixed by the student · allergy repeated · calm explanations.

Stretch: explain why the site is marked, in plain English. Support: checklist in view.

Homework: record an explanation of checklist P1.

Lesson 23 · B Practice · After surgery
Goal Ask about postoperative symptoms and report observations.
New words (9) postoperative, incision, sutures (stitches), staples, drain, recovery room, pain relief, dressing change, mobilize
Recycle dressing, drainage, redness
Grammar How is your pain compared with earlier? Passive perfect: Has the dressing been changed today?
Spark Listen and Answer (postoperative handoff)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the P1 problems. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Mobilize = get the patient moving safely.
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer (below). Grammar in 4 minutes.
30–50 F Round 1: postoperative check-in with teacher-patient PO1. Round 2: read PO1's observations and report them. Round 3 (new detail): the patient says My dressing feels wet; the student looks (card) and reports what they see, without guessing why.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 compared with + 1 passive-perfect question. Set homework.

Postoperative handoff (teacher reads): Mrs. Ismoilova came back from abdominal surgery at 11 a.m. Her pain was 7 out of 10 at noon and is 4 out of 10 now, after pain relief at 12:30. The dressing is dry. The drain has 40 milliliters of fluid. She hasn't passed urine since surgery. Questions: Pain at noon and now? Drain amount? What hasn't she done? Key: 7/10 → 4/10; 40 mL; passed urine.

Card PO1 (fictional): Zamira Ismoilova, 47, day 0 after abdominal surgery. 3 p.m.: pain 5/10; nausea, no vomiting; dressing dry; drain 60 mL total; has not passed urine since surgery; has not walked yet.

Observer checks: pain compared with earlier · drain amount with unit · urine asked · observations, not explanations.

Stretch: add When did you last have pain relief? Support: postoperative question card (Student Edition, Week 8 cards).

Homework: record a postoperative report for card PO1.

Lesson 24 · C Perform · Admission, discharge and teach-back
Goal Orient a new patient, then teach back discharge instructions.
New words (4) orientation, call button, teach-back, follow-up appointment
Recycle incision, sutures, pain relief, warning sign
Grammar First conditional for warning signs: If* you notice a fever over 38 degrees, call* the clinic.
Spark Mystery Patient (find what the patient misunderstood)
Perform task Recorded discharge teaching with teach-back
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: report card PO1.
5–12 H 4 new words. Teach-back = the patient explains the instructions in their own words, so you can check they understood. Admission orientation script: This is your call button. Press it if you need help. The bathroom is here. Your nurse today is Anna.
12–20 I Model discharge teaching from DS1 in chunks; check after each chunk.
20–50 F Round 1: orient the teacher-patient to the room. Round 2: discharge teaching with DS1. Spark: Mystery Patient; the teacher holds a hidden card of 2 misunderstandings, and the student must find them through teach-back. Then the performance: record Round 2 with teach-back.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Discharge sheet DS1 (fictional, after knee arthroscopy): keep the dressing dry for 48 hours, then shower; no bath for 2 weeks · ice for 20 minutes every 2 hours while awake · walk with crutches as shown · pain medicine as prescribed (see label) · follow-up: Tuesday 10:30 a.m., Dr. Brooks · call if: fever above 38 °C (100.4 °F), more redness or drainage, pain or swelling in the calf, pain not controlled.

Hidden misunderstandings (teacher only): the patient plans to take a bath tomorrow; thinks the follow-up is Thursday.

Observer checks: information in chunks · teach-back after each chunk · both misunderstandings found · warning signs with if.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): admission orientation, then the DS1 warning signs.

teacher.title: Medication Safety and Patient Education
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can confirm a medication list and find differences, read unclear labels and ask for clarification, and answer medicine questions safely by referring.

Prepare: medication lists ML1–ML2; labels LB-A and LB-B (two strengths of one medicine) and LB-C; question cards Q1–Q4. All medicine names are invented.

Find, report, never change. Students find differences and tell the nurse or pharmacist. They never advise a dose.

Lesson 25 · A Learn · Medication reconciliation
Goal Confirm a medication list accurately.
New words (9) reconciliation, home medications, prescription, over-the-counter (OTC), supplement, herbal remedy, discrepancy, medication list, last dose taken
Recycle dose, route, frequency
Grammar Question tags to confirm: You take it twice a day, don't you? You haven't taken it today, have you?
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the DS1 warning signs. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Always ask about herbal teas and remedies: many patients don't count them as medicine. Intonation: falling tag = confirming; rising tag = really asking.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Model going through ML1 line by line.
32–50 F Round 1: the student checks ML1 against what the teacher-patient says and finds 4 discrepancies. Spark (6 min): Error Hunt on the teacher's summary. Round 2: the student reports the discrepancies to the nurse. Round 3 (unseen): list ML2 and patient (below).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 question tags with correct intonation. Set homework.

List ML1 (fictional pharmacy list): METAVIL 500 mg tablet twice daily with meals · PRESSANOL 5 mg once daily in the morning · ATORIN 20 mg once daily at night.

What the patient says (teacher only): I take Metavil once a day, it upsets my stomach. Pressanol every morning. I stopped Atorin last month. I also take vitamin D and a herbal tea for my sugar every day. Discrepancies: Metavil once, not twice · Atorin stopped · vitamin D not listed · herbal tea not listed.

Error Hunt (teacher's summary): He takes Metavil twice a day. He stopped Pressanol last month. He takes no supplements. Key: Metavil once a day; it was Atorin he stopped; he takes vitamin D and a herbal tea.

List ML2 (unseen, fictional pharmacy list): KORDAPIN 5 mg once daily in the morning · ZELMAVIN 1,000 mg twice daily with meals · TASORIL 75 mg once daily. What the patient says (teacher only): I take Kordapin, but only half a tablet; a whole one makes me dizzy. Zelmavin morning and evening with food. Tasoril every day. And my daughter bought me some tablets for my knees at the pharmacy. Discrepancies: Kordapin half a tablet, not one · an over-the-counter medicine for her knees is not on the list. The student reports both to the nurse and gives no advice.

Observer checks: every line checked · OTC and herbal asked · discrepancies reported, not corrected · tags used to confirm.

Stretch: ask When did you take your last dose? for each medicine. Support: a 3-column list: on the list / what the patient says / match?

Homework: record a medication-list interview with ML1.

Lesson 26 · B Practice · Label instructions and clarification
Goal Spot unclear label wording and ask for clarification.
New words (8) maximum dose, extended-release, chewable, on an empty stomach, shake well, avoid alcohol, may cause drowsiness, expiry date
Recycle milligram, milliliter, as needed, strength (new meaning)
Grammar Reported instructions: The label says to take it on an empty stomach. It says not to drink alcohol.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the ML1 discrepancies. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Strength = the amount in each tablet (a recycled word with a new meaning). Maximum dose = the most you may take in a set time. Spark: Number Catch: 0.5 mg / 5 mg · 1.25 mL · half a tablet · every 4–6 hours · 8 tablets in 24 hours.
16–30 I Model comparing labels LB-A and LB-B. Grammar in 4 minutes.
30–50 F Round 1: the student reads both labels to the teacher-patient using The label says to… Round 2: the patient has both bottles and is confused; the student finds the risk (two strengths) and asks the pharmacist for clarification. Round 3 (unseen): label LB-C (below), with the strength missing; the student does not guess.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 says to / says not to sentences. Set homework.

Labels (fictional): LB-A – DOLOREX 5 mg tablets: take 1–2 tablets every 4–6 hours as needed for pain; no more than 8 tablets in 24 hours; may cause drowsiness; avoid alcohol. LB-B – DOLOREX 10 mg tablets: take 1 tablet every 6 hours as needed for pain; no more than 4 tablets in 24 hours; may cause drowsiness; avoid alcohol.

Clarification model: The patient has two bottles of Dolorex in different strengths, 5 mg and 10 mg. I'd like to check which one she should be taking.

Label LB-C (unseen, fictional): RESPIRAN extended-release tablets · strength: not printed · take 1 tablet twice a day with food · swallow whole; do not crush or chew · expiry date 03/2027. Key: the student says The strength isn't on this label. I won't guess; I'll check with the pharmacist.

Observer checks: strength read every time · maximum dose read · ambiguity spotted · no guessing.

Stretch: explain extended-release in plain English. Support: the label map (Student Edition, Week 9 cards).

Homework: record two label read-backs.

Lesson 27 · C Perform · Side effects and safe referral
Goal Answer medicine questions safely by referring.
New words (4) adverse reaction, interaction, prescriber, medication error
Recycle discrepancy, over-the-counter, supplement
Grammar Referral language: You should ask your pharmacist about that. I'm not able to advise on that, but I'll find someone who can.
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Perform task Recorded responses to 4 patient questions: answer from the card or refer
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: explain the Dolorex risk.
5–12 H 4 new words. Side effect = an expected unwanted effect; adverse reaction = a harmful reaction that must be reported.
12–20 I Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
20–50 F Round 1: the teacher asks Q1–Q4; the student sorts them: answer from the card, or refer. Round 2: swap roles. Round 3 (unseen): a rash after a new medicine; the student reports it as a possible adverse reaction to the nurse at once. Then the performance: record answers to Q1–Q4.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Uzbek Bridge:

Uzbek Model English
Bu dorini ichgandan beri ko‘p yo‘talyapman. Since I started this medicine, I've been coughing a lot.
Kecha dorimni ichishni unutdim, bugun ikkitasini ichsam bo‘ladimi? I forgot my medicine yesterday. Can I take two today?
Qo‘shnim menga o‘z dorisini berdi. My neighbor gave me her medicine.
Dori ichgandan keyin badanimga toshma toshdi. After taking the medicine, I got a rash on my body.

Question cards: Q1 – What time should I take Pressanol? (answer from list ML1: in the morning) · Q2 – Can I take two today because I missed yesterday? (refer) · Q3 – Can I drink alcohol with Dolorex? (label: avoid alcohol) · Q4 – Can I stop Atorin? I feel fine. (refer to the prescriber).

Observer checks: label answers exact · every clinical question referred · rash reported as urgent · no personal opinion.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the ML1 reconciliation report, then answers to Q2 and Q3.

teacher.title: Mental Health and Therapeutic Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can respond to emotions with empathy, respect privacy and cultural preferences, and report a mental-health concern using the patient's exact words.

Prepare: emotion cards MH1–MH2; the preferences text; card MH3.

Teacher note: keep role-plays calm and fictional. If a student finds a topic personally difficult, change the card; no student has to play a role they are uncomfortable with.

Lesson 28 · A Learn · Emotions and supportive language
Goal Respond with empathy and open questions.
New words (9) anxious, overwhelmed, frustrated, low mood, tearful, stress, coping, support, validate
Recycle worried, concern, reassure
Grammar Modal deduction: That must be difficult. You must be exhausted. It sounds like…
Spark Match and Speak (statement ↔ empathic response)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: What makes a nurse easy to talk to? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Validate = show the feeling makes sense. Tone: slower, lower, pauses allowed.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark (4 min): Match and Speak (below).
32–50 F Round 1: card MH1. Round 2: card MH2, no notes. Round 3 (new detail): the patient says I'm fine but looks tearful; the student names what they notice gently.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 must be + 1 It sounds like… Set homework.

Match and Speak: I haven't slept for days worrying about my son ↔ That must be exhausting. Would you like to tell me more? · Nobody here listens to me ↔ It sounds like you've felt ignored. I'm listening now. · I'm fine (crying) ↔ I notice you seem upset. Is something on your mind? · I can't do this anymore: the diet, the insulin, everything ↔ It sounds like you're feeling overwhelmed. What's been the hardest part?

Emotion cards (fictional): MH1 – Malika, 33, new mother: tired and anxious about her baby's weight. MH2 – Rustam, 60, newly diagnosed with diabetes: frustrated with insulin injections.

Observer checks: feeling named · no false promises · one open question · calm pace.

Stretch: follow with What has helped you cope before? Support: 3 empathy frames (Student Edition, Week 10 cards).

Homework: record 3 supportive responses.

Lesson 29 · B Practice · Sensitive conversations
Goal Ask permission and respect preferences.
New words (9) confidential, permission, preference, boundary, dignity, chaperone, culturally sensitive, same-gender, private
Recycle interpreter, privacy, respect
Grammar Would you prefer…? Would you mind if…? Is it OK if…?
Spark Listen and Answer (a patient's preferences)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: respond to card MH2. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Common preferences: a same-gender nurse, who may hear results, family presence, prayer times, religious fasting. Ask; don't assume.
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer (below). Grammar in 4 minutes.
30–50 F Round 1: the patient asks for privacy and an interpreter. Round 2: the patient asks for a female nurse for an examination; the student offers a chaperone and checks with the team. Round 3 (unseen): a relative insists on interpreting; the student politely explains why a professional interpreter is used.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 permission questions. Set homework.

Preferences text (teacher reads): I'd prefer a female nurse for the examination. My husband can stay, but please don't discuss my results in front of my mother-in-law. I'm fasting this month, so I'd like to know if my medicine times can change. Can you ask the doctor? Questions: Who should do the examination? What should not happen? What must be referred? Key: a female nurse; results discussed in front of her mother-in-law; medicine times during fasting (to the doctor).

Observer checks: permission asked before acting · preference respected or escalated · no judgment · clinical question referred.

Stretch: explain confidentiality in one plain sentence. Support: the three question frames.

Homework: write and record a short privacy-focused dialogue.

Lesson 30 · C Perform · Reporting mental-health concerns
Goal Report quotes and observations neutrally.
New words (4) stated, behavior, safety concern, notify
Recycle tearful, low mood, permission
Grammar Direct quotes in reports: The patient stated, "I don't see the point anymore." Observations in the past: He was tearful and had not eaten lunch.
Spark Error Hunt
Perform task Recorded supportive response, then a report to the nurse for card MH3
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: the preferences text from memory.
5–12 H 4 new words. Rule: if a patient says anything that suggests they may not be safe, stay with them and tell the nurse straight away. Use their exact words; never interpret them.
12–20 I Model the report (below). Spark: Error Hunt (below).
20–50 F Round 1: a supportive response to the teacher as MH3. Round 2: the report to the nurse, with the model in view. Round 3: no model; the teacher asks What exactly did he say? Then the performance: record Rounds 1 and 2.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Card MH3 (fictional): Shavkat Mirzayev, 58, room 9, 4 p.m. Has not eaten lunch; lying facing the wall; tearful. Stated: I don't see the point anymore. I'm just a burden to my family. No visitors today.

Model report: I'm concerned about Mr. Mirzayev in room 9. At 4 p.m. he was tearful and hadn't eaten lunch. He stated, "I don't see the point anymore. I'm just a burden to my family." I've stayed with him. Can you come and speak with him now?

Error Hunt: Mr. Mirzayev is depressed. He refused lunch because he is angry. Key: depressed is a diagnosis: report his words instead; he hasn't eaten, not refused; he was tearful, and nobody observed anger.

Observer checks: exact quote · observed facts with time · no diagnosis or interpretation · stays with the patient and notifies at once.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the MH3 report, then 2 supportive responses from Lesson 28.

teacher.title: Documentation and Professional Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can separate subjective from objective information in a note, give an end-of-shift SBAR, and pass information accurately by phone.

Prepare: the 8 sorting statements; cards DN1–DN2; handoff cards SH1–SH2; phone cards PH1–PH2 and caller script PH3; the phonetic alphabet sheet (below).

Lesson 31 · A Learn · Subjective and objective
Goal Separate reported facts from measured facts and write a 4-sentence note.
New words (9) subjective, objective, documented, denies, describes, abbreviation, accurate, chart (verb), late entry
Recycle reported, observed, stated, measured
Grammar Reporting verbs in notes: Patient reports hip pain 5/10. Denies nausea. Appears comfortable at rest.
Spark Match and Speak (sort S or O)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the MH3 report. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Subjective = what the patient tells you. Objective = what you measure or see. Abbreviation = a short form, such as BP or HR; use only standard ones. Note style drops the and he/she: Denies nausea.
24–32 I Spark (4 min): Match and Speak: the student sorts the 8 statements into S or O. Grammar in 4 minutes.
32–50 F Round 1: the student interviews teacher-patient DN1. Round 2: the student writes a 4-sentence note and reads it aloud; compare with the model. Round 3 (unseen): card DN2 (below); the note is written in 5 minutes.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 reports + 1 denies sentence. Set homework.

Sorting statements: I feel dizzy (S) · BP 150/95 (O) · pain 6/10 per patient (S) · wound 3 cm with red edges (O) · says she slept badly (S) · ate 50% of lunch (O) · appears anxious (O, an observed behavior) · denies nausea (S).

Card DN1 (fictional): Barno, 62, 9 a.m. Says she slept badly; left hip pain 5/10, worse when I turn. Denies nausea. BP 136/84, HR 82, T 36.9 °C. Ate half of breakfast. Walked to the bathroom with a walker and one assistant.

Model note: 09:00. Patient reports poor sleep and left hip pain 5/10, worse on turning. Denies nausea. BP 136/84, HR 82, T 36.9 °C. Ate 50% of breakfast; walked to bathroom with walker and assistance of one.

Card DN2 (unseen, fictional): Timur Ganiyev, 54, 2 p.m., day 3 after knee surgery. Says the wound feels hot and itchy; pain 4/10 at the incision. Denies fever. T 37.8 °C, HR 90, BP 128/80. Redness about 2 cm around the wound edges. Ate all of lunch. Model note: 14:00. Patient reports incision pain 4/10 and states the wound feels hot and itchy. Denies fever. T 37.8 °C, HR 90, BP 128/80. Redness approx. 2 cm around wound edges; ate 100% of lunch.

Observer checks: S and O kept apart · every value has a unit · time at the start · no opinions.

Stretch: add a late entry correctly: Late entry for 08:30… Support: the S/O note template (Student Edition, Week 11 cards).

Homework: write a 4-sentence mock note for card GI1 (Week 6) and record it.

Lesson 32 · B Practice · Professional SBAR
Goal Give an organized 1-minute end-of-shift SBAR.
New words (8) concise, relevant, pending, outstanding, escalate, acknowledge, end-of-shift, bedside handoff
Recycle situation, recommendation, read-back
Grammar I'm calling to give you an update on…; compact phrases: day 2 after hip surgery; results pending
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: read the DN1 note aloud. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Pending = waiting for a result. Outstanding = still to be done.
16–30 I Model the end-of-shift SBAR for SH1 (below). Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: SBAR for SH1 with the frame. Round 2: no frame, 1 minute timed; the teacher asks for exact values and times. Round 3 (unseen): handoff card SH2 (below); the receiving nurse (teacher) reads back and the student acknowledges.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: say what is pending and what is outstanding for SH1. Set homework.

Handoff card SH1 (fictional): Kamol Umarov, 71, room 12, day 2 after hip surgery. Pain 3/10 after pain relief at 2 p.m. Walked 10 m with a walker and the physiotherapist. Passed urine 3 times. Dressing dry. Blood test results pending. Family visiting at 7 p.m. Outstanding: blood sugar check at 9 p.m.

Error Hunt: Mr. Umarov is day 3 after hip surgery. He walked 100 meters. His blood results are normal. Key: day 2; 10 m; results are pending, not available.

Model SBAR (SH1): S: I'm handing over Mr. Umarov in room 12. B: He is 71, day 2 after hip surgery. A: His pain is 3 out of 10 after pain relief at 2 p.m. He walked 10 meters with a walker and the physiotherapist. He has passed urine 3 times, and his dressing is dry. R: His blood test results are pending. The blood sugar check at 9 p.m. is outstanding. His family is visiting at 7 p.m.

Handoff card SH2 (unseen, fictional): Gavhar Sultonova, 66, room 4, day 1 after gallbladder surgery. Pain 4/10 after pain relief at 5 p.m. Walked to the bathroom once with help. Drain: 30 mL since 7 a.m. Nausea at 4 p.m., none now. Pending: blood test results. Outstanding: blood pressure check at 10 p.m. Model SBAR: S: I'm handing over Mrs. Sultonova in room 4. B: She is 66, day 1 after gallbladder surgery. A: Her pain is 4 out of 10 after pain relief at 5 p.m. She walked to the bathroom once with help. Her drain has 30 milliliters since 7 a.m. She had nausea at 4 p.m. and has none now. R: Her blood test results are pending, and the blood pressure check at 10 p.m. is outstanding. Read-back: the teacher reads it back; the student acknowledges: Yes, that's correct.

Observer checks: under 60 seconds · pending and outstanding items named · numbers exact · read-back acknowledged.

Stretch: handle a question you can't answer: I don't have that information; I'll find out and call you back. Support: the SBAR frame.

Homework: record a 1-minute SBAR for SH1.

Lesson 33 · C Perform · Phone calls and messages
Goal Pass accurate information by phone.
New words (4) voicemail, extension, phonetic alphabet, recipient
Recycle read-back, callback, pending
Grammar Could you spell the last name, please? Could you read that back to me? I'm calling on behalf of…
Spark Number Catch
Perform task Recorded 45-second voicemail (PH1) and a written, read-back phone message (PH2)
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: the SH1 SBAR.
5–12 H 4 new words. Phonetic alphabet for Uzbek names: Kholmatov = K for Kilo, H for Hotel…; Yo'ldosheva = Y-O-apostrophe-L-D-O-S-H-E-V-A (say the apostrophe).
12–20 I Spark: Number Catch: phone numbers, an extension (2241), a record number (40817), and two names spelled with the phonetic alphabet.
20–50 F Round 1: leave the PH1 voicemail. Round 2: take the PH2 message, write it and read it back. Round 3 (unseen): caller script PH3 (below), a fast caller with a bad line; the student controls the call: Sorry, the line is bad. Could you repeat the room number? Then the performance: record the PH1 voicemail and hand in the PH2 message.
50–60 O Play the recording back and check the message. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Phone cards (fictional): PH1 – call the lab on behalf of nurse Anna, Unit 4, extension 2241, about Malika Yo'ldosheva, record number 40817: when will her blood results be ready? Leave a voicemail. PH2 – incoming: This is Tom from pharmacy, extension 3150, about Mr. Kholmatov in room 7. His Atorin is out of stock; it will arrive at 4 p.m.

Voicemail model: Hello, this is Dilnoza calling on behalf of nurse Anna on Unit 4. I'm calling about Malika Yo'ldosheva, record number 4-0-8-1-7. Could you let us know when her blood results will be ready? Please call us back on extension 2-2-4-1. That's extension 2-2-4-1. Thank you.

Phonetic alphabet sheet: A Alfa · B Bravo · C Charlie · D Delta · E Echo · F Foxtrot · G Golf · H Hotel · I India · J Juliett · K Kilo · L Lima · M Mike · N November · O Oscar · P Papa · Q Quebec · R Romeo · S Sierra · T Tango · U Uniform · V Victor · W Whiskey · X X-ray · Y Yankee · Z Zulu.

Caller script PH3 (unseen, fictional; the teacher speaks fast and drops words): Hi, it's radiology… about Mr. Bozorov… room… his X-ray's moved to half past three… can you tell his nurse… Full details (teacher only): Lola, radiology, extension 5170; Shuhrat Bozorov, room 15; X-ray moved to 3:30 p.m.; tell nurse Anna. Key: the student controls the call and gets every detail (caller and extension, patient's name spelled, room, new time, who to tell), then reads it all back.

Observer checks: name spelled · numbers in single digits · callback number given twice · message read back.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the PH1 voicemail, then read the DN1 note aloud.

teacher.title: Nursing-School Readiness · Final
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can read nursing-school assignment instructions and ask for help, complete a full multi-step simulation, and pass the five-task final assessment.

Prepare: assignment AS1; simulation card SIM1; the final cards (below); the Lesson 1 and Lesson 18 recordings; the completion certificate.

Lesson 34 · A Learn · Assignments and clinical instructions
Goal Read mock nursing-school instructions and ask for help.
New words (9) learning objective, criteria, word count, citation, APA format, submit, extension (2nd meaning), plagiarism, academic integrity
Recycle syllabus, due date, rubric
Grammar Modals in instructions: must include, should not exceed, may use. Could you clarify what is required?
Spark Listen and Answer (an instructor's spoken instructions)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: What will your first week of nursing school be like? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Plagiarism = using others' words or ideas without citing them; US schools treat it very seriously.
24–32 I Spark: Listen and Answer; the teacher reads AS1 as an instructor would say it. Questions: word range? how many Vocabulary Book words? format? late penalty? Key: 250–300 words; at least 8 B2 words; PDF by email; 10% per day.
32–50 F Round 1: the student summarizes the AS1 requirements. Round 2: the student asks the teacher-instructor 3 clarifying questions. Round 3 (new detail): the student was ill and asks for an extension, first by speaking, then in a 4-sentence email.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 must + 1 should not sentence about AS1. Set homework.

Assignment AS1: ShifoLife B2 Patient Education Leaflet. Choose one condition from your B2 weeks (for example asthma, diabetes or high blood pressure). Write 250–300 words explaining it for a patient with low health literacy. Must use at least 8 words from the B2 section of the Doc, each explained in plain English. Should not exceed 300 words. Send it as a PDF to your teacher by email by 11:59 p.m. Sunday. Late work loses 10% per day. Rubric: content 40%, clarity 30%, vocabulary 20%, format 10%.

Observer checks: all requirements found · questions polite and specific · extension request gives a reason and a new date · email has a greeting and closing.

Stretch: explain the rubric weights in your own words. Support: the requirements checklist (Student Edition, Week 12 cards).

Homework: record a request for clarification about AS1.

Lesson 35 · B Practice · Integrated patient simulation
Goal Complete a multi-step patient simulation.
New words (8) scenario, standardized patient, debrief, prioritize, sequence, critical information, time limit, reflect
Recycle closed-loop communication, teach-back, situation
Grammar Sequencing and plans: First I'll check your name and date of birth. Then I'll ask about… Let me summarize…
Spark Mystery Patient (unseen standardized patient)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the AS1 requirements. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Debrief = talking through what happened after a simulation.
16–30 I Explain the 5 stages (below) and the time limit: 15 minutes.
30–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient; the teacher plays SIM1 (unseen) and the student runs all 5 stages. Debrief: What went well? What would you change? What language did you need?
50–60 O Two errors, then retry the weakest stage. Set homework.

The 5 stages: (1) intake and identity · (2) focused interview (OLDCARTS) · (3) read the vital-signs card · (4) explain the supplied instruction with teach-back · (5) SBAR to the nurse with the supplied request.

Card SIM1 (unseen, fictional): Nargiza Usmonova, 56, type 2 diabetes. Noticed a wound on her right foot 5 days ago; now red and painful 5/10, some yellow drainage; feels feverish. Vitals: T 38.2 °C, HR 102, BP 142/88, glucose 245 mg/dL. Supplied instruction: Keep your foot raised and don't walk on it. The doctor will see you in 30 minutes. Supplied request: Please come and assess her foot.

Observer checks: all 5 stages · within 15 minutes · values with units · no diagnosis named.

Homework: review your recordings and write 3 improvements.

Lesson 36 · C Perform · Final assessment
Goal Complete five tasks without help.
New words None. Review Weeks 1–12.
Assessment Final. Score with the section 4 rubric; compare with Lessons 1 and 18; decide the certificate and the C1 recommendation.
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S Relaxed warm-up: What can you do now that you couldn't do in Week 1?
5–8 — Explain the 5 tasks and the rubric. No coaching. Record everything.
8–18 Task 1 Advanced interview with card FB1 (unseen), 5 minutes.
18–24 Task 2 Report the FB1 vital-signs and fluid card (1 minute).
24–30 Task 3 1-minute SBAR for FB1 with the supplied request.
30–38 Task 4 Teach discharge sheet DS2 with teach-back; in the teach-back the teacher (as patient) leaves out one detail, and the student notices it and teaches it again.
38–43 Task 5 Ask the teacher-instructor 2 questions about AS1.
43–50 Review Play 20 seconds each from Lessons 1, 18 and 36. The student names 3 improvements.
50–60 O Scores; certificate and C1 decision; next-step plan: 10 words and 3 goals.

Card FB1 (unseen, fictional): Abdulla Karimov, 63. Chest discomfort when walking uphill and more short of breath for 3 weeks; both ankles swollen in the evenings; smokes 10 cigarettes a day; hypertension; one blood-pressure tablet daily; no allergies. Vitals and fluids (8 a.m.–2 p.m.): BP 156/94, HR 92, RR 22, SpO2 93% on room air; intake 900 mL, urine output 500 mL. Supplied request: Could you come and review him before lunch?

student.title: Introduction
student.html:
Welcome to C1 Professional Medical English

C1 prepares you for life inside a US nursing program: following lectures, reading textbooks, presenting cases, writing care plans and reflections, handling difficult conversations, speaking up in the team, and interpreting between Uzbek and English. This book is yours: write in it and bring it to every lesson.

My details
Name
Level C1 Professional
Teacher
Class days and time
Start date
My B2 final score
My nursing school / target date

What's new in C1

  • Reading and writing every week. One short written task a week: a summary, a care plan, a report or a reflection. Log them at the end of this book.
  • Register matters. You'll learn to say the same thing to a doctor, a patient, a family member and in Uzbek (Register Switch).
  • Make your own examples. At C1 you write your own example sentence for each new word: it's how words stay with you.
  • Interpreting at a professional level. Week 11 trains you as a medical interpreter: accuracy, completeness, ethics.
  • Final OSCE. Lesson 36 is a five-station exam, just like nursing school.
  • Homework: 20–25 minutes a day. Lectures or reading after Lesson A; speaking and recording after Lesson B; your written task and voice note after Lesson C.

Grammar help: look up any grammar point in the Doc (Part 3 for C1; the reference tables cover all 12 tenses).

Word help: every word in your week tables has an English definition and an example in the Doc (C1 section). Read the definition and example, then write your own sentence in the table.

All patients, documents and cases in this book are fictional. This course teaches English, not clinical skills.

Mini-lecture ML1, hand hygiene (read after you listen; Lesson 1 Round 1): Today I'd like to talk about hand hygiene, and I'll cover three points: why it matters, when to do it, and why people forget. Firstly, why does it matter? Hands are the most common way germs move between patients. Consequently, hand hygiene is one of the simplest ways to prevent infection in hospital. Secondly, when should you do it? To illustrate, think of five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean procedure, after contact with body fluids, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings. Thirdly, why do people forget? In contrast to what we might expect, it's usually not lack of knowledge but time pressure and habit. So, to sum up: hands carry germs, there are five key moments, and the main barrier is habit, not knowledge.

Reading text RT1, Type 2 diabetes: an overview (Lessons 4–6): Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose. Its etiology involves both genetic and lifestyle risk factors, including obesity and physical inactivity. The underlying pathophysiology is insulin resistance: the body's cells do not respond normally to insulin. Clinical manifestations may include thirst, frequent urination and fatigue, although many patients have no symptoms at diagnosis. Research suggests that lifestyle interventions, such as increased activity and dietary change, can delay its onset in high-risk individuals. Long-term complications are associated with damage to the eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels. The rationale for regular monitoring is therefore to detect these changes early.

• ☐ I can understand what exam questions are really asking.

Lesson New words My example sentences
34 stem, option, distractor, priority, initial action, most appropriate, further teaching is needed, select all that apply, indicates understanding, except

Key language: Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? = find the wrong statement · first / priority = one action before all others · Before I begin, may I clarify…? I've finished; is there anything you'd like me to add?

Final OSCE (Lesson 36): (1) lecture summary · (2) case presentation · (3) patient education with teach-back · (4) a difficult conversation or complaint · (5) an interpreted exchange.

Final voice note: your 2-minute introduction as a future nurse.

Cards and texts · Week 12

Q1 (language practice, Lesson 34): A patient with diabetes makes the following statements about foot care. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. I will check my feet every day. B. I will walk barefoot at home to let my feet breathe. C. I will tell my nurse about any cuts. D. I will dry carefully between my toes.

Stem bank ST1–ST20 (language practice, not nursing content). ST1–ST5: Lesson 34 Round 1 · ST6–ST10: Round 3, timed · ST11–ST20: homework. Underline the key words, say what the question really asks, then choose.

ST1. A patient using insulin at home checks her sugar before breakfast. It is 62 mg/dL. According to leaflet LF2, what should she do first? A. Inject her morning insulin. B. Take 4 glucose tablets. C. Eat breakfast and check again tomorrow. D. Wait 2 hours and check again.

ST2. A patient has been taught to use an inhaler with a spacer. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I shake the inhaler before I use it." B. "I breathe out fully before I press." C. "I press twice quickly, then breathe in." D. "I rinse my mouth after my steroid inhaler."

ST3. According to lecture ML2, which patients have a higher risk of pressure injuries? Select all that apply. A. a patient after surgery who cannot move easily B. a very ill older adult C. a patient with poor nutrition and moist skin D. a young adult who walks every day

ST4. Lecture ML1 lists five moments for hand hygiene. They include all of the following except: A. before touching a patient B. after touching the patient's surroundings C. after contact with body fluids D. after reading the patient's chart at the desk

ST5. Which statement by a patient indicates understanding of leaflet LF2? A. "I'll keep the pen I'm using in the freezer." B. "I'll inject into the same spot every day." C. "I'll put used needles in the sharps container." D. "I'll check my feet once a month."

ST6. A patient asks a nursing student, "Am I going to die?" What is the most appropriate response? A. "No, everything will be fine." B. "That's an important question. Can you tell me what's making you think about it? I'll make sure the doctor talks with you today." C. "You should ask the doctor, not me." D. "Let's talk about something happier."

ST7. A student sees a colleague about to give room 4's medicine to the patient in room 6. What is the student's initial action? A. Report it at the end of the shift. B. Speak up now and ask to check the ID band together. C. Tell the patient not to take any medicine today. D. Say nothing, because the colleague is senior.

ST8. During a history, Mrs. Tursunova mentions several problems. Which one should the student report as the priority? A. knee pain when she walks B. a new sore on her big toe that she did not notice for a week C. the clinic is far from her home D. she finds sweets hard to refuse at weddings

ST9. A professional interpreter should do all of the following except: A. interpret everything that is said B. speak in the first person C. give the patient advice about treatment D. use a transparency statement to ask for a repetition

ST10. A nursing student is learning to respond to complaints. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I'm sorry this happened." B. "Let me find out what happened." C. "It was the night nurse's fault." D. "I'll come back by 5 p.m. with an update."

ST11. Which actions are part of the nurse's role in informed consent in the USA? Select all that apply. A. witnessing the patient's signature B. checking that the patient understands C. explaining the risks of the procedure instead of the provider D. telling the provider if the patient does not understand

ST12. A relative phones and asks for a patient's test results. What is the most appropriate response? A. Read the results to the caller quickly. B. "I'm sorry, I can't share any information over the phone." C. Give the results if the caller knows the patient's date of birth. D. "The results are fine; don't worry."

ST13. Mrs. Ahmedova ran out of her blood-pressure tablets a week ago. Her BP is 178/102. What is the most appropriate action for a nursing student? A. Give her a tablet from another patient's supply. B. Report the reading to the nurse and the physician. C. Tell her the reading is normal. D. Advise her to take two tablets tonight.

ST14. A patient has been taught to use an inhaler with a spacer. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I wait 30 seconds before a second puff." B. "I hold my breath for 10 seconds." C. "I don't need to rinse my mouth after a steroid inhaler." D. "I attach the spacer before I press."

ST15. A relative becomes threatening. The student should do all of the following except: A. step back to a safe distance B. leave the room C. call the charge nurse or security D. stand close and argue until he calms down

ST16. After teaching, which statement indicates that the patient understands what an HbA1c test measures? A. "It shows my sugar right now." B. "It shows my average blood sugar over about 3 months." C. "It measures my blood pressure." D. "It shows whether I have an infection."

ST17. Which sentences are written correctly for an incident report (IR1)? Select all that apply. A. "At 03:10 the patient was found on the floor beside his bed." B. "The patient fell because the night nurse forgot the bed rails." C. "He stated, 'I wanted to go to the toilet.'" D. "He was silly to get up alone."

ST18. A patient's son starts adding his own opinions while he interprets. What is the nurse's initial action? A. Continue, because the family knows best. B. Offer a professional interpreter. C. Ask the patient to speak English. D. End the visit.

ST19. Mr. Mirzaev often forgets his evening doses. Which question is most appropriate? A. "Why are you non-compliant?" B. "What gets in the way of taking your evening medicines?" C. "You should have taken them, shouldn't you?" D. "Do you want to get worse?"

ST20. Lecture ML2 lists three ways to prevent pressure injuries. They include all of the following except: A. changing the patient's position regularly B. keeping the skin clean and dry C. checking the skin every day D. keeping the patient in one position all night

1 uses the reading time and asks to clarify if needed

3 completes the station task (lecture summary, case, teaching, conversation or interpreting)
4 uses the right register for the listener
