teacher.title: Introduction
teacher.html:
1. About this book

This is the teacher's book for C1 Professional Medical English, the third ShifoLife level (B1 → B2 → C1). It covers 12 weeks, 36 lessons of 60 minutes, three per week. A matching Student Edition holds the timetable, the word lists and every card and text students use (in Cards and texts · Week N at the end of each week), without answer keys or hidden and unseen cards.

Who it is for: students who completed B2, or scored 28+ on the placement check (printed in the B1 Teacher Edition, section 3). They can already run patient interviews and SBAR handoffs. C1 prepares them for life inside a US nursing program: lectures, textbooks, case presentations, academic writing, difficult conversations, teamwork and professional interpreting.

What it is not: clinical training or exam preparation for content. Students learn the language of nursing school, exams and the ward; nursing knowledge comes from their program. All patients, documents and cases are fictional.

Grammar companion: C1 grammar is explained in full in the Doc (Part 3, Units 28–34), plus reference tables for all 12 tenses.

Vocabulary companion: every new word and word part in this book has an English definition, a word type and an example sentence in the Doc (C1 section, by week and lesson). Use it for Register Switch, Odd One Out and the weekly word review.

Copyright. © 2026 Shifo Life. All rights reserved. ShifoLife Medical English, the SHIFO Lesson Cycle, the Learn · Practice · Perform week, Uzbek Bridge and Register Switch are proprietary to Shifo Life. No part of this book may be copied, adapted or used to teach outside Shifo Life without written permission. Version 1.0 (draft for review).

2. The C1 level and what changes

By Week 12 the student can take usable notes from short lectures (2–5 minutes), summarize a textbook passage in their own words, present a full case in 3 minutes and answer questions, educate a patient with low health literacy, support a patient after difficult news, de-escalate a complaint, speak up in rounds, write a care plan, incident report and reflection, and interpret an encounter between Uzbek and English.

B2 C1
Student talk time 60–70% 70–80%
New words 8–9 per A/B, 4 per C 8–10 per A/B (clinical and academic), 4 per C
Start stage (S) 60 seconds of free speaking 90 seconds on a prompt, often a news item or a case
Skills Mostly speaking and listening Speaking, listening, reading and writing: one short written task a week
Teacher's role Patient, colleague, instructor Also lecturer, examiner, angry relative, physician on rounds
Feedback focus Accuracy Accuracy plus register: is this right for a patient, a doctor, an instructor?
Grammar band Perfect continuous, passive, reported speech, conditionals Discourse markers, nominalization, reduced relatives, cleft sentences, advanced hedging, tentative requests

The SHIFO timings stay the same as in B1 and B2. At C1 the I stage often holds a mini-lecture or a reading text, and Lesson C sometimes ends with a written task instead of a voice note.

New Spark for C1: Register Switch. The student gets one piece of information and says it four ways: to a doctor (clinical), to the patient (plain English), to a family member (gentle), and in Uzbek. Score accuracy, register and warmth. Hot Seat Interpreting and all B1 Sparks stay in use.

Groups: C1 works well in groups of 3–5. Seminar lessons (17, 27) need at least 2 students; with one student, the teacher takes the opposing view.

3. C1 timetable: 36 lessons at a glance

# Wk Type Lesson Goal: the student can… Grammar / language (C1) Spark

4. Assessment: Lessons 1, 18 and the final OSCE

At C1 the four skills are widened to cover register and professional interaction. Students complete C1 with 10 or more out of 12 at Lesson 36 and no skill below 2.

Skill 1 2 3 (C1 standard)
Vocabulary and register Correct words, but the wrong register for the listener Mostly right register; some shifts Switches easily between clinical, plain and academic English
Fluency and clarity Long pauses; listeners lose the thread Fluent, with some hesitation on complex points Fluent, organized and easy to follow at natural speed
Listening and interaction Follows the main points only Follows detail; responds appropriately Follows lectures and fast talk; handles questions, emotion and interruption
Accuracy and precision Errors in facts or meaning Rare errors, self-corrected Precise facts; nothing added or lost, including when interpreting

Score 0 when the skill is not yet shown.

Scoring at Lessons 18 and 36: score each of the 4 skills once across all the tasks or stations, using the best evidence from any of them. The total is out of 12. The OSCE station checklist (Lesson 35) helps you note evidence; it adds no points.

When Tasks Recording kept

Lesson 18 (midpoint) 3-minute case presentation; plain-language explanation of a consent form; 2-minute seminar contribution All three
Lesson 36 (final OSCE) Five timed stations: lecture summary; case presentation; patient education with teach-back; difficult conversation or complaint; interpreted exchange All five

Every week: one short written task (summary, note, care plan, report or reflection), marked for accuracy and register.

Completion: attend at least 32 of 36 lessons and reach the score above for the ShifoLife C1 Professional Medical English certificate of completion. It is a course certificate, not a CEFR, licensing or clinical qualification. For admission, students still need the English test their school requires.

teacher.title: Lectures and Note-taking
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can follow a lecture's structure, take notes that can be rebuilt into the lecture, summarize it in 1 minute and ask academic questions.

Written task: a 60-word summary of mini-lecture ML2.

Prepare: mini-lectures ML1 and ML2 and the falls lecture FP1 (read them aloud at natural speed; they are written to be spoken); a voice-note recording of ML1 for the Lesson 1 homework; the Cornell notes template and the symbol sheet (both printed in the Student Edition, Cards and texts · Week 1).

Lesson 1 · A Learn · Lecture signposting
Goal Follow the structure of a mini-lecture.
New words (10) signpost, outline, key concept, furthermore, in contrast, consequently, to illustrate, to sum up, digress, emphasize
Recycle (B2) learning objective, syllabus, debrief
Language Discourse markers that open, order, contrast, give examples and close a talk
Spark Listen and Answer
Assessment Baseline: the 90-second introduction (Start) and the Round 2 summary. Record both.
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Introduce yourself as a new nursing student to your class. Record it.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words in 5 groups: open (outline), order (furthermore), contrast (in contrast), example (to illustrate), close (to sum up).
24–32 I Spark: Listen and Answer on ML1, heard once at natural speed. Questions: How many points? What are they? Which phrase introduced the example? What is the main barrier?
32–50 F Round 1: the student underlines the signposts on the ML1 transcript. Round 2: the student gives a 1-minute summary of ML1 from memory (record it). Round 3: the student gives their own 1-minute mini-lecture on Why I chose nursing, using 5 signposts.
50–60 O Two priority errors, then retry. Exit check: 3 signposts from 3 groups. Set homework.

Mini-lecture ML1, hand hygiene (teacher reads): Today I'd like to talk about hand hygiene, and I'll cover three points: why it matters, when to do it, and why people forget. Firstly, why does it matter? Hands are the most common way germs move between patients. Consequently, hand hygiene is one of the simplest ways to prevent infection in hospital. Secondly, when should you do it? To illustrate, think of five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean procedure, after contact with body fluids, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings. Thirdly, why do people forget? In contrast to what we might expect, it's usually not lack of knowledge but time pressure and habit. So, to sum up: hands carry germs, there are five key moments, and the main barrier is habit, not knowledge.

Key: 3 points: why, when, why people forget · To illustrate introduced the example · the main barrier is time pressure and habit.

Stretch: spot the lecturer's emphasis words (the most common, simplest). Support: signpost table in view.

Homework: listen to the teacher's ML1 voice note again and write the outline in 5 lines.

Lesson 2 · B Practice · Note-taking from lectures
Goal Take usable notes and rebuild the lecture from them.
New words (9) Cornell notes, cue column, abbreviation, symbol, condense, reconstruct, key term, main idea, supporting detail
Recycle signpost, consequently, outline
Language Note style: drop articles and verbs; use symbols (↑ ↓ → ∴ ≈) and abbreviations (pt, hx, dx, tx, sx, w/, w/o, q2h)
Spark Error Hunt (teacher's notes vs the lecture)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: give the ML1 outline from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words and the symbol sheet. Cornell layout: notes on the right, key terms in the cue column, summary at the bottom.
16–30 I The teacher reads ML2 twice; the student takes Cornell notes. Compare with the model notes.
30–50 F Spark: Error Hunt (below). Round 1: the student rebuilds ML2 aloud from their notes only. Round 2: the teacher asks 3 detail questions; the student answers from the notes. Round 3 (unseen): lecture FP1 on falls prevention (below, about 2 minutes), heard once; notes, then a 30-second rebuild.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: write 5 symbols or abbreviations with their meanings. Set homework.

Mini-lecture ML2, pressure injuries (teacher reads): Today: pressure injuries: what they are, who is at risk, and prevention. A pressure injury is damage to the skin and the tissue underneath, caused by pressure over a long time, usually over a bone, such as the heels, the hips or the base of the spine. Who is at risk? Mainly patients who can't move easily: older adults, people after surgery, and people who are very ill. Poor nutrition and moist skin increase the risk. Prevention has three parts. First, change the patient's position regularly; many hospitals use a schedule of about every two hours. Second, keep the skin clean and dry. Third, check the skin every day, especially over bones. The key message: prevention is much easier than treatment.

Model notes: Pressure injuries (PI). Def: skin + tissue damage ← long pressure over bone (heels, hips, base of spine). Risk: ↓ mobility (elderly, post-op, very ill); poor nutrition + moist skin ↑ risk. Prevention: 1) reposition ≈ q2h; 2) skin clean + dry; 3) daily skin check over bones. Key: prevention > treatment.

Error Hunt (teacher's notes): PI: damage ← short pressure · risk ↑ w/ good nutrition · reposition q4h. Key: long pressure; poor nutrition; about every 2 hours.

Mini-lecture FP1, falls prevention (unseen; teacher reads, about 2 minutes): Today I'd like to talk about falls in hospital. I'll cover three things: why falls matter, who is most at risk, and what nurses can do. Firstly, why do falls matter? Falls are one of the most common safety incidents in hospital. Even a simple fall can cause a fracture, a head injury or a longer stay, and many patients become afraid of walking again. Secondly, who is at risk? The main risk factors are older age, a previous fall, confusion, weak legs, and medicines that can cause dizziness, such as sleeping tablets. Needing the toilet often, especially at night, also increases the risk. In contrast to what many people expect, most falls happen in the patient's own room, not in the corridor. Thirdly, what can nurses do? To illustrate, think of a patient who wants to go to the toilet at 3 a.m. First, keep the bed low and the call button within reach. Second, make sure the patient has non-slip footwear and their glasses. Third, keep the floor dry and the path to the bathroom clear, with a night light on. Finally, check high-risk patients regularly and offer the toilet before they ask. Consequently, many falls can be prevented with small, simple actions. So, to sum up: falls are common and harmful, the risk is highest for older, confused or dizzy patients, and simple checks at the bedside make a real difference.

Model notes (FP1): Falls: common + harmful (fracture, head injury, longer stay, fear of walking). Risk ↑: older, prev. fall, confusion, weak legs, meds → dizziness (sleeping tabs), toilet at night. Most falls in pt's room. Prevention: bed low + call button in reach; non-slip footwear + glasses; dry floor, clear path, night light; regular checks, offer toilet. ∴ small actions prevent falls. Rebuild key: 3 points (why, who, what to do), at least 3 risk factors and 3 actions.

Observer checks: notes rebuild the whole lecture · numbers kept · symbols used correctly · cue column filled.

Homework: make Cornell notes on C1 Week 1 in the Vocabulary Book: each word in the cue column, its meaning in the notes column, and a 2-line summary at the bottom.

Lesson 3 · C Perform · Summarizing and asking in class
Goal Give a 1-minute lecture summary and ask 2 academic questions.
New words (4) elaborate, query, synthesize, takeaway
Recycle Cornell notes, main idea, key term
Language Tentative academic questions: I was wondering whether you could expand on… Could you clarify what you meant by…? Am I right in thinking that…?
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded 1-minute ML2 summary and 2 questions; written 60-word summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: What makes a lecture easy or hard to follow?
5–12 H 4 new words. Model the summary (below): main idea first, then supporting points, then the takeaway.
12–20 I Teach the three question frames. The teacher, as lecturer, answers one question too briefly; the student follows up.
20–50 F Spark: 60-Second Report on ML2. Round 1: summary plus 2 questions to the teacher-lecturer. Round 2: lecture FP1 from Lesson 2, same task. Then the performance: record the ML2 summary and questions; write the 60-word summary in 10 minutes.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the written summary. Two errors, then retry.

Model summary (ML2): The lecture explained pressure injuries: damage to skin and tissue caused by long pressure over bony areas. The main risk is reduced mobility, with poor nutrition and moist skin adding to it. Prevention involves regular repositioning, keeping the skin clean and dry, and checking it daily. The main takeaway was that prevention is far easier than treatment.

Observer checks: main idea first · no copied sentences · questions tentative and specific · within 60 seconds.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): your own 1-minute mini-lecture on a health topic, using 5 signposts.

teacher.title: Reading Nursing Textbooks
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can skim and scan a textbook passage, decode unfamiliar medical terms from their parts, and summarize a passage in their own words without plagiarizing.

Written task: a 50-word summary of reading text RT1.

Prepare: reading text RT1 (below; students' copy in Cards and texts · Week 2); unseen paragraph RT2 on hypertension (below, Lesson 4 Round 3); the word-parts sheet (Lesson 5, also printed in the Student Edition).

Lesson 4 · A Learn · Academic words in nursing texts
Goal Use key textbook vocabulary.
New words (10) etiology, pathophysiology, clinical manifestation, risk factor, intervention, rationale, evidence-based, contraindication, outcome, complication
Recycle key concept, main idea, consequently
Language Academic verbs: indicates, suggests, demonstrates, is associated with, is characterized by
Spark Match and Speak (term ↔ plain definition)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: How do you read a long English text? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words. Sounds: e-ti-OL-o-gy, PATH-o-phys-i-OL-o-gy, con-tra-IN-di-CAY-tion.
24–32 I Skim RT1 in 30 seconds: What is it about? Then scan: find 3 risk factors and 3 manifestations. Underline the academic verbs.
32–50 F Spark (6 min): Match and Speak: each term ↔ a plain definition (rationale ↔ the reason for doing something). Round 1: the student explains RT1 to a classmate (the teacher) using 5 new words. Round 2: the teacher asks why questions; the student answers from the text. Round 3 (unseen): paragraph RT2 (below); the student finds the etiology, manifestations and complications.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 sentences with academic verbs. Set homework.

Reading text RT1, Type 2 diabetes: an overview: Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose. Its etiology involves both genetic and lifestyle risk factors, including obesity and physical inactivity. The underlying pathophysiology is insulin resistance: the body's cells do not respond normally to insulin. Clinical manifestations may include thirst, frequent urination and fatigue, although many patients have no symptoms at diagnosis. Research suggests that lifestyle interventions, such as increased activity and dietary change, can delay its onset in high-risk individuals. Long-term complications are associated with damage to the eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels. The rationale for regular monitoring is therefore to detect these changes early.

Scan key: risk factors: genetics, obesity, physical inactivity · manifestations: thirst, frequent urination, fatigue.

Unseen paragraph RT2, Hypertension (written for this book): Hypertension is a chronic condition characterized by persistently raised blood pressure in the arteries. In most adults its etiology is unknown, but risk factors include older age, obesity, a high-salt diet, physical inactivity and a family history of the condition. Many patients have no clinical manifestations, which is why hypertension is often called a silent condition; some report headaches or dizziness. If it is not controlled, it is associated with serious complications, including stroke, heart attack, heart failure and kidney disease. Key: etiology: usually unknown; risk factors: older age, obesity, high-salt diet, inactivity, family history · manifestations: often none; sometimes headache or dizziness · complications: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, kidney disease.

Stretch: explain why many patients have no symptoms matters for nurses. Support: glossary strip.

Homework: read RT1 aloud and record it; mark the stressed syllables in the 10 words.

Lesson 5 · B Practice · Medical word building
Goal Decode unfamiliar medical terms.
New word parts (9) hyper-, hypo-, tachy-, brady-, -itis, -ectomy, -ostomy, -algia, -emia
Roots (review sheet) cardi (heart), gastr (stomach), nephr (kidney), hepat (liver), neur (nerve), derm (skin), oste (bone), pneum / pulmon (lung)
Recycle etiology, complication, rationale
Language Word building and stress shift: CAR-di-ac → car-di-OL-o-gy
Spark Odd One Out
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: explain RT1 to a family member. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 parts with the root sheet. Spark: Odd One Out: appendectomy, tonsillectomy, colostomy, mastectomy (colostomy: -ostomy = an opening, not a removal).
16–30 I Decode 10 terms (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student decodes the 10 terms aloud. Round 2: the teacher gives definitions; the student builds the term (inflammation of the stomach → gastritis). Round 3 (unseen): 5 new terms; the student guesses from the parts, then checks with the key.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: decode 3 terms. Set homework.

Decode list: bradycardia (slow heart rate) · tachypnea (fast breathing) · hepatitis (liver inflammation) · nephrectomy (kidney removal) · neuralgia (nerve pain) · hyperglycemia (high blood sugar) · hypotension (low blood pressure) · gastritis (stomach inflammation) · colostomy (an opening from the colon) · dermatitis (skin inflammation).

Round 3 terms and key: pericarditis (inflammation around the heart; peri- = around) · cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal; chole = bile, cyst = bladder) · polyuria (passing a lot of urine; poly- = many) · dysphagia (difficulty swallowing; dys- = difficult, -phagia = eating) · hematuria (blood in urine; hemat = blood).

Stretch: build 3 new terms of your own and test the teacher. Support: parts sheet in view.

Homework: make 20 word-part flashcards and record 10 terms with their meanings.

Lesson 6 · C Perform · Paraphrase and summary
Goal Write a 50-word summary in your own words.
New words (4) paraphrase, quotation, cite, original wording
Recycle plagiarism, synthesize, condense
Language Paraphrasing: synonyms, a new word form, a new structure, a new order
Spark Register Switch
Perform task Written 50-word summary of RT1 and a recorded 60-second oral version
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: decode 5 terms from Lesson 5 and use each in a sentence.
5–12 H 4 new words. Show a good paraphrase and a patchwriting example (below). Patchwriting counts as plagiarism in US schools.
12–20 I Spark: Register Switch with one RT1 fact (below).
20–50 F Round 1: paraphrase 3 RT1 sentences. Round 2: plan the summary (main idea → 3 points). Then the performance: write the 50-word summary (10 minutes) and record a 60-second oral version.
50–60 O Mark the summary: own words, accuracy, length. Two errors, then retry.

Paraphrase examples. Original: Clinical manifestations may include thirst, frequent urination and fatigue. Good: Patients might notice that they are thirsty, need to urinate often and feel tired. Patchwriting (too close): Clinical signs may include thirst, frequent urination and tiredness.

Model summary (RT1, about 50 words): Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition in which the body does not use insulin properly, so blood sugar is high. Genes, weight and inactivity raise the risk. Many people have no symptoms at first. Lifestyle changes can delay it, and regular checks find damage to eyes, kidneys and nerves early.

Register Switch (fact: Long-term complications are associated with damage to the eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels): to a doctor: Long-term complications include retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy and vascular disease. · to the patient: Over many years, high sugar can damage your eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels. That's why check-ups matter. · to family: Helping her keep her sugar steady protects her eyes, kidneys and feet over time. · in Uzbek: Yillar davomida qondagi qand miqdori yuqori bo‘lsa, ko‘z, buyrak, nervlar va qon tomirlari zararlanishi mumkin.

Observer checks: no sentence copied · meaning unchanged · main idea first · 50 words, plus or minus 5.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the Register Switch for one RT1 fact of your choice.

teacher.title: Case Presentations
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can order a case presentation correctly, speak in compact clinical style, and present a 3-minute case and handle questions.

Written task: a written case summary (120 words) of CP2.

Prepare: case CP1 (teacher presents); jumbled case cards CP2 (students' copy in Cards and texts · Week 3); unseen card CP4 (Lesson 7); unseen handoff RH1 (Lesson 8); hidden case CP3; the presentation frame.

Presentation frame: identifying data → presenting complaint → history of present illness → past medical history → medicines and allergies → social history → findings → plan (as documented by the team).

Lesson 7 · A Learn · Case presentation structure
Goal Order a case presentation correctly.
New words (10) case presentation, identifying data, presents with, history of present illness (HPI), past medical history (PMH), review of systems, pertinent positive, findings, plan, as documented
Recycle (B2) chief complaint, pertinent negative, social history
Language The standard opening with a reduced relative clause: Mrs. X is a 64-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, presenting with a 3-day history of… (full form: …who presents with…)
Spark Listen and Answer
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: decode 5 word-part terms in a sentence each. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words on the frame.
24–32 I Spark: Listen and Answer; the teacher presents CP1. The student labels each part of the frame and answers: age? key history? main findings? plan?
32–50 F Round 1: the student sorts the jumbled CP2 cards into frame order. Round 2: the student presents CP2 with the frame in view. Round 3 (unseen): card CP4 (below), 5 minutes to prepare, then present.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: the opening sentence for CP2 without notes. Set homework.

Case CP1 (teacher presents): Mrs. Karima Yusupova is a 64-year-old retired teacher with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension who presents with a 3-day history of a red, painful area on her left lower leg. The redness started near a small scratch and has spread. She reports pain of 6 out of 10 and feeling feverish. She denies chest pain or shortness of breath. She takes a diabetes tablet and a blood-pressure tablet and has no known allergies. She lives with her husband and doesn't smoke. On assessment, her temperature is 38.1, heart rate 96, blood pressure 138 over 84, and the red area measures about 10 by 6 centimeters and is warm to touch. The plan, as documented by the team, is blood tests and review by the physician.

Jumbled case CP2 (fictional): Islom Rakhimov, 47, construction worker · asthma · cough and shortness of breath for 5 days, worse at night · yellow sputum; fever 38.4 °C · rescue inhaler 6 times a day · no allergies · smokes 10 cigarettes a day · SpO2 93% on room air, RR 24; wheeze heard on the physician's examination · plan as documented: chest X-ray and nebulizer as ordered.

Case CP4 (unseen, fictional): Gulnora Ismoilova, 35, accountant · no significant past medical history · burning on urination and passing urine often for 2 days · since this morning, pain in the right side of her back and fever 38.6 °C; nausea, no vomiting · no regular medicines · allergy: penicillin (rash) · lives with her husband and two children; doesn't smoke · HR 104, BP 118/76, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air · plan as documented: urine test, blood tests and physician review. Model opening: Mrs. Ismoilova is a 35-year-old woman with no significant past medical history, presenting with a 2-day history of burning on urination and frequency, and right-sided back pain and fever since this morning.

Stretch: add one pertinent negative to CP2. Support: frame with sentence starters.

Homework: record the CP2 presentation (2 minutes).

Lesson 8 · B Practice · Concise clinical language
Goal Compress long sentences into presentation style.
New words (9) notable for, significant for, unremarkable, otherwise well, ongoing, worsening, x-day history, onset of, associated with
Recycle presents with, HPI, pertinent positive
Language Nominalization: She has been coughing for 5 days and it's getting worse → a 5-day history of worsening cough
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: present CP2 from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Unremarkable = normal, nothing important found.
16–30 I Compression drill (below). Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student rewrites CP2 in compressed style. Round 2: delivers it in under 2 minutes. Round 3 (unseen): the teacher reads handoff RH1 (below); the student compresses it into a 3-sentence presentation.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: compress 2 sentences aloud. Set homework.

Compression drill (key in brackets): She started having pain 3 days ago and it's getting worse (3-day history of worsening pain) · He has had diabetes for 10 years (10-year history of diabetes) · The chest X-ray didn't show anything important (chest X-ray unremarkable) · Apart from that she is healthy (otherwise well) · The main thing in his history is asthma (PMH notable for asthma) · She feels sick, and it comes with the headache (headache associated with nausea).

Error Hunt (teacher presents): Mr. Rakhimov is a 47-year-old man who is presenting for a cough since 5 days which is worst at night. His history is remarkable. Key: presents with; a 5-day history of cough; worse at night; notable for asthma (remarkable on its own sounds like praise; clinical English says remarkable for asthma or notable for asthma).

Handoff RH1 (unseen; teacher reads it in a rambling way): OK, so, the lady in bed 7, Mrs. Abdullaeva, she's 71, she came in, when was it, yesterday afternoon I think, because she'd been really short of breath, for about four days she said, and it's got worse, especially when she walks to the bathroom, and she's got heart failure, that's in her notes, and diabetes too, and her ankles are quite swollen, both of them, and her oxygen was 91 on room air earlier, so she's on 2 liters now and she's 95, and the doctor's seen her and they've started the water medicine through the IV, and, oh, she's allergic to aspirin, it gives her a rash, and her daughter's coming at six. Model 3-sentence presentation: Mrs. Abdullaeva is a 71-year-old woman with heart failure and diabetes, admitted yesterday with a 4-day history of worsening shortness of breath on exertion and swelling of both ankles. Her SpO2 was 91% on room air and is 95% on 2 L, and an IV diuretic has been started as documented. She is allergic to aspirin (rash), and her daughter is visiting at 18:00.

Observer checks: compressed but complete · numbers exact · frame order kept · under 2 minutes.

Homework: write the 120-word CP2 case summary.

Lesson 9 · C Perform · Presenting a case
Goal Present a 3-minute case and answer questions.
New words (4) attending physician, clarifying question, in summary, defer
Recycle notable for, unremarkable, presents with
Language Hedged answers: I didn't assess that, but I can find out. As far as I know… I'd defer to the physician on that.
Spark Mystery Patient
Perform task Recorded 3-minute presentation of CP3 and answers to 2 questions
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: compress handoff RH1 from Lesson 8.
5–12 H 4 new words. It is fine not to know; it is not fine to guess.
12–20 I Spark: Mystery Patient; the student interviews the teacher as CP3 (hidden) for 5 minutes.
20–50 F Round 1: 5 minutes to prepare, then the 3-minute presentation. Round 2: the teacher, as attending physician, asks the 2 questions (below). Then the performance: record Rounds 1 and 2 together.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Case CP3 (hidden, fictional): Dildora Ahmedova, 58, teacher; hypertension; 2 days of dizziness and headache; home BP 182/104 this morning; denies chest pain, weakness or vision changes; ran out of her blood-pressure tablets 1 week ago; lives alone; no allergies. Now: BP 178/102, HR 84, alert and oriented, speech clear. Plan as documented: physician review.

Attending's questions: When did she last take her tablets? (answerable: 1 week ago) · What's her kidney function? (not assessed: That wasn't available to me, but I can check the labs.)

Observer checks: frame order · compressed style · honest when unsure · 3 minutes, plus or minus 20 seconds.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the CP3 presentation, improved.

teacher.title: Chronic Illness and Complex Histories
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can discuss multiple long-term conditions, explore barriers to self-management without judging, and run a 10-minute complex history with a prioritized summary.

Why this week matters: many Uzbek patients live with diabetes and several other conditions. Nurses who speak Uzbek will meet this patient group often.

Written task: a 100-word nursing summary of case CI3.

Prepare: chronic-illness cards CI1–CI2; hidden case CI3.

Lesson 10 · A Learn · Chronic illness and polypharmacy
Goal Discuss complex long-term conditions.
New words (10) chronic disease, comorbidity, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, adherence, self-management, glycemic control, neuropathy, retinopathy, foot care
Recycle complication, risk factor, outcome
Language Complex noun phrases: a 70-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease, taking nine medicines
Spark Match and Speak (term ↔ meaning)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: present CP3 from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words. Adherence = taking treatment as agreed (preferred to compliance, which sounds like blame).
24–32 I Spark (6 min): Match and Speak (polypharmacy ↔ taking many medicines at once; self-management ↔ what the patient does day to day…). Model one complex noun phrase per card.
32–50 F Round 1: interview teacher-patient CI1 about his conditions and how he manages them. Round 2: describe CI1 in 3 complex noun phrases. Round 3 (unseen): card CI2.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one complex noun phrase for CI2. Set homework.

Cards (fictional): CI1 – Mr. Ergash Mirzaev, 70: type 2 diabetes for 15 years, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (documented); takes 9 medicines; often forgets evening doses; burning feet at night; blurred vision; lives with his son's family. CI2 – Mrs. Nodira Sobirova, 61: heart failure (documented), type 2 diabetes, arthritis; short of breath on stairs; swollen ankles; finds the low-salt diet hard.

Stretch: ask Which of your conditions worries you most? Support: term sheet in view.

Homework: record a description of CI1 in complex noun phrases.

Lesson 11 · B Practice · Lifestyle, barriers and motivation
Goal Ask about barriers without judging.
New words (9) barrier, affordability, transport, routine, motivation, readiness, ambivalence, non-judgmental, social support
Recycle adherence, self-management, polypharmacy
Language Tentative questions: I was wondering whether… What gets in the way of…? On a scale of 0 to 10, how ready do you feel to…?
Spark Uzbek Bridge (barrier statements)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: describe CI2. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Ambivalence = wanting and not wanting to change at the same time; it is normal.
16–30 I Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below). Model 4 non-judgmental questions.
30–50 F Round 1: explore CI1's barriers. Round 2: ask the readiness question and follow up: Why a 4 and not a 2? Round 3 (new detail): the patient gets defensive: Are you saying it's my fault? The student rephrases without blame.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 tentative questions. Set homework.

Uzbek Bridge:

Uzbek Model English
Dorilar juda qimmat, shuning uchun ba’zan yarim dozada ichaman. The medicines are very expensive, so sometimes I take half the dose.
Kechqurun charchab qolaman va dori ichishni unutaman. In the evening I get tired and forget to take my medicine.
To‘ylarda va mehmonda shirinlikdan voz kechish qiyin. At weddings and when visiting people, it's hard to say no to sweets.
O‘g‘lim ishda, klinikaga olib boradigan odam yo‘q. My son is at work, so there's no one to take me to the clinic.

Observer checks: no blame words (should have, non-compliant) · open and tentative questions · the patient's own reasons explored · cultural context respected.

Stretch: reflect ambivalence: Part of you wants to…, and part of you… Support: question frames.

Homework: record 5 non-judgmental barrier questions.

Lesson 12 · C Perform · The complex history
Goal Run a 10-minute history and give a prioritized summary.
New words (4) prioritize, salient, overarching, collateral history
Recycle barrier, adherence, comorbidity
Language Cleft sentences for priorities: What concerns me most is*… It's the evening doses that* he misses.
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded 10-minute interview with CI3 and a 90-second prioritized summary; written 100-word summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: What makes a history "complex"?
5–12 H 4 new words. Collateral history = information from family or carers.
12–20 I Model the prioritized summary (below). Cleft sentences in 4 minutes.
20–50 F Spark: 60-Second Report on CI1's main problem. Then the performance: a 10-minute interview with CI3 (hidden; the teacher also plays the daughter) and a 90-second prioritized summary, recorded. Then 10 minutes to write the 100-word summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the summary. Two errors, then retry.

Case CI3 (hidden, fictional): Mrs. Rano Tursunova, 66: type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension, knee arthritis; 8 medicines, buys only some because of cost; skips insulin when her sugar "feels fine"; a new sore on her left big toe for 1 week that she didn't notice at first; meter readings 220–300 mg/dL this week. Daughter: Mom is more forgetful lately. Lives alone; her daughter visits weekly.

Model prioritized summary: What concerns me most is the new sore on her left big toe, which she didn't notice for a week. Second, her glucose has been 220 to 300 this week, and she skips insulin when she feels fine and buys only some of her tablets because of cost. Third, her daughter reports that she is more forgetful. I'd like the team to look at the foot today, and I'd suggest involving a social worker about medication costs.

Observer checks: foot sore found and prioritized · cost barrier found · collateral history used · summary in priority order.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the CI3 summary, improved.

teacher.title: Patient Education and Health Literacy
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can turn medical jargon into plain English, teach a complex home routine in chunks with teach-back, and teach a patient through an interpreter.

Written task: rewrite leaflet paragraph LF1 in plain language (30–50 words).

Prepare: leaflet paragraph LF1 and leaflet LF2 (fictional; students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 5); the Hot Seat lines (Lesson 15); paper for drawing simple visuals.

Lesson 13 · A Learn · Plain language
Goal Turn jargon into plain English without losing meaning.
New words (10) health literacy, jargon, plain language, numeracy, chunk, visual aid, everyday equivalent, simplify, misconception, empower
Recycle rationale, intervention, adherence
Language Plain-language rules: short sentences, active voice, everyday words, concrete numbers, one idea per sentence
Spark Register Switch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: give the CI3 summary. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words with the jargon list (below). Warn about traps: to patients, a negative result can sound like bad news.
24–32 I Model rewriting LF1 (below). Spark: Register Switch on one LF1 sentence.
32–50 F Round 1: the student rewrites LF1 aloud, sentence by sentence. Round 2: explains it to a teacher-patient with low health literacy. Round 3 (unseen): My report says HbA1c 8.5%. What does that mean? The student explains what the test measures (average blood sugar over about 3 months) and refers the meaning of the number to the doctor.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 3 jargon words → plain. Set homework.

Jargon → plain: hypertension → high blood pressure · glucose → blood sugar · adhere to → take as agreed · monitor → check · oral → by mouth · prior to → before · edema → swelling · hypoglycemia → low blood sugar · benign → not cancer · negative result → nothing worrying was found.

LF1 (original): Patients with hypertension should adhere to their prescribed antihypertensive regimen and monitor their blood pressure regularly. Sodium intake should be limited to reduce cardiovascular risk. Plain model: If you have high blood pressure, take your blood pressure tablets every day, as your doctor told you. Check your blood pressure often. Eat less salt: this helps protect your heart.

Stretch: add a visual: draw a simple daily tablet chart. Support: jargon list in view.

Homework: write the LF1 plain-language version (30–50 words).

Lesson 14 · B Practice · Chunk and check
Goal Teach a complex routine in chunks with teach-back.
New words (9) regimen, injection site, rotate, storage, sharps container, glucose tablets, foot inspection, return demonstration, reinforce
Recycle chunk, plain language, teach-back
Language Softened instructions and conditionals: It's best to… Try to… If your sugar is under 70, the leaflet says to…
Spark Listen and Answer
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: explain HbA1c in plain English. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Return demonstration = the patient shows (or describes) how they will do it.
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer: the teacher teaches LF2 as a nurse. Questions: Where is the unopened pen stored? What does the leaflet say to do if sugar is under 70? How often are the feet checked?
30–50 F Round 1: the student teaches LF2 in 3 chunks (insulin → low sugar → feet), with teach-back after each. Round 2: return demonstration: the patient describes injecting into the same spot every day; the student gently corrects (rotate sites). Round 3 (unseen): a patient with low numeracy struggles with 70; the student uses a visual aid.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one chunk with teach-back. Set homework.

Leaflet LF2, Starting insulin at home (fictional, supplied by the clinic): keep unopened pens in the fridge; the pen you are using can stay at room temperature for up to 28 days · inject into the abdomen or thigh and rotate sites · check your sugar before breakfast and before dinner · if it is under 70 mg/dL, take 4 glucose tablets and check again in 15 minutes · check your feet every day for cuts or redness · put used needles in the sharps container.

Observer checks: 3 chunks · teach-back after each · only leaflet content · correction kind and clear.

Stretch: handle Can I skip insulin if I feel fine? by referring to the team. Support: chunk cards.

Homework: record the LF2 teaching (3 minutes).

Lesson 15 · C Perform · Teaching through an interpreter
Goal Teach a patient with limited English through an interpreter.
New words (4) briefing, pacing, first-person address, cultural broker
Recycle health literacy, chunk, teach-back
Language Speak to the patient, not the interpreter: Mrs. Tursunova, how do you store your insulin? (not Ask her how…). Short turns; pause.
Spark Hot Seat Interpreting
Perform task Recorded LF2 teaching through an interpreter, then 3 turns as the interpreter
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: What makes interpreted conversations go wrong?
5–12 H 4 new words. Briefing model (below).
12–20 I Spark: Hot Seat Interpreting: the three LF2 sentences (English → Uzbek), then the three patient questions (Uzbek → English) below.
20–50 F Round 1: brief the interpreter (the teacher). Round 2: teach LF2 through the interpreter, with teach-back. Round 3: swap roles; the student interprets the 3 patient questions (below) and the nurse's answers. Then the performance: record Rounds 2 and 3. In groups: nurse, interpreter, patient, rotating.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Briefing model: Before we start: I'll speak in short sentences and pause after each one. Please interpret everything, in the first person. If anything is unclear or you need a repeat, just tell me.

Hot Seat lines (Lesson 15) with Uzbek models:

Turn English Uzbek
LF2 sentence 1 Keep unopened pens in the fridge. Ochilmagan insulin shprits-ruchkalarini muzlatkichda saqlang.
LF2 sentence 2 The pen you are using can stay at room temperature for up to 28 days. Hozir ishlatayotgan shprits-ruchkangizni xona haroratida 28 kungacha saqlasangiz bo‘ladi.
LF2 sentence 3 If your sugar is under 70, take 4 glucose tablets and check again in 15 minutes. Agar qandingiz 70 dan past bo‘lsa, 4 ta glyukoza tabletkasini qabul qiling va 15 daqiqadan keyin yana tekshiring.
Patient question 1 Can I inject the insulin in the same place every day? Insulinni har kuni bitta joyga ukol qilsam bo‘ladimi?
Patient question 2 If I don't have a fridge at home, where do I keep the pen? Uyda muzlatkichim bo‘lmasa, shprits-ruchkani qayerda saqlayman?
Patient question 3 If I don't have glucose tablets, what do I do? Glyukoza tabletkasi bo‘lmasa, nima qilaman?

The nurse answers from LF2 only (question 1: rotate sites) and refers questions 2 and 3 to the team.

Observer checks: briefing given · patient addressed directly · short turns · teach-back done through the interpreter.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the LF1 plain-language version, read aloud, then the briefing.

teacher.title: Consent, Ethics and Patient Rights · Midpoint
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can explain consent and confidentiality in plain English, argue a position politely in a seminar, and complete the midpoint tasks.

Written task: a 150-word position paragraph on dilemma ED1.

Prepare: consent form excerpts CF1 and CF2 (fictional); dilemmas ED1 and ED2; midpoint case CP-M (CF1 and ED1 are in Cards and texts · Week 6; CF2, ED2 and CP-M are unseen until Lesson 18: copy them from this book); the Lesson 1 recordings.

The nurse's role in consent (US): the provider doing the procedure explains it and obtains consent. The nurse may witness the signature, checks that the patient understands, and tells the provider if they don't.

Lesson 16 · A Learn · Consent and patient rights
Goal Use the language of consent and rights.
New words (10) informed consent, capacity, autonomy, voluntary, witness, withdraw, advance directive, health care proxy, confidentiality, HIPAA
Recycle consent form, dignity, permission
Language Formal register and the passive in documents: Consent must be obtained… The risks have been explained to me.
Spark Match and Speak
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Who decides about a patient's treatment in Uzbekistan, and who in the USA? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words. HIPAA = the US law protecting patients' health information. Health care proxy = the person chosen to decide if the patient can't.
24–32 I Spark (6 min): Match and Speak (term ↔ plain meaning). Read CF1 and its plain version (below).
32–50 F Round 1: the student explains CF1 in plain English. Round 2: the patient says I don't really understand what they'll do; the student doesn't witness yet and tells the provider. Round 3 (unseen): a relative phones and asks for the patient's results; the student answers within confidentiality rules (below).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: explain capacity and withdraw in plain words. Set homework.

CF1 (fictional): I, ___, consent to a colonoscopy to be performed by Dr. Hughes. The nature of the procedure, its expected benefits, material risks (including bleeding and perforation) and alternatives have been explained to me. I understand that I may withdraw consent at any time before the procedure. Plain version: This form says you agree to a colonoscopy, a camera test of the bowel, by Dr. Hughes. It says the doctor explained what will happen, why, the main risks, like bleeding or a small tear, and other options. You can change your mind at any time before the test.

Confidentiality model: I'm sorry, I can't share any information over the phone. If your mother agrees, she can tell us who may receive information, and the team can speak with you then.

Stretch: explain an advance directive to a family. Support: term sheet.

Homework: record the CF1 plain explanation.

Lesson 17 · B Practice · Ethics seminar
Goal Argue a position politely in a seminar.
New words (9) dilemma, stance, counter-argument, concede, justify, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, cultural norms
Recycle autonomy, capacity, confidentiality
Language Hedged argument: It could be argued that… While I take your point,… On balance,… I see it slightly differently.
Spark Error Hunt (repair rude or absolute statements)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: explain confidentiality to a relative. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words, including the four principles: autonomy, beneficence (do good), non-maleficence (do no harm), justice (fairness).
16–30 I Spark: Error Hunt: You're wrong. → I see it differently. · Doctors always know best. → In many cases… · Everybody knows that… → Research suggests… Read dilemma ED1.
30–50 F Round 1: prepare a position: 2 reasons and 1 concession. Round 2: a 2-minute seminar contribution. Round 3: the teacher challenges; the student concedes a point and defends the rest. One student alone: the teacher takes the opposite view throughout.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 concession + 1 counter-argument. Set homework.

Dilemma ED1 (fictional): An adult Uzbek patient's family asks the team not to tell their father about his serious diagnosis, because in their culture it would take away his hope. The patient has capacity and has asked the nurse: "What's wrong with me?" Possible lines of argument: autonomy and the right to know; family and cultural norms; asking the patient how much he wants to know; the nurse's role (refer to the provider, never decide alone).

Observer checks: position clear · reasons given · a concession made · polite, hedged language throughout.

Homework: write the 150-word position paragraph.

Lesson 18 · C Perform · Midpoint check
Goal Present a case, explain a form plainly, and contribute to a seminar.
New words None. Review Weeks 1–6.
Assessment Midpoint. Score each of the 4 skills once across the three tasks, using the best evidence (total /12); compare with Lesson 1.
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: Which C1 skill has grown most for you?
5–8 — Explain the 3 tasks and the rubric. No coaching. Record everything.
8–20 Task 1 5 minutes to prepare, then a 3-minute presentation of CP-M; the teacher asks 1 question.
20–30 Task 2 Explain CF2 in plain English to a teacher-patient, with teach-back.
30–40 Task 3 A 2-minute seminar contribution on ED2, then a reply to one challenge.
40–50 Review Play 20 seconds of the Lesson 1 summary, then today's presentation. The student names 2 improvements.
50–60 O Scores, 2 strengths, 2 goals for Weeks 7–12.

Case CP-M (fictional): Bahodir Saidov, 52, driver; type 2 diabetes; 4-day history of fever, cough and right-sided chest pain on breathing; T 38.7 °C, RR 26, SpO2 92% on room air, HR 110. Plan as documented: chest X-ray, blood cultures, physician review.

CF2 (fictional): I understand that blood products carry a small risk of reactions, including fever and allergic reactions, and a very small risk of infection. Alternatives have been discussed with me.

Dilemma ED2: Should nurses ever use a family member as an interpreter?

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): your ED2 contribution, improved.

teacher.title: Difficult Conversations
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can respond to strong emotion with a full range of empathic statements, support a patient and family after difficult news, and hold a 5-minute supportive conversation.

The nurse's role: the physician gives a diagnosis and prognosis. The nurse supports, checks understanding, notices needs and refers. Students never guess an answer to Am I going to die?

Written task: a 120-word factual note of the concerns the patient expressed in Lesson 21.

Prepare: card DN-A and patient lines PL1–PL5 (Lesson 19; students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 7); the family dialogue; hidden card DN-B. Keep the tone calm; change any card a student finds personally difficult.

Lesson 19 · A Learn · The language of empathy
Goal Use a full range of empathic statements.
New words (10) acknowledge, empathic statement, name the emotion, legitimize, explore, silence, presence, grief, hope, distressing
Recycle validate, coping, support
Language NURSE statements. Name: It sounds like you're frightened. Understand: I can understand why you'd feel that way. Respect: You've been so strong through all of this. Support: I'll be here, and we'll go through this together. Explore: Tell me more about what worries you most.
Spark Match and Speak (patient line ↔ NURSE type)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Describe a time someone listened to you well. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words and NURSE. Silence is a skill: count to 5 before speaking.
24–32 I Spark (6 min): Match and Speak; patient lines PL1–PL5 (below), each matched to the best NURSE response.
32–50 F Round 1: respond to PL1–PL5 in your own words, one per NURSE type. Round 2: a conversation with card DN-A. Round 3 (new detail): the patient is angry, not sad: Why did nobody find this earlier? The student names the anger and doesn't defend or blame.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one statement of each NURSE type. Set homework.

Card DN-A (fictional): Mrs. Feruza Alimova, 52. An hour ago the doctor told her that her biopsy shows cancer and explained the plan. She is tearful: I keep thinking about my children.

Patient lines PL1–PL5 (fictional) and NURSE responses a–e (for matching):

Line The patient says Response
PL1 I just keep shaking. I don't even know what I'm feeling. a. You've done so much for your family.
PL2 Anyone would be upset, wouldn't they? Or am I overreacting? b. Take your time. Tell me more about what's on your mind.
PL3 I looked after my husband for ten years, and now this. c. It sounds like this has been a real shock.
PL4 I'm scared of going through this alone. d. You won't be on your own. I'll be here, and the team will be with you.
PL5 There's something else bothering me, but it's hard to say. e. I can understand why you'd feel this way. It's a lot to take in.

Key: PL1 c (Name) · PL2 e (Understand) · PL3 a (Respect) · PL4 d (Support) · PL5 b (Explore).

Observer checks: emotion named · silence used · no false reassurance (Everything will be fine) · at least one exploring question.

Stretch: combine two NURSE types in one turn. Support: NURSE card.

Homework: record 5 NURSE responses to DN-A.

Lesson 20 · B Practice · After difficult news
Goal Support a patient and family after difficult news.
New words (9) absorb, understanding, family meeting, decision-maker, palliative care, comfort, uncertainty, spiritual care, chaplain
Recycle dignity, preference, empathic statement
Language What's your understanding of what's happening? I wonder if… Would it help if…? Some people like to hear everything themselves; others prefer their family to be involved. What would you like?
Spark Listen and Answer (a family conversation)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: respond to DN-A with three NURSE types. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Palliative care = care focused on comfort and quality of life. In many Uzbek families the eldest son speaks for the family: ask the patient what they want, never assume.
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer (below).
30–50 F Round 1: check DN-A's understanding after the doctor's visit. Round 2: a family meeting role-play (the teacher plays the patient and the son); the student asks the patient's preference first. Round 3 (new detail): Am I going to die? The student responds (model below).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 understanding question + 1 preference question. Set homework.

Family dialogue (teacher reads): Patient (Mr. Akbar Nurmatov, 74): My son Jasur handles these things. Tell him everything; I'll listen. Son: We'd like to know about palliative care, and my father would like an imam to visit. Questions: Who does the patient want informed? What two kinds of support are requested? Who should each request go to? Key: his son, with the patient present; palliative-care information (to the team) and spiritual care (chaplaincy can arrange an imam).

Model response to Am I going to die?: That's a really important question, and I don't want to guess. Can I ask what's making you think about that? I'll make sure the doctor talks with you about it today.

Observer checks: the patient's preference asked first · no prognosis given · requests referred to the right person · respectful of culture.

Homework: record the response to Am I going to die? and one preference question.

Lesson 21 · C Perform · A supportive conversation
Goal Hold a 5-minute supportive conversation and pass on what the patient needs.
New words (4) reflective listening, therapeutic silence, compassionate, self-care
Recycle NURSE, acknowledge, explore
Language Reflecting back: So what I'm hearing is… It sounds as if the hardest part is…
Spark Mystery Patient (a hidden concern)
Perform task Recorded 5-minute conversation and a 30-second handoff to the nurse; written 120-word note
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: How do nurses look after themselves after hard conversations? (self-care)
5–12 H 4 new words. Model reflecting back.
12–20 I Explain the task: the patient's first worry may not be the real one.
20–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient with card DN-B. Then the performance: a 5-minute conversation and a 30-second handoff to the nurse, recorded. Then 10 minutes to write the 120-word note.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the note. Brief debrief: How did that feel?

Card DN-B (hidden, fictional): Mrs. Lobar Qodirova, 67, admitted for tests. She talks first about pain (3/10, managed). Her real worry, which she shares only if the student explores and reflects: Who will look after my son? He has a disability and I'm his only carer.

Handoff model: Mrs. Qodirova's pain is 3 out of 10. Her main worry is care for her son, who has a disability; she is his only carer. Could we ask the social worker to see her?

Observer checks: the real concern found · reflecting back used · silence allowed · a correct referral in the handoff.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): a NURSE-based response to DN-A, then the DN-B handoff.

teacher.title: Complaints and De-escalation
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can respond to a complaint without blaming anyone, calm an angry relative while staying safe, and write a factual summary of a complaint.

Written task: an 80-word factual summary of complaint C3.

Prepare: complaint cards C1–C3 and angry-relative card AR1 (students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 8).

The five steps: Listen → Acknowledge → Apologize for the experience → Act (or find someone who can) → Follow up with a time.

Lesson 22 · A Learn · Complaints and apologies
Goal Respond to a complaint without blaming anyone.
New words (10) complaint, grievance, patient relations, service recovery, accountability, fault, inconvenience, resolve, expectation, sincere
Recycle acknowledge, escalate, empathic statement
Language Apologize for the experience, not with blame: I'm sorry this happened. I'm sorry you've had to wait. ✗ It was the night nurse's fault. Let me find out what happened.
Spark Register Switch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Describe good customer service you've received. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words and the five steps. Patient relations = the hospital office that handles complaints.
24–32 I Model a response to C1 (below). Spark: Register Switch on C1: to the patient, to the charge nurse (factual), to the family, in Uzbek.
32–50 F Round 1: respond to C1 with the five steps. Round 2: complaint C2. Round 3 (new detail): Give me the name of the night nurse. I'm reporting her. The student answers: You have every right to raise this. I can put you in touch with patient relations.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 sincere apology without blame. Set homework.

Complaint cards (fictional): C1 – I've been waiting three hours for my pain medicine! Nobody answers the call button! C2 – My mother's meals arrive cold every day, and nobody helps her eat.

Model response to C1: I'm really sorry you've been waiting in pain; that shouldn't happen. Let me check your medicine with your nurse right now. I'll come back in 10 minutes to tell you what's happening.

Register Switch on C1 (model): to the patient: I'm really sorry you've been waiting in pain. I'm checking your medicine with your nurse right now. · to the charge nurse (factual): My patient has waited three hours for his pain medicine and says the call button wasn't answered. Could you check his order with me now? · to the family: I'm sorry your father has been waiting. I'm checking his pain medicine with his nurse now, and I'll come back to you in 10 minutes. · in Uzbek (to the patient): Og‘riq qoldiruvchi doringizni uch soat kutganingiz uchun uzr so‘rayman. Hozir hamshirangiz bilan tekshiraman va 10 daqiqadan keyin qaytib kelib aytaman.

Observer checks: all 5 steps · no blame on colleagues · a concrete action · a follow-up time.

Stretch: handle a complaint that is partly unfair, politely. Support: five-step card.

Homework: record responses to C1 and C2.

Lesson 23 · B Practice · De-escalation
Goal Calm an angry relative, set limits and stay safe.
New words (9) de-escalate, raised voice, personal space, body language, threatening, security, safe distance, cool down, limit-setting
Recycle boundary, frustrated, grievance
Language Calm and firm: I can see you're very upset. I want to help you. I can't help while you're shouting at me. Would you like to sit down and tell me what happened?
Spark Error Hunt (inflaming phrases)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: respond to C2. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Body language: open hands, side-on, at a safe distance, a lower voice. Safety first: if there is a threat, step away and call for help.
16–30 I Spark: Error Hunt; the student repairs each phrase: Calm down! · That's not my job. · You'll have to wait like everyone else. · There's nothing I can do.
30–50 F Round 1: angry relative AR1. Round 2: AR1 raises his voice; the student sets a limit calmly and offers a choice. Round 3 (unseen): a relative becomes threatening; the student steps back, leaves the room and calls the charge nurse or security.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 limit-setting sentence + 1 choice. Set homework.

Error Hunt key: Calm down! → I can see you're upset. · That's not my job. → Let me find the right person for you. · You'll have to wait like everyone else. → I know waiting is hard. Here's what's happening… · There's nothing I can do. → Here's what I can do right now…

Card AR1 (fictional): Mr. Jahongir Sultonov, 40, son of a patient: My father has been here since morning and no doctor has seen him! This is unacceptable!

Observer checks: no inflaming phrases · the feeling named · the limit set calmly · safety chosen over finishing the conversation.

Homework: record the AR1 de-escalation.

Lesson 24 · C Perform · Handling a complaint
Goal Handle a complaint and write a factual summary.
New words (4) verbatim, chronological, factual account, follow-up action
Recycle grievance, patient relations, de-escalate
Language Neutral past narrative: At 14:10 Ms. X stated that… I apologized… I informed… at 14:25.
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded complaint conversation (C3) and a written 80-word factual summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: the AR1 de-escalation.
5–12 H 4 new words. Verbatim = in the person's exact words.
12–20 I Model the written summary (below).
20–50 F Spark: 60-Second Report on C3 to the charge nurse. Then the performance: handle C3 with the five steps (recorded), then write the 80-word summary in 10 minutes.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the summary. Two errors, then retry.

Complaint C3 (fictional): Mrs. Sevara Hamidova, daughter of Mrs. Dilnoza Ergasheva (room 15): her mother's upper dentures went missing during the transfer from the ED yesterday; My mother can't eat properly. She is upset and asks who will pay.

Model summary: At 14:10 on 11/07, Mrs. Hamidova, daughter of Mrs. Ergasheva (room 15), reported that her mother's upper dentures were missing after transfer from the ED on 11/06. She stated, "My mother can't eat properly." I apologized, searched the room and bedside locker (not found), and informed charge nurse Anna at 14:25. Patient relations was contacted at 14:40. She asked who would pay for new dentures. I told Mrs. Hamidova I would update her by 17:00.

Observer checks: chronological · a verbatim quote · no opinions or blame · follow-up action and time.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the C3 conversation, improved.

teacher.title: Interprofessional Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can give a concise update on rounds and make a tactful suggestion, read back orders and speak up about safety, and represent the nursing view in a care conference.

Written task: a 100-word action-point summary of care conference CC1.

Prepare: the rounds script; card RN1, orders TO1–TO3 and the CC1 role cards (students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 9); the unseen CUS scenario.

Lesson 25 · A Learn · Ward rounds
Goal Give a concise nursing update and make a tactful suggestion.
New words (10) rounds, multidisciplinary team, physiotherapist, dietitian, social worker, case manager, overnight events, plan of care, tactful, input
Recycle concise, attending physician, prioritize
Language Tactful suggestions: Would it be worth…? Could we consider…? I wonder whether… might help.
Spark Listen and Answer (a round)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: the C3 complaint summary. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words: who does what in the team.
24–32 I Spark: Listen and Answer; the teacher reads the round (below). Questions: What is the oxygen plan? What is the walking goal? Who leads discharge planning?
32–50 F Round 1: a 30-second nursing update on RN1 in rounds. Round 2: add a tactful suggestion. Round 3 (new detail): the physician disagrees; the student acknowledges, gives one reason, and escalates later if still concerned.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 tactful suggestions. Set homework.

Round script (teacher reads): Physician: Mrs. Yuldasheva, day 3 after admission with pneumonia. Overnight, temperature 37.6, saturations 95% on 1 liter. Plan: continue antibiotics and wean the oxygen. Physiotherapist: She walked 20 meters today; the goal is 40 tomorrow. Dietitian: She's eating about 30% of meals; we'll start supplements. Social worker: She lives alone, and her daughter is abroad, so we need to start discharge planning. Key: wean the oxygen; 40 m tomorrow; the social worker.

Card RN1 (fictional): Mr. Usmon Karimov, 77, day 2 after hip-fracture surgery. Confused 2–4 a.m. overnight and pulled at his IV; pain 4/10; eating 25%; passing urine; his daughter speaks only Uzbek. Model suggestions: Could we consider booking an interpreter for the family meeting? I wonder whether a review of his night-time confusion might help.

Observer checks: update under 30 seconds · overnight events first · suggestion tactful · disagreement handled respectfully.

Homework: record the RN1 update and 2 suggestions.

Lesson 26 · B Practice · Read-back and speaking up
Goal Read back orders exactly and voice a safety concern.
New words (9) verbal order, telephone order, CUS, two-challenge rule, speak up, safety culture, near miss, hierarchy, assertive
Recycle closed-loop communication, read-back, escalate
Language CUS: I'm Concerned… I'm Uncomfortable… This is a Safety issue. The two-challenge rule: say it at least twice.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Why is it hard to question a senior doctor? Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Nursing students never take verbal or telephone orders; they say: "I'm a nursing student, so I can't take orders. Let me get my nurse." Read-back is practiced here in the role of a licensed nurse, for later. Spark: Number Catch: 0.5 mg / 5 mg · 15 units / 50 units · every 6 hours · 3 L/min. Always say units in full.
16–30 I Model reading back TO1–TO3 (below).
30–50 F Round 1: in the role of a licensed nurse, the student reads back TO1–TO3 exactly. Round 2: first, the teacher, as a physician, phones the student with an order; the student declines within scope and fetches the nurse. Then, in the licensed-nurse role, the teacher gives an unclear order (Give him 10 of insulin); the student clarifies the unit and the route. Round 3 (unseen): the CUS scenario; the student speaks up twice.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one full CUS statement. Set homework.

Fictional orders and read-back (practiced in the role of a licensed nurse; students never take orders): TO1 – Give KALIXOR 20 milligrams IV once, now. · TO2 – Recheck blood glucose in 2 hours. · TO3 – Increase oxygen to 3 liters per minute via nasal cannula. Read-back: Let me read that back: Kalixor 20 milligrams IV, once, now. Recheck blood glucose in 2 hours. Increase oxygen to 3 liters per minute via nasal cannula. Is that correct?

CUS scenario (fictional): Akmal Rakhimov (room 4) and Akbar Rakhimov (room 6). A colleague is about to give room 4's medicine to the patient in room 6. Model: Excuse me, I'm concerned: this is Akbar Rakhimov, not Akmal. I'm uncomfortable going ahead. This is a safety issue: can we check the ID band together?

Observer checks: numbers and units exact · Is that correct? asked · concern raised calmly · repeated if ignored.

Homework: record the 3 read-backs and the CUS statement.

Lesson 27 · C Perform · Care conference
Goal Represent the nursing view and summarize agreed actions.
New words (4) agenda, consensus, compromise, action point
Recycle multidisciplinary team, tactful, plan of care
Language From a nursing perspective… Could we compromise by…? So, to summarize, we've agreed that…
Spark Mystery Patient (hidden team views)
Perform task Recorded care-conference contribution and summary; written 100-word action-point summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: the CUS scenario from memory.
5–12 H 4 new words. Model a summary of agreed actions.
12–20 I Spark: Mystery Patient; the student asks each "team member" (the teacher or classmates with role cards) for their view on CC1.
20–50 F Then the performance: a 10-minute care conference on CC1. The student gives the nursing view, suggests a compromise, and closes with a summary of action points. Recorded. Then 8 minutes to write the 100-word summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the summary. Two errors, then retry.

Care conference CC1, Mr. Karimov's discharge (role cards): Daughter (through an interpreter): wants him home with her now. Physiotherapist: he needs about 2 more weeks of rehabilitation. Social worker: a rehab bed is available on Monday. Patient (through an interpreter): wants to go home. Nursing view (the student): confused at night; needs supervision at night. A possible agreement: rehab for 2 weeks, then home with his daughter; a home-safety visit; an interpreter for every family meeting.

Observer checks: everyone's view heard · the nursing view clear · a compromise offered · action points with names.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the CC1 summary of agreed actions.

teacher.title: Clinical and Academic Writing
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can write a care-plan entry with a SMART goal, an objective incident report, and a structured 250-word reflection.

Written task: the 250-word reflection (Lesson 30).

Prepare: the care-plan template, patient card PI1, incident IR1, the flawed report and the Gibbs cycle sheet (all printed in the Student Edition, Cards and texts · Week 10).

A note on terms: a nursing diagnosis is a nursing-school writing format about the patient's response and needs. It is not a medical diagnosis.

Lesson 28 · A Learn · Nursing care plans
Goal Write a care-plan entry.
New words (10) nursing diagnosis, related to, as evidenced by, short-term goal, long-term goal, measurable, time-bound, nursing intervention, evaluation, NANDA-I
Recycle rationale, intervention, outcome
Language The formula: [Problem] related to [cause] as evidenced by [signs]. SMART goals: Patient will walk 40 m with a walker by day 3.
Spark Match and Speak (care-plan parts ↔ examples)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: the CC1 action points. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words. NANDA-I = the standard list of nursing diagnoses many US schools use. Risk for… diagnoses list risk factors and have no as evidenced by.
24–32 I Spark (6 min): Match and Speak (diagnosis, goal, intervention, rationale, evaluation ↔ examples). Read the model (below).
32–50 F Round 1: the student explains the model care plan aloud. Round 2: writes an entry for patient card PI1 (below): Impaired skin integrity related to… as evidenced by… Round 3: fixes vague goals: Patient will feel better → a SMART goal.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one SMART goal. Set homework.

Model care plan (Mr. Karimov, RN1): Nursing diagnosis: Risk for falls related to night-time confusion and recent hip surgery. Goal: Patient will remain free from falls during the hospital stay. Interventions: bed in the lowest position; call button within reach; hourly checks at night; the call button explained through an interpreter. Rationale: reduces the chance of unassisted getting up at night. Evaluation: no falls recorded at discharge.

Patient card PI1 (fictional): Mr. Rustam Aliev, 81, day 5 after a stroke · cannot turn himself in bed · eats about half of his meals · incontinent of urine · on assessment, a 3 × 2 cm area of red, broken skin over the sacrum (base of the spine) · pain 3/10 when turned. Model entry: Nursing diagnosis: Impaired skin integrity related to immobility and moisture as evidenced by a 3 × 2 cm area of broken skin over the sacrum. Goal: The wound will not increase in size, and no new pressure injuries will develop, by day 10. Interventions: reposition about every 2 hours; keep the skin clean and dry; check the skin over bones daily; report any change to the RN. Rationale: less pressure and moisture protect the skin. Evaluation: wound measured and documented on day 10.

Stretch: write a second goal for mobility. Support: the formula card.

Homework: write one complete care-plan entry for case CI3.

Lesson 29 · B Practice · Incident reports
Goal Write an objective, chronological incident report.
New words (9) incident report, occurrence, witness statement, contributing factor, harm, no-harm event, just culture, root cause, unwitnessed
Recycle near miss, chronological, factual account
Language Facts only, no blame or guessing. Patient was found on the floor beside the bed at 03:10 (not fell, if nobody saw it).
Spark Error Hunt (a flawed report)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: explain your CI3 care plan. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Just culture = reports are for learning, not punishment.
16–30 I Spark: Error Hunt on the flawed report (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student lists IR1's facts in order. Round 2: writes the report (12 minutes). Round 3: reads it aloud; the teacher, as manager, asks factual questions.
50–60 O Compare with the model. Two errors, then retry. Set homework.

Incident IR1 (fictional): 03:10, Mr. Karimov found on the floor beside his bed; bed rails down; call button out of reach. He said, I wanted to go to the toilet. A 2 cm skin tear on the left forearm. Vital signs within his usual range. Physician notified at 03:20. Daughter informed at 08:00 through an interpreter.

Flawed report: The patient fell because the night nurse forgot the bed rails. He was confused and silly to get up alone. He wasn't hurt badly. Key: blame on a colleague; a judgment (silly); fell is a guess, as nobody saw it; the injury is vague; no times.

Model report: At 03:10 on 11/07, Mr. Karimov was found on the floor beside his bed. The bed rails were down and the call button was out of reach. He stated, "I wanted to go to the toilet." A 2 cm skin tear was noted on the left forearm. Vital signs were within his usual range. The physician was notified at 03:20. His daughter was informed at 08:00 through an interpreter.

Observer checks: times for every event · found not fell · a verbatim quote · no blame or opinion.

Homework: rewrite the flawed report correctly.

Lesson 30 · C Perform · Reflective writing
Goal Write a 250-word reflection using the Gibbs cycle.
New words (4) Gibbs cycle, on reflection, in hindsight, learning point
Recycle debrief, self-care, contributing factor
Language At the time I felt… On reflection,… In hindsight, I would… This links to… Next time I will…
Spark Register Switch
Perform task Written 250-word reflection and a recorded 60-second oral version
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: What did you learn from the hardest role-play in this course?
5–12 H 4 new words. Gibbs: Description → Feelings → Evaluation → Analysis → Conclusion → Action plan.
12–20 I Spark: Register Switch: one event (complaint C3) told to a classmate in a debrief, in a reflection, in an incident report and in Uzbek to the daughter (model below). Read the model excerpt.
20–50 F The student chooses one course role-play (for example DN-B or C3), plans the 6 stages, then writes 250 words (20 minutes). Then the performance: a 60-second oral version, recorded.
50–60 O Mark the reflection for structure, honesty and an action plan. Set the weekly voice note.

Model excerpt: During a role-play, a patient's daughter complained that her mother's dentures had been lost. At the time I felt defensive, because it was not my fault. On reflection, my first sentence sounded like an excuse rather than an apology. In hindsight, I would have acknowledged her frustration before explaining anything. This links to the service-recovery steps we studied. Next time I will listen fully first and give a clear follow-up time.

Register Switch on C3 (model): to a classmate (debrief, no patient names): The daughter in my role-play was really upset about her mom's lost dentures, and I got defensive at first. · in a reflection: At the time I felt defensive; on reflection, I should have acknowledged her frustration first. · in an incident report: At 14:10 the patient's daughter reported that her mother's upper dentures were missing after transfer from the ED. · in Uzbek (to the daughter): Onangizning tish protezi yo‘qolgani uchun juda afsusdaman. Bu haqda katta hamshiraga xabar berdim va soat 17:00 gacha sizga javob beraman.

Observer checks: all 6 stages · honest feelings · one concrete action plan · 250 words, plus or minus 20.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the oral version of your reflection.

teacher.title: Medical Interpreting (Uzbek ↔ English)
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can explain and follow interpreter ethics, interpret long turns with notes, sight-translate a short form, and interpret a full doctor–patient encounter.

Why this week matters: this is the ShifoLife signature skill. Bilingual nurses are often asked to interpret. Doing it well protects patients; doing it badly puts them at risk.

Written task: a written Uzbek translation of leaflet LF2.

Prepare: the ethics situations and the Uzbek Bridge lines (students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 11); leaflet LF2; Hot Seat turns HS1–HS3, long turns LT1–LT2 and the sample LF2 translation (Lesson 32); encounter ENC1 and the flawed interpretation (unseen). The teacher must be a fluent Uzbek speaker for this week.

Lesson 31 · A Learn · The interpreter's role
Goal Explain and follow interpreter ethics.
New words (10) accuracy, completeness, impartiality, transparency, conflict of interest, consecutive interpreting, sight translation, positioning, intervention, ad hoc interpreter
Recycle confidentiality, first-person address, cultural broker
Language Transparency statements in the third person: The interpreter needs to ask for a repetition. The interpreter would like to clarify a term.
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Have you ever interpreted for family? What was hard? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words as rules: interpret everything, add nothing, take no side, keep it confidential, speak in the first person, step out of the role only with a transparency statement. Ad hoc interpreter = an untrained person (often family) used to interpret.
24–32 I Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
32–50 F Round 1: the student explains the rules to a nurse (the teacher). Round 2: ethics situations (below); the student responds as the interpreter. Round 3 (unseen): the patient whispers something to the interpreter only.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 transparency statements. Set homework.
